question: 2141. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will respond to the queries raised in correspondence (details supplied) and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59762/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2141, 2227, 2311 and 2312 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Last year, my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. These guidelines set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or has Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department's website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. In April 2025, 1,358 fair procedures letters were issued to applicants, affording them the opportunity to provide a submission or submit additional documentation in support of their Irish Association application. All submissions received have been reviewed and added to the relevant applications. I can advise the Deputy that, in devising and introducing the new guidelines, full policy and operational consideration was undertaken, including transitional arrangements. Under the provisions of Section 16 of the Act, the Minister is afforded absolute discretion. I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications and decisions based on Section 16 'Irish Association' received each year, during the past four years. This would require the manual examination of hundreds of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time to compile. Following the recent introduction of the new Section 16 'Irish Association' guidelines, arrangements to separately record such applications have been put in place. The total number of decisions issued on Irish Association applications since the introduction of the guidelines in April 2025 is 444, of which 300 were refusals and 144 were approvals.

question: 2142. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the progress that has been made regarding updating Prison Rules 2007 by 31 December 2025; when he plans to publish the updated rules; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59824/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration A review of the Prison Rules 2007 has been completed to take account of the European Prison Rules 2020. The review considered draft amendments arising from the European Prison Rules 2020, proposals identified within the Irish Prison Service and amendments arising from the stakeholder consultation. My Department and the Irish Prison Service are working closely together to progress the next phases of the work, including refining the policy proposals required to underpin the amendments to the Prison Rules. A further phase will also include engagement with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel in relation to the drafting of the necessary Statutory Instrument. The work is progressing and every effort is being made to advance the amendments as efficiently as possible. Given the scale and complexity of the review and the legislative drafting process involved, the timeline for completion and publication is subject to the outcome and progression of this work, including engagement with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel.

question: 2143. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the report on the external review of the chaplaincy service; if he has received the report; the timeline for when it will be published; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59835/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised that a 14-month review of the Chaplains Service was commissioned by the Irish Prison Service and conducted by the Jesuit Centre for Faith and Justice from January 2024 to March 2025. A copy of that review has now been issued to prison chaplains and to the Prisons Liaison of the Irish Episcopal Conference. I am further advised that the recommendations contained within the review will need to be fully considered and approved by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The implementation of any of those recommendations, once approved, would fall under the scope of the Head Chaplain.

question: 2144. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total allocation provided to An Garda Síochána for EU Presidency policing; the amount drawn down to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59656/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is also the Accounting Officer for An Garda Síochána under Section 72 of the Act, and is responsible for the Garda budget. As Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, I am committed to ensuring a successful and safe Irish Presidency and I am working closely with other Departments and State agencies in the planning and delivery of Ireland’s programme. The scale and significance of Presidency events planned to take place in Ireland, mean that unprecedented security considerations arise. The security arrangements being put in place will necessarily reflect the wider backdrop of a changed EU security landscape and a more complex threat environment. I am regularly briefed by the Garda Commissioner on the policing and security aspects of planning for and delivering a successful Presidency and I have engaged extensively with my colleague, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Deputy Jack Chambers TD, to ensure An Garda Síochána have what is needed to provide for the security needs for all events, and high-level visits hosted in Ireland during Ireland's Presidency. I secured €125 million in the Revised Estimates for 2026 for An Garda Síochána to cover the additional policing and security costs that are expected to arise. An Garda Síochána has been engaged in detailed planning of all aspects of the security and policing requirements for many months now. This work includes the operational and logistics planning, interagency engagement and continuous liaison with policing and security partners across the EU, and officials from my Department, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Office of Public Works.

question: 2150. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any means that biometric testing can be carried out in a location other than an Irish embassy or consulate (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59928/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2135, 2136, 2150 and 2151 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted leave to land and gain entry to the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. Immigration officials conduct passport checks, and run operations as required, to ensure passengers arriving in the State are properly documented in accordance with Section 11 of the Immigration Act 2004. A non-EEA national must be in possession of a valid passport or other equivalent document, issued by or on behalf of an authority recognised by the Government, which establishes his or her identity and nationality. There are no biometric requirements. For Irish visa purposes, biometric enrolment may be carried out outside an Irish Embassy or Consulate through designated Visa Application Centres, currently operated by VFS Global in certain countries, where fingerprints and facial images are captured on behalf of the Irish authorities. More information is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/biometrics/.

question: 2153. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide the number of participants in each initiative currently operated by or within the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, the Parole Board and the Garda Youth Diversion Programme which are designed to address violent behaviour, raise awareness of the impact of physical assaults on victims and families, promote non-violence and reduce reoffending from the most recent year for which figures are available, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59949/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2153 and 2216 together. This Government has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026. Following a significant increase of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding as part of Budget 2026, the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. Part 4 of the Children Act 2001 provides the statutory basis for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The intention of this programme is to divert children, aged 12-17 years old, who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the criminal justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Young people who are deemed suitable by the Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme are referred to local youth diversion projects, where, in collaboration with a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer, these projects provide supports to children to address their behaviour, engage in positive self-development, and connect with their communities. While there has been an approximate 25% increase in the population of 12-17 year olds over the past ten years, I am advised that the number or children coming to the attention of the Garda National Youth Diversion Bureau has remained steady, pointing to an actual reduction in youth offending. I am advised that between 2012 and 2022, there has been a drop in total criminal incidents involving children of 35% and a reduction of 31% in the number of children in detention over the past ten years. With the official opening of POINT YDP on 18th June 2026, youth diversion is available to all children and young people across the country. There are currently 92 youth diversion projects and 4 targeted youth diversion projects across the country that are funded by my Department. In 2025, these youth diversion projects and targeted youth diversion projects engaged with 4,786 young persons. Details of the projects and participant numbers are contained in Table 1. The locations of 2 specialist targeted YDPs are excluded in Table 1 for confidentiality, to protect the identity of the young people engaged in their services. The department, in collaboration with the Probation Service, also operates a number of initiatives distinctly designed to address serious and prolific youth offending for those who may be deemed unsuitable for diversion, these are: the Greentown Programme, the Bail Supervision Scheme and targeted interventions for children who are harder to reach in terms of addressing prolific and serious offending. The Department also funds specialised Youth Justice Workers and Programmes in youth diversion projects catering to Early Intervention, Family Support and Harder-to-Reach, serious and prolific young offenders. Within the Irish Prison Service, I am advised that measures to prevent and manage violence include early intervention, rehabilitation and multidisciplinary responses within individual prisons. The Irish Prison Service Psychology Service provides specialist, proactive interventions for people convicted of general and sexual violence, young people at increased risk of recidivism, people serving life sentences, and people convicted of violent offences who are serving sentences of more than two years. The Psychology Service provides primary and secondary care mental health interventions, alongside assessment and intervention for people presenting with neurodivergence, histories of trauma and personality difficulties. Irish Prison Service Healthcare and Merchants Quay Ireland also provide healthcare and addiction interventions, including opioid agonist treatment (OAT) and addiction counselling. The National Forensic Mental Health Service provides specialist psychiatric care to people in custody experiencing major mental illness. Collectively, these services address a range of factors that may contribute to the risk, occurrence or management of violent behaviour and support broader rehabilitation and efforts to reduce re-offending. I am advised that 2,786 individuals were referred in 2025 to the Irish Prison Service Psychology Service, across all interventions, of whom 1,619 were seen for intervention. The Alternatives to Violence Project (AVP) is a voluntary organisation comprising trained volunteers from within prisons and the wider community. Teams deliver workshops in Irish prisons aimed at helping participants build better relationships and develop ways of resolving conflict without resorting to violence. During 2025, I am advised that AVP delivered 43 full workshops across 11 prisons, accounting for 402 participations. A further 11 support sessions were delivered across 10 prisons, accounting for 93 participations and encompassing taster, debrief and refresher sessions. The Traveller Mediation Service (TMS) is a partnership initiative supported by Restorative Justice in the Community and funded by the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. It provides mediation and conflict-skills training within the community, including mediation between Travellers, and between Travellers, agencies and the Settled Community. I am advised that since establishment, the peer-mediation programme has worked with 412 people in custody, with 160 participants attending the programme in 2025. The National Violence Reduction Unit (NVRU), based in the Midlands Prison, accommodates some of the most complex and high-risk men in custody with significant histories of violence. It is a psychologically informed, co-led unit specifically designed to reduce and manage violence. The capacity of the unit is 9 and there are currently 9 prisoners accommodated on the unit. The Irish Prison Service also operates a number of other initiatives that contribute to violence prevention. The Community-Based Health and First Aid (CBHFA) programme, which has operated since 2009, uses trained peer volunteers to deliver health and wellbeing initiatives within prisons. In 2025, 272 CBHFA volunteers implemented 252 projects addressing areas including mental health, anti-bullying, violence prevention and health awareness. The Irish Prison Service has also established a Violence Management Steering Group in 2025. The Group aims to reduce violence in all its forms across the prison estate and to ensure that effective prevention and response mechanisms are in place. Given the breadth of these interventions, and the extent to which violence prevention and reduction are embedded within wider clinical, rehabilitative and multidisciplinary work, the IPS have advised that it is not possible to provide a single accurate figure representing the total number of people who engaged in work specifically directed towards all of the objectives referenced in the Deputy’s question. I am further advised that with regard to the Probation Service, work was undertaken with 17,686 people in the community. At every level of engagement, the focus on re-offending and the impact of crime on victims is paramount. In addition to this, Probation Service-funded Community Based Organisations work alongside the Service to provide a diverse range of services, addressing offending behaviour while supporting sustainable change and reintegration. These services and participant numbers are contained in the attached Table 2. question: 2154. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of short-stay visa applications submitted through the Moscow Visa Office that are currently being processed by the Dublin Visa Office; the number of decisions on these visa applications that have issued in 2026 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59960/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2154 and 2155 together. I can advise the Deputy that there are currently seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. They are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated sanction from my Department. I can confirm that the 37-day average processing time was for all Type C short stay visas, submitted by all nationalities, processed in Visa Offices and Irish Embassies globally. The tables below outline the figures requested by the Deputy. Table 1. Type C short stay visit visa applications from Russian nationals processed in the Moscow Visa Office and the Dublin Visa Office. ISD / Moscow Visa Office Visit Applications Received Visit Applications Granted Visit Applications Refused Average Processing Time 2025 2,212 1,628 9 42 days 2026* 01/01/26 - 31/07/2026 839 103 301 246 days * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. * All figures are calendar days and based on a 7-day week. There is no allowance made for weekends, public, bank or religious holidays in the various jurisdictions. * A decision made in a particular year may relate to an application received in a previous year. All visa applications which are submitted to the Moscow Visa Office are now sent to the Dublin Visa Office for processing. This change took place in late 2025. Processing times for all applications are influenced by a number of factors. The time it can take varies depending on the type and complexity of application; individual circumstances; peak application periods; such as holidays or the start of the school year; and, crucially, the quality and completeness of the application lodged. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system and the checks involved can take time to complete.

question: 2158. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expedite short-stay C visit visa applications (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60028/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the visa applications referred to have been refused. The reasons for these decisions were set out in the refusal letters sent to the applicants at that time. Appeals were received on 21 May 2026. All visa applicants are advised that the responsibility is on them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they feel is necessary. Guidelines in this regard are posted on our website. People that carefully follow these guidelines have an improved prospect of receiving a positive decision. It should be noted that visa appeals are dealt with in strict chronological order. Decisions will be issued to the applicants as soon as full consideration has been given by a Visa Appeals Officer. The people concerned can now directly check the status of their visa appeals on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. question: 2159. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any review of the allowances for Ukrainian citizens to qualify for housing supports while under temporary protective status; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60032/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2159 and 2160 together. My Department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. Under section 60 of the International Protection Act 2015, beneficiaries of Temporary Protection who are living independently and are not accommodated in State-provided accommodation are entitled to access social welfare supports on the same basis as Irish citizens. Beneficiaries may seek accommodation in the private rental sector through their own means and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement, which is a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Long-term housing supports, including the Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) and access to social housing, are matters for the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage. Ukrainian beneficiaries of Temporary Protection are not eligible for long-term housing supports, such as Housing Assistance Payment (HAP). The Government has approved a phased transition from State-funded accommodation for certain cohorts of beneficiaries of Temporary Protection, with information and supports being provided to assist affected individuals in securing alternative accommodation arrangements. Ongoing accommodation supports continue to be available for people whose particular circumstances make it difficult for them to move to independent accommodation. Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection may also seek hosted accommodation through their local authority or through the Irish Red Cross.

question: 2161. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider introducing attachment orders, or a similar mechanism, on social welfare payments for persons convicted of ten or more offences; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60064/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2161 and 2162 together. My Department understands that the Deputy's queries are related to the attachments of earnings relating to the payment of child maintenance. The Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders, completed by my officials, was published in 2024. The Review put forward 26 recommendations focused on generating maximum compliance with child maintenance orders, to ensure security and stability for children and to aid poverty prevention. The key recommendations include: • Development of a set of child maintenance guidelines. • Running an awareness campaign highlighting the importance of paying child maintenance and promoting a ‘culture of paying’. • Strengthening attachment of earnings orders, including by exploring the possibility of attaching an order to a PPS number rather than employing entities, so that orders do not lapse when there is a change in employer; permitting attachments on social welfare payments and benefits; as well as enabling the court to grant attachment of earnings orders automatically, without representation, if the paying parent defaults. • Introduction of a single enforcement procedure when the receiving parent makes an enforcement application, allowing the judge to choose the most appropriate enforcement option based on the circumstances of the case. This would enable the courts to ensure enforcement difficulties and patterns of non-compliance with court ordered maintenance orders are addressed by the court in the most timely and effective manner possible. • Simplification of the bench warrant process. • Placing the onus on paying parents to pay costs associated with enforcement proceedings. • Introduction of an information sharing agreement between Revenue, the Department of Social Protection and the Courts Service. • Allowing for deductions from social welfare, the paying parent’s bank accounts, from government grants and subsidies and allowing for the recovery of arrears from tax refunds. • Consolidating and simplifying maintenance legislation, which would be particularly beneficial for unrepresented litigants navigating maintenance proceedings. The Programme for Government commits to enhancing the enforcement mechanisms for child maintenance orders to ensure that children receive the financial support they need from both parents. In line with this commitment, the development of legislative amendments required to give effect to the Review’s recommendations is under way. On 19 January this year, I published Ireland’s first set of Child Maintenance Guidelines, along with the report on the public consultation. The published guidelines and accompanying report can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/. In line with another recommendation in the Review, my Department also undertook a social media campaign in October 2025, to reinforce the importance of paying child maintenance and complying with Child Maintenance orders.

question: 2163. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeframe for court reform, including but not limited to increasing the number of judges, and accelerating the establishment and operation of the family courts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60073/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Management of the courts and operational matters, including matters pertaining to the maintenance and use of court buildings, are the responsibility of the Courts Service which is independent in the exercise of these functions. The Courts Service is midway through a ten-year Modernisation Programme, designed around the needs of the court user, with clear, standardised services and accessible data to inform decisions. To ensure that our judiciary is resourced appropriately, 24 additional judges were appointed in 2023 on foot of the Judicial Planning Working Group report. On December 10 2025, the Courts and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2025 was signed into law by the President, and the relevant provisions to allow for the recruitment of additional judges were commenced on 30 January 2026. The Act provides for the increase in the number of judges in each Court jurisdiction by a further 21 posts and I intend to ask the Judicial Appointments Commission to commence the recruitment process for these additional judges in the coming months. As a result, the number of judges across all Irish courts now stands at 219, representing an increase of approximately 25% since 2023. The Family Courts Act 2024 is a key component of the Department's Family Justice Strategy and contains a number of provisions designed to make the family court process more focussed on the needs of children as well as user-friendly, safer and less costly. On 22 April 2026, I published the Implementation Plan for the Family Courts that sets out the timeline for implementation on a phased basis. Preparatory work is currently ongoing to establish the first family courts in early 2027. The Dublin Family Courts Complex will be delivered by way of Public Private Partnership; it is being procured by the NDFA in conjunction with the OPW, using the competitive dialogue procurement procedure pursuant to EU and national procurement law. The Complex is a flagship project within the overall programme of family justice reform and will directly support the implementation of the Family Courts Act, 2024. Subject to the successful completion of the procurement process in 2026, the current timescale indicates that construction is set to commence in 2027.

question: 2164. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will amend section 12 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 to provide that any vehicle suspected of having been used in the commission of a crime be automatically forfeited to the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60091/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Section 61 of the Criminal Justice Act 1994 provides a statutory power for the forfeiture of property, where the applicable statutory requirements are satisfied. Following conviction, the court may make a forfeiture order in respect of property which has been lawfully seized from the offender, or which was in the offender’s possession or under his or her control at the relevant time, where the court is satisfied that the property was used for the purpose of committing or facilitating the commission of an offence, or was intended by the offender to be so used. In considering whether to make such an order, the court is required to have regard to the value of the property and to the likely financial and other effects of the order on the offender. The legislation also affords a person claiming ownership of, or another interest in, the property an opportunity to show cause why a forfeiture order should not be made. I can assure the Deputy that relevant legislation is kept under review.

question: 2165. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider removing responsibility for the preparation and prosecution of District Court matters from members of An Garda Síochána, expanding the role and resources of the State prosecutions service to assume these functions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60102/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration While the Commission on the Future of Policing in Ireland (CoFPI) recommended that responsibility for the prosecution of offences should be removed from the Gardaí, the Government sought a further evaluation of its implications, including the impact on resources. That subsequent evaluation, which was undertaken by a ‘High-Level Review Group’ (HLRG), concluded that the CoFPI change was not appropriate and recommended, instead, the implementation of what they termed the “Reform Model”. Under the Reform Model, the HLRG recommended that An Garda Síochána retain responsibility for the conduct of prosecutions in court. The HLRG also recommended that the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) be supported in substantially enhancing quality assurance of the prosecution functions by An Garda Síochána in the name of the DPP. A Summary Prosecution Reform Steering Committee was then established, under the auspices of the Department of the Taoiseach, to drive forward the detailed design and implementation of the Reform Model and this work is continuing. The composition of the High-level Review Group is listed in the Report of the High Level Review Group on the Role of An Garda Síochána in the Public Prosecution System (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/report-of-the-high-level-review-group-on-the-role-of-an-garda-s%C3%ADoch%C3%A1na-in-the-public-prosecution-system/). As the Deputy will note, the Group comprised representatives from a wide range of interested parties bringing considerable experience and expertise to bear on the Group's deliberations.

question: 2166. Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of gardaí stationed in County Kildare, by station after the latest Garda allocations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60128/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2166 and 2174 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of all Garda personnel, including the allocation of newly attested Gardaí throughout the State. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Historical data on the allocation of Gardaí allocated to the Kildare/Carlow Division from 2006-2025, and probationer Gardaí from 2015-2025, along with the same data for 2026 can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/. Newly attested Gardaí are allocated to specially designated training stations which have the required training and development structures and resources in place, including trained Garda tutors and access to a permanently appointed supervisory Sergeant who is thoroughly familiar with their responsibilities under the training programme. I have been informed by the Garda authorities that in the latest attestation held on 24 July 2026 there were 19 probationer Gardaí allocated to the Kildare/Carlow Division, bringing the total number of probationer Gardaí allocated to the Division so far in 2026 to 41. As well as increasing the number of Gardaí in our communities, the allocation of newly attested Gardaí from Templemore facilitates serving Garda members to move on transfer to other Divisions across the country and into specialist units.

question: 2173. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the increased measures being taken to protect our borders from migration, especially through Northern Ireland; the level of checks carried out on individuals and families trying to enter the country; what happens when people arrive without passports or documentation; his position in relation to the number coming into Ireland in the context of capacity and pressure on services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60200/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2174. Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide updated staffing levels for Garda stations serving north Kildare, including Celbridge, Leixlip and Maynooth; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60130/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2166 and 2174 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of all Garda personnel, including the allocation of newly attested Gardaí throughout the State. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Historical data on the allocation of Gardaí allocated to the Kildare/Carlow Division from 2006-2025, and probationer Gardaí from 2015-2025, along with the same data for 2026 can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/. Newly attested Gardaí are allocated to specially designated training stations which have the required training and development structures and resources in place, including trained Garda tutors and access to a permanently appointed supervisory Sergeant who is thoroughly familiar with their responsibilities under the training programme. question: 2175. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on the adequacy of the provisions contained within section 23 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60214/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Tackling drug misuse is a whole-of-Government responsibility, and I regularly engage with the Minister for Health, the Minister of State with special responsibility for Public Health, Wellbeing and the National Drugs Strategy and the Garda Commissioner on matters relevant to the work of my Department in this area. The Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 (as amended) falls under the remit of the Minister for Health. This Act is an important legislative tool in our efforts to combat the sale and supply of illegal drugs in our communities. Section 23 of the Act provides a statutory power for a member of An Garda Síochána to search, without warrant, any person, vehicle, vessel or aircraft that the member has a reasonable suspicion that the person is in possession of a controlled substance so defined under the Act, or that such a substance is present in a vehicle, vessel or aircraft. The section also provides powers of detention and examination. Work is under way in my Department on the Garda (Powers) Bill, which will codify police search powers and procedural rights of suspects through rationalising and modernising those powers to take into account developments in modern technology to provide clarity and transparency. Sections 9, 10 and 11 of the Bill will provide for Garda powers of search, where there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a person is in possession of a relevant article, such as illegal drugs, and powers to search persons and vehicles for evidence of an offence where there are reasonable grounds to suspect that an offence has been, is being or is about to be committed. Sections 12 and 13 provide a clear right to be informed of the reason(s) for a search under Section 9 or 10, as well as an obligation on An Garda Síochána to record details of such a search. The Bill has already completed all stages in the Seanad and I hope to progress the Bill later this year through the Dáil.

question: 2179. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the evidence or analysis that informed the decision to introduce the revised citizenship residency requirement and family reunification provisions in the International Protection Act 2026; the assessment that was made of how these measures would support the integration of people granted international protection; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60459/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2179 and 2180 together. Migration plays an important role in Ireland's economic, social and community life. For those granted international protection, the ability to reunite with close family members can be a significant factor in supporting stability and integration. At the same time, family reunification policy must operate within the context of finite public resources. The State has a responsibility to manage migration in the interests of the country's economic and social wellbeing and to promote independence and self-sufficiency in support of positive integration outcomes. As the Deputy will be aware, Ireland has experienced unprecedented numbers of international protection applicants over the last few years. I introduced family reunification provisions in the International Protection Act 2026 that reflect these objectives and more closely align Ireland's approach with that of other EU Member States. The provisions have been carefully developed to ensure compliance with all relevant constitutional and European Convention on Human Rights obligations. Following the grant of international protection, sponsors will not be entitled to seek family reunification for a defined period of two years. I have also introduced a range of conditions relating to self-sufficiency, alongside a waiting period before any such application may be made. Recognising the challenges faced by those who have been granted international protection, a number of exemptions are provided in relation to the self-sufficiency criteria. The purpose of these exemptions is to allow for a short period of reliance on State supports where an applicant would otherwise be unable to provide for themselves without recourse to those supports. Furthermore, I propose to exempt minors from the income thresholds and to allow for the exercise of discretion in relation to all criteria when considering applications for family reunification from unaccompanied minors. Last November, Government approved the introduction of new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland's migration and asylum system and ensure that it is rules-based, efficient and more closely aligned with other EU Member States. One such policy change related to the residence requirements applying to a person granted refugee status who subsequently wishes to apply for Irish citizenship. This change came into effect on 8 December 2025. Previously, individuals granted international protection could apply for citizenship after a period of three years. Since 8 December 2025, refugees have generally been required to have five years of reckonable residence in the State in order to meet the eligibility criteria for citizenship. This policy change relates solely to the length of reckonable residence required following the grant of international protection. The extension of the reckonable residence requirement reinforces the principle that Irish citizenship reflects a sustained and meaningful connection with the State, demonstrated over time. This approach supports the Government's objective of achieving positive integration outcomes for both sponsors and their family members. In that context, my Department continues to invest in a range of integration measures, including community-led initiatives that promote the participation and inclusion of migrants and their families in Irish society.

question: 2181. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to urgently intervene and assist in a case (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60571/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally. My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. Section 26(1) sets out that: “ the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential ”. As I am sure you will appreciate, these confidentiality requirements are especially important for an asylum-seeker, whose claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and whose situation, or that of their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if the protection of their personal information is not ensured. An applicant for such protection status, or their legal representative, should contact either the International Protection Office (IPO) or the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) directly, as appropriate if they wish to receive an update on the status of their case. Contact information for The International Protection Office can be found at: https://ipo.irishimmigration.ie/contact-us/. Contact information for The International Protection Appeals Tribunal can be found at: www.protectionappeals.ie/contact-us/. Both the International Protection Office (IPO) and the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) are fully independent in deciding whether or not to grant international protection. Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. They are also bound by confidentiality provisions in respect of applicants as set out in the International Protection 2015 Act. Alongside this, should an international protection applicant have queries on the labour market access permission works, they can direct any queries in relation to Labour Market Access eligibility to the Labour Market Access Unit of this Department at Lmauqueries@justice.ie. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: • They are an international protection applicant; and • They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and • They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. Lastly, should an international protection applicant have any queries in relation to their state provided accommodation, they can contact the International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) at ipasinbox@justice.ie.

question: 2182. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status and occupancy of the rapid-build modular housing sites at Ballinure Way, Mahon, Cork city, and at Charleville, County Cork; the number of units at each site; the number currently occupied; and the number of residents accommodated at each site as of the most recent date available. [60594/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2182, 2183, 2184 and 2648 together. The rapid build programme has delivered 654 homes at 11 sites nationwide which are providing temporary accommodation for just over 2,600 people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Together, the two sites in Co Cork, referred to by the Deputy, comprise a total of 130 units designed for families of four, with 64 units at Ballinure Way in Mahon and 66 units at Charleville. These rapid build sites have a combined maximum occupancy of 520 people and there are currently no vacant units. A licence agreement is signed by each adult occupant allowing them to remain in their allocated unit while the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) is in force. Residents must adhere to the conditions of the agreement and fulfil satisfactory annual unit inspections undertaken by the Approved Housing Body, Tuath Housing, who manage all rapid builds across the 11 sites. At present, the licence agreements are dated to 4th March 2027. Now that the TPD has been extended to 4th March 2028, these licenses can be extended on expiry of the current license period. Contributions are payable at a rate of 16% of income plus a flat fee of €40 per household per week towards utility costs. The same contribution is payable at all rapid build sites and there has been no change in the contribution percentage or utility amount since the sites were initially occupied. These contributions are offset against the management costs of the sites. The rapid build sites fall outside of the scope of the commercial accommodation wind down and, subject to meeting license conditions, current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until the end of the TPD. Rapid build residents will be able to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process becomes available. In order to meet the conditions of the scheme, however, they must first surrender their unit and leave state-provided accommodation. This same requirement also applies to those in commercial accommodation.

question: 2185. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will approve visas for students from Gaza who have been granted scholarships to Irish universities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60604/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. Short Stay (C) Study Received 6 Long Stay (D) Study Received 134 Short Stay (C) Study Granted 5 Long Stay (D) Study Granted 41 Short Stay (C) Study Refused <5 Long Stay (D) Study Refused 108 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. * A decision made in 2026 may relate to an application received in a previous year. * It is the policy of my Department not to release numbers where there are fewer than 5 in respect of any nationality, as there is a possibility that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. * The Department does not collate information on the sponsorship details of applicants.

question: 2188. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures his Department is taking to address the use of fireworks in the leadup to Halloween 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60818/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am aware of the distress the use of illegal fireworks can cause around Halloween. The use of illegal fireworks is of serious concern in terms of anti-social behaviour and they pose a real risk to the health and safety children, teenagers and older or more vulnerable people. They also cause distress to family pets, service dogs and other animals. All pyrotechnics in Europe, including fireworks, fall under the EU Pyrotechnic Directive 2013/29/EU. Under Article 4, Member States are permitted to restrict the availability of hazardous fireworks to the general public. In Ireland, the only fireworks available to the general public are Category F1 fireworks which present a 'very low hazard' and negligible noise level. Only professional pyrotechnic operators are permitted to use more hazardous Category F2, F3 and F4 fireworks for public displays at festivals and weddings, following the successful conclusion of a risk assessment and consultation with relevant local authorities including the Fire Service and An Garda Síochána. Anyone importing or selling fireworks of any kind must have a licence, and licences are only issued for hazardous fireworks if they are to be used in organised displays conducted by professional and competent operators. The penalties for importing, selling or using unlicensed fireworks are significant. The Criminal Justice Act 2006, specifically Part 6, grants members of An Garda Síochána the power to arrest individuals found with unlicensed fireworks and impose significant penalties, including fines up to €10,000 or up to five years' imprisonment for possession with intent to sell or supply, or for igniting them. These penalties, which can also apply to those convicted or throwing an ignited firework at a person or property, demonstrate the seriousness attached to breaches of the legislation governing the importation and use of fireworks. My Department runs an annual Fireworks Awareness Raising Campaign that informs the public about the serious dangers associated with fireworks and the penalties that people can face for selling or using illegal fireworks. An Garda Síochána, through Operation Tombola, runs a nationwide policing plan focused on the prevention and detection of the sale of fireworks and associated public order and anti-social behaviour issues during the Halloween period. Operation Tombola combats the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, through intelligence-led operations, visits to local car boot sales, searches and seizures of fireworks, as well as focusing on preventing associated public disorder and anti-social behaviour through the incremental deployment of resources. Since 2016, An Garda Síochána have carried out 1,883 fireworks seizures, with a value of €347,516. These seizures have undoubtedly contributed to reducing harm associated with the illegal use of fireworks. A key component of Operation Tombola is active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each Garda division, and gardaí collaborate closely with these stakeholders to ensure a unified approach to preventing anti-social behaviour during the Halloween period. In addition, very good work is undertaken by local authorities and community groups to organise safe fun events for children and young people in our communities around Halloween and these often include firework displays by professional pyrotechnic operators.

question: 2194. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the recommendation in the first annual report of the Special Rapporteur on Racial Equality and Racism for an urgent update to incitement to hatred legislation is under consideration by his Department, given the removal of the incitement to violence or hatred provisions from the legislation enacted as the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60944/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Any discrimination or criminal action taken against a person because of their race, religion, gender or sexual orientation is unacceptable and will not be tolerated. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 was commenced at the end of 2024 and placed specific hate offence provisions in Irish law for the first time, in line with EU obligations. This provided for increased prison sentences for certain offences, where proven to be motivated by hatred, or where hatred is demonstrated, based on personal identity characteristics like race, colour, nationality, religion, national or ethnic origin, descent, disability, gender, sex characteristics or sexual orientation. Ireland has had incitement to hatred legislation in place for 37 years, which remains in force. It is an offence under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 to incite hatred based on a person’s race, colour, nationality, religion, ethnic or national origins, membership of the travelling community or sexual orientation. The protections against incitement to hatred are in line with Ireland’s constitutional obligation and democratic tradition of protecting freedom of speech. This means that people are free to express opinions that we may find deeply offensive as long as there is no intention to incite others to hatred or what is done or said is not likely to incite hatred. This is an important protection for democratic processes, where it is essential that opinions can be freely expressed. However, whenever anyone incites hatred against a person or any group of persons on the basis of a personal characteristic such as their gender or religion, that is an offence.

question: 2195. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department, or any body under its aegis, has assessed the evidence base for the effectiveness of unconscious bias training prior to any endorsement of the recommendation for mandatory, continuous unconscious bias training across all public sector staff; if his Department is aware of the decision taken in 2020 to phase out such training across the United Kingdom civil service on the basis of a commissioned evidence review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60949/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Recommended Public and Civil Service-wide training is developed and delivered through OneLearning, in partnership with the Institute of Public Administration (IPA). OneLearning delivers a range of training programmes for public and civil servants and supports the ongoing development of capability across the Civil Service. The Department is aware of the decision taken by the UK Civil Service in 2020 to discontinue mandatory standalone unconscious bias training following a review of the available evidence. However, the Department does not provide standalone mandatory unconscious bias training. Instead, unconscious bias is addressed within the wider context of intercultural awareness and inclusive workplace practices. While the Department provides a suite of Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (ED&I) training programmes, including mandatory programmes such as Equality and Human Rights in the Public Service and Intercultural Awareness – Building Competence for Inclusive Workplaces, the Department recognises that sustainable behavioural change is achieved through a combination of leadership, organisational culture, practical workplace measures and skills development. The Intercultural Awareness programme is informed by research and practical approaches to developing intercultural competence and fostering inclusive workplaces. It equips staff with the knowledge, skills and tools required to work effectively in increasingly diverse environments and to contribute to a culture of respect, inclusion and belonging across the organisation. Strengthening intercultural competence across the organisation supports the delivery of responsive, inclusive and accessible services for all. With regard to the agencies under the remit of my Department, I am informed that, similarly, they do not provide standalone mandatory unconscious bias training. Instead, unconscious bias is addressed within the wider context of intercultural awareness and inclusive workplace practices. As the Deputy will be aware, under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána, including Garda training matters. I am informed by their HR Directorate that unconscious bias training is undertaken. It has not yet been assessed.

question: 2212. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if supports are available for a victim of domestic violence seeking a divorce who is above the income threshold for legal aid but can not afford divorce proceedings. [61163/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2126, 2212, 2509 and 2524 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. A range of civil legal issues are covered by the scheme, including domestic violence applications, which are prioritised by the Board. While contributions from those legally aided are an aspect of the scheme, the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 2017 provide that no contribution is payable for those who are applying solely for orders under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. In particular, the majority report recommends increasing the disposable income threshold from €18,000 to €23,500. Having the Civil Legal Aid Scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. However, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. A critical aspect will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Officials in my Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process. Potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy will be taken into account. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis is underway, with officials in my Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 2216. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide details of any programmes, education initiatives, behavioural interventions or awareness campaigns currently operated by or within the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, the Parole Board and the Garda Youth Diversion Programme which are designed to address violent behaviour, raise awareness of the impact of physical assaults on victims and families, promote non-violence and reduce reoffending; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59946/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2153 and 2216 together. This Government has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026. Following a significant increase of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding as part of Budget 2026, the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. Part 4 of the Children Act 2001 provides the statutory basis for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The intention of this programme is to divert children, aged 12-17 years old, who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the criminal justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Young people who are deemed suitable by the Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme are referred to local youth diversion projects, where, in collaboration with a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer, these projects provide supports to children to address their behaviour, engage in positive self-development, and connect with their communities. While there has been an approximate 25% increase in the population of 12-17 year olds over the past ten years, I am advised that the number or children coming to the attention of the Garda National Youth Diversion Bureau has remained steady, pointing to an actual reduction in youth offending. I am advised that between 2012 and 2022, there has been a drop in total criminal incidents involving children of 35% and a reduction of 31% in the number of children in detention over the past ten years. With the official opening of POINT YDP on 18th June 2026, youth diversion is available to all children and young people across the country. There are currently 92 youth diversion projects and 4 targeted youth diversion projects across the country that are funded by my Department. In 2025, these youth diversion projects and targeted youth diversion projects engaged with 4,786 young persons. Details of the projects and participant numbers are contained in Table 1. The locations of 2 specialist targeted YDPs are excluded in Table 1 for confidentiality, to protect the identity of the young people engaged in their services. The department, in collaboration with the Probation Service, also operates a number of initiatives distinctly designed to address serious and prolific youth offending for those who may be deemed unsuitable for diversion, these are: the Greentown Programme, the Bail Supervision Scheme and targeted interventions for children who are harder to reach in terms of addressing prolific and serious offending. The Department also funds specialised Youth Justice Workers and Programmes in youth diversion projects catering to Early Intervention, Family Support and Harder-to-Reach, serious and prolific young offenders. Within the Irish Prison Service, I am advised that measures to prevent and manage violence include early intervention, rehabilitation and multidisciplinary responses within individual prisons. The Irish Prison Service Psychology Service provides specialist, proactive interventions for people convicted of general and sexual violence, young people at increased risk of recidivism, people serving life sentences, and people convicted of violent offences who are serving sentences of more than two years. The Psychology Service provides primary and secondary care mental health interventions, alongside assessment and intervention for people presenting with neurodivergence, histories of trauma and personality difficulties. Irish Prison Service Healthcare and Merchants Quay Ireland also provide healthcare and addiction interventions, including opioid agonist treatment (OAT) and addiction counselling. The National Forensic Mental Health Service provides specialist psychiatric care to people in custody experiencing major mental illness. Collectively, these services address a range of factors that may contribute to the risk, occurrence or management of violent behaviour and support broader rehabilitation and efforts to reduce re-offending. I am advised that 2,786 individuals were referred in 2025 to the Irish Prison Service Psychology Service, across all interventions, of whom 1,619 were seen for intervention. The Alternatives to Violence Project (AVP) is a voluntary organisation comprising trained volunteers from within prisons and the wider community. Teams deliver workshops in Irish prisons aimed at helping participants build better relationships and develop ways of resolving conflict without resorting to violence. During 2025, I am advised that AVP delivered 43 full workshops across 11 prisons, accounting for 402 participations. A further 11 support sessions were delivered across 10 prisons, accounting for 93 participations and encompassing taster, debrief and refresher sessions. The Traveller Mediation Service (TMS) is a partnership initiative supported by Restorative Justice in the Community and funded by the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. It provides mediation and conflict-skills training within the community, including mediation between Travellers, and between Travellers, agencies and the Settled Community. I am advised that since establishment, the peer-mediation programme has worked with 412 people in custody, with 160 participants attending the programme in 2025. The National Violence Reduction Unit (NVRU), based in the Midlands Prison, accommodates some of the most complex and high-risk men in custody with significant histories of violence. It is a psychologically informed, co-led unit specifically designed to reduce and manage violence. The capacity of the unit is 9 and there are currently 9 prisoners accommodated on the unit. The Irish Prison Service also operates a number of other initiatives that contribute to violence prevention. The Community-Based Health and First Aid (CBHFA) programme, which has operated since 2009, uses trained peer volunteers to deliver health and wellbeing initiatives within prisons. In 2025, 272 CBHFA volunteers implemented 252 projects addressing areas including mental health, anti-bullying, violence prevention and health awareness. The Irish Prison Service has also established a Violence Management Steering Group in 2025. The Group aims to reduce violence in all its forms across the prison estate and to ensure that effective prevention and response mechanisms are in place. Given the breadth of these interventions, and the extent to which violence prevention and reduction are embedded within wider clinical, rehabilitative and multidisciplinary work, the IPS have advised that it is not possible to provide a single accurate figure representing the total number of people who engaged in work specifically directed towards all of the objectives referenced in the Deputy’s question. I am further advised that with regard to the Probation Service, work was undertaken with 17,686 people in the community. At every level of engagement, the focus on re-offending and the impact of crime on victims is paramount. In addition to this, Probation Service-funded Community Based Organisations work alongside the Service to provide a diverse range of services, addressing offending behaviour while supporting sustainable change and reintegration. question: 2217. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider legislative amendments to ensure that deliberate misrepresentation of qualifications, insurance, accreditation or business identity by contractors can be better prosecuted as fraud rather than treated solely as a civil matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61227/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The deliberate misrepresentation of qualifications, insurance, accreditation, or business identity is not solely a civil matter under Irish law. Where an individual dishonestly makes false representations with the intention of securing business, making a financial gain, or causing a loss to another, such conduct may, depending on the circumstances, be addressed under existing criminal fraud legislation. Under Sections 6 and 7 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, it is an offence to dishonestly induce a person by deception to do or refrain from doing an act, with the intention of making a gain or causing a loss to another, or to dishonestly obtain services by deception with the intention of making a gain or causing a loss to another. On conviction on indictment, a person guilty of an offence under Section 6 or 7 is liable to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both. Where the conduct involves the making or use of a false instrument, offences of forgery and using a false instrument under Sections 25 and 26 of the Act may also be applicable. A person guilty of an offence under Section 25 or 26 is liable, on conviction on indictment, to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, or both. It should also be noted that should a report be submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), that office is responsible for deciding whether a person should be prosecuted and, if so, for which offence. The DPP is wholly independent of my role as Minister and the Department of Justice under the Prosecution of Offences Act 1974 (as amended). I have no role in the operations, functions, oversight or governance of the Office of the DPP and cannot provide any information relating to the decisions made by that Office.
