question: 2221. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to address the issues raised correspondence (details supplied); the supports available to make the transition into private accommodation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61252/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2221 and 2223 together. Following the Government decision in May of this year, my department is progressing the next phase of withdrawal of state-supported commercial accommodation for people benefitting from Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland before March 2024. This is being progressed on a phased basis over the coming months and people who are residents in state-supported Ukraine accommodation will be given a notice period on changes to their accommodation. My department recognises that there will be people who, for various reasons may require continued accommodation which may be in an alternative setting. An application process has opened to people in these centres who can demonstrate that they continue to require temporary accommodation post-commercial accommodation wind-down. The self-declaration application process is open from August 4th – September 11th 2026 online. Successful applications will be offered accommodation in a designated accommodation centre. Anyone not availing of continued accommodation will be required to vacate the centres by the agreed date. People with Temporary Protection continue to have access to public services in accordance with the Temporary Protection Directive and Irish law, including access to healthcare and, where eligible, social protection supports such as rent supplement administered by the relevant Departments. Integration supports are provided by a number of stakeholders and supports will be further mobilised and coordinated to harness inputs and support the integration of people with Temporary Protection and to assist them in moving to independent living. Local Authorities coordinate the supports of wider agencies through their Community Integration Forums. Supports are provided by: • The HSE on health • Department of Social Protection on PPSN and Social Welfare supports • Intreo on employment supports and jobs advice • Department of Education, ETBs and Regional Education and Language Teams (REALTs) for schooling, youth services and English Language supports. Further supports are also provided by the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). A blended model of online and in-person engagement are being delivered by the IRC and IOM to inform people of policy changes and give guidance on options available to people. For more information on these supports please visit www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/state-contracted-commercial-accommodation-en/. People with Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own private arrangements for accommodation through their own means, using supports provided by the Department of Social Protection, or by asking their Local Authority or Irish Red Cross for alternative accommodation offered by hosts. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation in any given area should contact the Local Authority in that area or the Irish Red Cross. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted by email at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or by phoning 1800 753 343. I have also obtained Government approval to develop an alternative permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland, which will be granted for a period of up to two years, renewable for periods of two years thereafter. This permission is known as the Temporary Protections Transition Scheme. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year as person with Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the application process. Applicants who are self-employed must provide satisfactory evidence such as revenue records that they were, and continue to be, self-employed for 6 months prior to the opening of the Scheme. There is no time requirement on how long an applicant is living independently from state supported accommodation prior to applying. However, an applicant must provide evidence of independent accommodation at the time of application. Further information is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. This webpage will be updated over the next few weeks to include details of the application process. It is also important to note that the alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Persons who cannot meet the requirements of the scheme remain entitled to and benefit from the Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. For the avoidance of doubt, the eligibility requirements for the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme do not apply to those remaining under Temporary Protection. While Temporary Protection is currently in place until March 2027, an extension until March 2028 has recently been agreed by the Council of the European Union. Those granted Temporary Protection in Ireland will remain entitled to this protection and associated rights to include employment and education while the Directive is in effect.

question: 2222. Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration regarding the family reunification visa system whether he acknowledges the concerns of healthcare assistants who work full-time, pay tax, and serve the needs of Irish society but who are refused reunification visas as their income is deemed insufficient under the terms of the scheme; whether he accepts the view that Ireland accepts healthcare labour as essential, but the immigration system often treats family reunification as unaffordable; and his plans to examine the fairness of the thresholds. [60049/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2223. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to respond to issues raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61164/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2221 and 2223 together. Following the Government decision in May of this year, my department is progressing the next phase of withdrawal of state-supported commercial accommodation for people benefitting from Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland before March 2024. This is being progressed on a phased basis over the coming months and people who are residents in state-supported Ukraine accommodation will be given a notice period on changes to their accommodation. My department recognises that there will be people who, for various reasons may require continued accommodation which may be in an alternative setting. An application process has opened to people in these centres who can demonstrate that they continue to require temporary accommodation post-commercial accommodation wind-down. The self-declaration application process is open from August 4th – September 11th 2026 online. Successful applications will be offered accommodation in a designated accommodation centre. Anyone not availing of continued accommodation will be required to vacate the centres by the agreed date. People with Temporary Protection continue to have access to public services in accordance with the Temporary Protection Directive and Irish law, including access to healthcare and, where eligible, social protection supports such as rent supplement administered by the relevant Departments. Integration supports are provided by a number of stakeholders and supports will be further mobilised and coordinated to harness inputs and support the integration of people with Temporary Protection and to assist them in moving to independent living. Local Authorities coordinate the supports of wider agencies through their Community Integration Forums. Supports are provided by: • The HSE on health • Department of Social Protection on PPSN and Social Welfare supports • Intreo on employment supports and jobs advice • Department of Education, ETBs and Regional Education and Language Teams (REALTs) for schooling, youth services and English Language supports. Further supports are also provided by the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). A blended model of online and in-person engagement are being delivered by the IRC and IOM to inform people of policy changes and give guidance on options available to people. For more information on these supports please visit www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/state-contracted-commercial-accommodation-en/. People with Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own private arrangements for accommodation through their own means, using supports provided by the Department of Social Protection, or by asking their Local Authority or Irish Red Cross for alternative accommodation offered by hosts. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation in any given area should contact the Local Authority in that area or the Irish Red Cross. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted by email at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or by phoning 1800 753 343. I have also obtained Government approval to develop an alternative permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland, which will be granted for a period of up to two years, renewable for periods of two years thereafter. This permission is known as the Temporary Protections Transition Scheme. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year as person with Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the application process. Applicants who are self-employed must provide satisfactory evidence such as revenue records that they were, and continue to be, self-employed for 6 months prior to the opening of the Scheme. There is no time requirement on how long an applicant is living independently from state supported accommodation prior to applying. However, an applicant must provide evidence of independent accommodation at the time of application. Further information is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. This webpage will be updated over the next few weeks to include details of the application process. It is also important to note that the alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Persons who cannot meet the requirements of the scheme remain entitled to and benefit from the Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. For the avoidance of doubt, the eligibility requirements for the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme do not apply to those remaining under Temporary Protection. While Temporary Protection is currently in place until March 2027, an extension until March 2028 has recently been agreed by the Council of the European Union. Those granted Temporary Protection in Ireland will remain entitled to this protection and associated rights to include employment and education while the Directive is in effect.

question: 2225. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the strategies he has in place to address the growing problem of shoplifting; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61280/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2225 and 2306 together. I take any risk to retailers, retail staff and communities very seriously and I am acutely aware of the personal and economic impact that retail crime is having on businesses, retail workers and communities. I recognise that shoplifting and organised retail crime pose a significant threat to the economic welfare of Irish retailers and that retail theft is not a victimless crime. The Government is taking a number of strategic, tactical and integrated measures to address retail crime. The Programme for Government makes several commitments in relation to retail crime. Together with the ongoing roll-out of high visibility policing by An Garda Síochána, further measures are also under consideration. These include: • Improving data sharing between retailers and Gardaí to support enforcement; • Expanding the use of community sanctions for retail crime; and • Updating the Public Order Acts to allow prolific offenders to be excluded from retail premises for a certain period of time. My Department is in the process of drafting a Retail Crime Strategy and work is well advanced. I expect to receive a draft copy of this strategy in the coming weeks for my consideration. The Government intends to publish the Strategy within the next few months. An Garda Síochána commenced a dedicated operation in 2023, ‘Operation Táirge’, to tackle organised retail crime. Under ‘Táirge’, Gardaí nationwide use an intelligence-led approach to identify criminals engaging in retail crime. The approach is to disrupt the most prolific groups using organised crime legislation and proceeds of crime legislation and to work with retailers to strengthen their security and prevent them becoming victims of this criminality. It should also be noted that my Departments work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions, probation supervision schemes and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment and increasing high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Additionally, An Garda Síochána is currently developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy for 2026-2029. On a tactical level, getting more Gardaí on our streets is my first priority. The overall Garda workforce has increased from 15,980 in 2016 to over 18,500 in 2026. With three recruitment competitions to join An Garda Síochána in the last 18 months, there is a strong pipeline of recruits regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College. More Gardaí proactively patrolling in our cities, towns and rural areas as well as more Garda staff will help to maintain law and order and make everyone feel safer.

question: 2227. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will report on operation of naturalisation via Irish association; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60460/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2141, 2227, 2311 and 2312 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Last year, my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. These guidelines set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or has Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department's website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. In April 2025, 1,358 fair procedures letters were issued to applicants, affording them the opportunity to provide a submission or submit additional documentation in support of their Irish Association application. All submissions received have been reviewed and added to the relevant applications. I can advise the Deputy that, in devising and introducing the new guidelines, full policy and operational consideration was undertaken, including transitional arrangements. Under the provisions of Section 16 of the Act, the Minister is afforded absolute discretion. I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications and decisions based on Section 16 'Irish Association' received each year, during the past four years. This would require the manual examination of hundreds of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time to compile. Following the recent introduction of the new Section 16 'Irish Association' guidelines, arrangements to separately record such applications have been put in place. The total number of decisions issued on Irish Association applications since the introduction of the guidelines in April 2025 is 444, of which 300 were refusals and 144 were approvals.

question: 2228. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued at a static speed camera (details supplied) from 1 July 2026 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60107/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, the use of technology is a vital component of reducing speeding on our roads. The aim of road safety cameras across Ireland is to encourage safer driving practices, reduce collisions and protect road users by promoting compliance with speed limits. Nine static speed safety cameras are in operation across the country since 2024. The locations of these cameras were selected based on fatal and serious injury collision data and speed data, as well as feedback from stakeholders. I am informed by Garda Authorities that there has been 4,569 Fixed Charge Penalty Notices (FCPN) issued for speeding for the month of July 2026 for this camera. All information contained in this report is based upon operational data from the FCPS system as was available on 14 August 2026 and is liable to change.

question: 2229. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left, State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number who left Ireland, including the number who returned to Ukraine, where this information is available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61305/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2229, 2230, 2231, 2232, 2233, 2234, 2235, 2240 and 2365 together. My department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My department has no role in private accommodation arrangements and cannot assist with long-term housing matters. Those granted Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own accommodation arrangements through their own means, with the support of schemes and services provided by other bodies where appropriate. People may seek private rented accommodation independently and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Further information on Rent Supplement is available through local Intreo Centres and Department of Social Protection offices. Alternatively, people with Temporary Protection may seek hosted accommodation through their Local Authority or through the Irish Red Cross. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation should contact their Local Authority or the Irish Red Cross directly. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or on 1800 753 343. Information on the Offer a Home scheme is available at www.offerahome.ie. Once a person with Temporary Protection leaves State-provided accommodation, my department does not have a role in, or visibility of, their subsequent private accommodation arrangements. Accordingly, my department cannot track whether an individual has returned to Ukraine, secured accommodation through private means, or accessed accommodation supports through other agencies. Further information regarding accommodation supports and policy updates is available at gov.ie under the Ukraine Updates portal.

question: 2236. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in light of the Government's decision that the accommodation recognition payment, ARP, scheme will end on 31 March 2027 and the phased withdrawal of State-contracted accommodation for beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine, the protections, accommodation supports and transition arrangements the Government intends to put in place for beneficiaries of temporary protection who remain dependent on ARP-supported accommodation when the scheme ends. [61320/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2236, 2238 and 2242 together. The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced in July 2022 to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to people arriving in Ireland from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive. It is intended that the ARP will end on 31 March 2027. From 1 September 2026, the ARP monthly contribution rate will be reduced from €600 per month to €400 per month per eligible property. As the payment is made monthly in arrears, the first payment at the reduced rate will be made in October 2026. S.I. No. 368 of 2026 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/si/368/made/en/pdf) gives effect to this change. The planned reduction in the contribution rate is expected to reduce the numbers participating in the scheme. However, as the scheme is demand-led, it is not possible to produce a robust estimate of the numbers expected to remain in the scheme. The previous reduction from €800 per month to €600 per month in June 2025 did not have a significant impact on numbers engaged in the scheme. The number of active claims continued to increase in the months following the reduction until December 2025 when it plateaued. However, participation in the scheme is currently trending downward. The impact of the reduction will be monitored. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, I would like a situation whereby people will have the ability to continue to share their homes with beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine. Other measures are in place in this regard, including the rent a room scheme. Hosts and beneficiaries of temporary protection will hopefully make agreements to continue their private arrangements that will enable this valuable source of accommodation to be retained beyond the termination of the scheme. In recognition of the valuable contribution many people who have come from Ukraine since the outbreak of the war have made, Ireland is introducing an alternative permission to live and work here. This alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation.

question: 2237. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if an application for a certificate of naturalisation (details supplied) will be examined; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60134/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application cited was returned to the person concerned on 10 September 2025 as it was incomplete. I am informed that further documentation was requested from the person concerned and this documentation was not provided. It is open to the person cited to make a new application at any time. To maintain the integrity of the file on record, Citizenship Division do not return documentation submitted. However, should applicants wish to lodge a new application, they may request all relevant documents previously submitted to be associated with the new application. My Department has recently launched a new webpage to help people better understand the naturalisation application process, including the key documents required for identity and residency. The page also provides guidance on how to have documents certified. Your constituent can view it at: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2238. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has undertaken an assessment of the number of individuals and families who are currently accommodated through ARP who may be unable to secure alternative accommodation without State assistance. [61322/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2236, 2238 and 2242 together. The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced in July 2022 to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to people arriving in Ireland from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive. It is intended that the ARP will end on 31 March 2027. From 1 September 2026, the ARP monthly contribution rate will be reduced from €600 per month to €400 per month per eligible property. As the payment is made monthly in arrears, the first payment at the reduced rate will be made in October 2026. S.I. No. 368 of 2026 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/si/368/made/en/pdf) gives effect to this change. The planned reduction in the contribution rate is expected to reduce the numbers participating in the scheme. However, as the scheme is demand-led, it is not possible to produce a robust estimate of the numbers expected to remain in the scheme. The previous reduction from €800 per month to €600 per month in June 2025 did not have a significant impact on numbers engaged in the scheme. The number of active claims continued to increase in the months following the reduction until December 2025 when it plateaued. However, participation in the scheme is currently trending downward. The impact of the reduction will be monitored. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, I would like a situation whereby people will have the ability to continue to share their homes with beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine. Other measures are in place in this regard, including the rent a room scheme. Hosts and beneficiaries of temporary protection will hopefully make agreements to continue their private arrangements that will enable this valuable source of accommodation to be retained beyond the termination of the scheme. In recognition of the valuable contribution many people who have come from Ukraine since the outbreak of the war have made, Ireland is introducing an alternative permission to live and work here. This alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation.

question: 2239. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number who moved into accommodation supported by the accommodation recognition payment, ARP; to provide a breakdown of the above figures by year, county and household type, where available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61300/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I cannot provide the information sought by the Deputy in respect of the number of temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine who left State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022 and have moved into accommodation supported by the Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP). This information is not collated by this Department. Hosting arrangements are a private matter between the host and the temporary protection beneficiaries living in the accommodation. The arrangements can be terminated at any stage by either party. I can provide a breakdown of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who are in accommodation supported by the Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP), however we have no information on where they resided previously. (Please see attached spreadsheet). No of BoTPs per year per county

question: 2240. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number who moved into private rented accommodation; the number receiving rent supplement or other housing related State support; to provide a breakdown of the above figures by year, county and household type and financial support category where available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61299/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2229, 2230, 2231, 2232, 2233, 2234, 2235, 2240 and 2365 together. My department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My department has no role in private accommodation arrangements and cannot assist with long-term housing matters. Those granted Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own accommodation arrangements through their own means, with the support of schemes and services provided by other bodies where appropriate. People may seek private rented accommodation independently and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Further information on Rent Supplement is available through local Intreo Centres and Department of Social Protection offices. Alternatively, people with Temporary Protection may seek hosted accommodation through their Local Authority or through the Irish Red Cross. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation should contact their Local Authority or the Irish Red Cross directly. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or on 1800 753 343. Information on the Offer a Home scheme is available at www.offerahome.ie. Once a person with Temporary Protection leaves State-provided accommodation, my department does not have a role in, or visibility of, their subsequent private accommodation arrangements. Accordingly, my department cannot track whether an individual has returned to Ukraine, secured accommodation through private means, or accessed accommodation supports through other agencies. Further information regarding accommodation supports and policy updates is available at gov.ie under the Ukraine Updates portal.

question: 2241. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applicants from Palestine for student visas for the 2026/2027 academic year; the number that were granted; the number refused; the primary reasons for refusal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61119/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. question: 2243. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether discussions have taken place with local authorities, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Department of Social Protection, and relevant housing and homelessness services regarding the potential consequences of the withdrawal of the accommodation recognition payment, ARP; if he will publish a detailed transition plan setting out the accommodation and support pathway available to each category of beneficiary currently dependent on ARP before the scheme terminates; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61328/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Since the outbreak of the conflict in Ukraine on 24 February 2022, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration continues to work as part of the whole-of-Government response with a focus on meeting the immediate needs of those fleeing the conflict. A number of Government decisions and actions that I have taken on the gradual phasing out of accommodation supports have involved discussion with other Departments and Local Authorities as referenced by the Deputy. These include: The monthly contribution rate per property was reduced from €800 to €600 from 1 June 2025. (S.I. No. 228 of 2025 www.irishstatutebook.ie/2025/en/si/0228.html). This reduction aimed to ensure that temporary and timebound supports for temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine are proportionate and equitable. From 10 November 2025 Ireland’s accommodation offering to newly arriving people fleeing the war in Ukraine was reduced to a maximum of 30 days. They will be provided with food, laundry, other services and integration supports in Designated Accommodation Centres. From the 1 January 2026, I made regulations to limit the period that retrospective claims for the ARP scheme can be made to six months from the date of application. S.I. No. 672 of 2025 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2025/si/672/made/en/print?q=21&years=2025) gives effect to this change. This intended to support more effective administration of the scheme and compliance matters. Under Part 3 of the Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/3/enacted/en/) from 3 March 2026, new applications for properties that have been registered with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) at any time since March 2022 no longer meet the ARP scheme’s eligibility criteria. Tenants in rental properties are no longer eligible to make new applications for the scheme. In March 2026, following approval of both Houses of the Oireachtas, I made a regulation [ S.I. No. 120 of 2026 ] (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/si/120/made/en/print)to set the ARP scheme termination date to 31 March 2027. Following the Government decision of May 2026 concerning the coordinated approach to transition from Temporary Protection, i made regulations in S.I. No. 368 of 2026 to confirm a reduction of the monthly ARP contribution rate from €600 to €400 from September 2026. The Government continues to support Ukraine in its long-term recovery. This will include a new alternative permission to live and work here, under the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme, for those who wish to remain in Ireland. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, hosts can continue to have private arrangements with Ukrainians if they so wish. Measures such as the rent a room scheme are also available. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation.

question: 2244. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the proposed voluntary return and rei-ntegration programme for Ukrainian beneficiaries of Temporary Protection; the amount of funding his Department has requested or provided for this programme as part of the 2027 Estimates process; whether any funding has been specifically identified or ring-fenced for the programme; the proportion of the estimated cost expected to be met from Exchequer funding and the proportion expected to be met from EU funding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61331/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2245. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of a naturalisation application by a person (details supplied), that has been pending since 2022 and has reportedly reached final processing; when the applicant can expect a final decision; the estimated date for completion, given the exceptional length of time the application has remained outstanding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60979/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation applications referred to by the Deputy continue to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2246. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of farm theft incidents in each county in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60218/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2246 and 2248 together. This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. Rural crime covers a range of issues, ranging from burglary and theft, to animal crime and road traffic offences. An Garda Síochána are committed to tackling all these forms of crime. The Rural Safety Plan 2025-2027 brings together and strengthens all of the various strands of work being carried out in relation to rural safety. It has been developed by my Department, in conjunction with the National Rural Safety Forum. The Plan's vision is to ensure people and communities in rural Ireland feel safe and are safe in their homes, places of work and their local environments. It does this by identifying four key priority areas that we will focus on to achieve this goal. These areas are Community Safety and Engagement, Property Crime, Roads Policing, and Animal and Wildlife Crime. A number of Garda operations support these objectives, including Operation Thor, which provides an intelligence-led response to burglary and related offences. Gardaí also conduct high-visibility patrols and checkpoints in identified hotspot locations, gather intelligence on known offenders, and regularly engage with rural communities on crime prevention measures. Local Garda Crime Prevention Officers also provide practical advice to farmers, businesses and householders on securing property and reducing opportunities for theft. I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that there is no specific incident type or crime classification of "farm theft" and therefore no corresponding definition. An Garda Síochána compiled figures using a combination of incident types, object categories and location information to provide an indication of theft-related incidents affecting farms. Specifically, the figures include incidents involving the theft of livestock, poultry, farming equipment or vehicles from locations such as farmland, fields, yards and outhouses/sheds, as well as incidents where the term "farm" was identified in the incident narrative. question: 2247. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, in light of the particular circumstances of elderly beneficiaries of temporary protection, TP, who remain dependent on State-supported accommodation and who have limited or no capacity to supplement their income through employment, he will seek a review of the categories exempted from the revised weekly payment of €38.80, with a view to including persons of pensionable age; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60901/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2247 and 2249 together. The BOTP weekly payment was introduced, following consultation with the Minister for Social Protection, for residents in Full Board Designated Accommodation Centres (DACs) in September 2024. Residents in Full Board DACs have all costs related to food and utilities covered by the State and the rate reflects that. This change was made to bring equivalence, as far as possible, between Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection who had arrived in Ireland before and after the introduction of the Timebound Accommodation Policy on 14 March 2024. The payment is subject to an income test and the rate is €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child, with an additional supplement of €70 per adult and €35 per child weekly to defray the cost of the mandatory contribution towards food in serviced accommodation. Following Government Decision in May 2026, a phased wind-down of state contracted commercial accommodation has commenced. My Department recognises that some residents will require ongoing accommodation support. Where a person feels they cannot source independent accommodation, they can apply to the Department for ongoing accommodation. Such applications require information on a person’s circumstances and supporting evidence. It is important to note that all State contracted commercial accommodation will cease in the coming months. Therefore, the window for applications applies to everyone currently in State accommodation who has a need for ongoing accommodation. Where a person’s application is successful, ongoing accommodation support will be provided in DACs and residents will be entitled to the BOTP weekly payment. These benefits are being maintained for successful applicants, including elderly people. No further review of these rates is being carried out at this time. More information regarding ongoing accommodation support can be found at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/ongoing-supports-en/. Persons who leave state accommodation may apply for standard social welfare payments on the same basis as Irish Citizens.

question: 2250. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the current responsibilities of his Department in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection, TP, in Ireland; the responsibilities which now rest with other Departments in relation to their accommodation, income supports, housing and integration; and if he will provide clarity as to the lead Department responsible for the overall co-ordination of Government policy concerning beneficiaries of temporary protection. [60897/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2250, 2253 and 2254 together. My Department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My Department also registers arrivals at points of entry and provides Temporary Protection Certificates. Under the Local Integration Model, my Department funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including those with Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in 2025. Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Other Departments and Agencies are also involved in the whole-of-Government response to this crisis: The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage and local authorities provide assistance to people with Temporary Protection in sourcing hosted accommodation. The Department of Health has responsibility for policy relating to the healthcare needs of people fleeing the conflict. The Department of Social Protection has responsibility for the provision of access to social welfare benefits and income supports. The Government has approved the phased withdrawal of State-funded accommodation for people from Ukraine who arrived before March 2024 and who have been in receipt of State accommodation on an ongoing basis. Ireland's State-funded accommodation model for people fleeing Ukraine has been more extensive than that available in many other EU Member States. There are currently over 13,000 people in non-time bound State-contracted commercial accommodation who will be affected by the accommodation wind-down. An application process for people currently residing in State-contracted commercial accommodation who require ongoing State accommodation support and who meet specified criteria opened on 4 August 2026 and will remain open until 11 September 2026. Individuals seeking continued State-supported accommodation are required to self-declare their need for support and provide appropriate documentary evidence in support of their circumstances. As the application process remains open, data on the number of applicants seeking ongoing State accommodation will not be available until the application period has closed and all applications have been assessed and processed. Accordingly, the number of people with Temporary Protection who will remain eligible for State-supported accommodation on grounds such as age, disability or other vulnerability criteria is not yet available. My Department will remain in contract with a number of accommodation centres to accommodate those who are eligible for ongoing accommodation support. The changes are being introduced on a phased basis to allow residents who are impacted time to access the information and supports available to them. My Department is not currently procuring any further new accommodation centres for use as Designated Accommodation Centres. Based on current assessments of accommodation demand, my Department is satisfied that sufficient accommodation capacity is available at present and will continue to keep requirements under review as applications are processed. People with Temporary Protection who are no longer eligible for State-supported accommodation may apply for housing and income supports, subject to the statutory eligibility criteria applying to those schemes. Responsibility for the administration of these supports and any guidance relating to their operation rests with the relevant Department. My Department will continue to work closely with all relevant Government Departments to ensure a coordinated approach to supporting beneficiaries of Temporary Protection in Ireland.

question: 2251. Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when applications for tourism or visit a family and-or friend received in Dublin on 2 June 2026 may be completed. [60893/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2251 and 2252 together. I can assure the Deputy that, while processing times vary across Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visa applications are processed within the published target timeframes. The average processing time for all Type C short-stay visas in 2025 was 37 days. My Department's website recommends that visa applications be submitted three months before the intended date of travel. While applications may be submitted earlier than this, applicants are advised to ensure that all supporting documentation is as up to date as possible. Applicants may also use my Department's Customer Service Portal to upload updated documentation after an application has been submitted. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. In 2025, approximately 206,000 visa applications of all types were received by the Visa Division of my Department. This represented an increase of 2% compared with 2024, with more than 3,900 additional applications received. This followed a 21% increase in applications in 2024 compared with 2023. During the first six months of 2026, the Visa Division received approximately 102,000 visa applications and issued approximately 85,200 decisions. Processing times are influenced by a range of factors, including the type and complexity of the application, the individual circumstances of the applicant, peak application periods such as holiday seasons or the beginning of the academic year, and, importantly, the quality and completeness of the application submitted. Verification of application details is a critical component of the immigration system, and the necessary checks can take time to complete. Information on current processing times for visa applications being processed in Dublin is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/. The website currently indicates that tourism and visit family/friend visa applications received by the Dublin Visa Office on 11 August 2025 are being processed. It should be noted that the date published on the website represents the oldest application currently under consideration within a particular category. Visa officers continue to process and decide applications received after the published processing date. Where an individual application requires additional examination and takes longer to finalise, the published processing date may remain unchanged for a period. This should not be interpreted as indicating that processing of applications within that category has ceased. Unfortunately, it is not possible to provide a definitive date for the finalisation of any individual application. Applications are generally processed in chronological order based on their date of receipt. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This enables applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency.

question: 2253. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of beneficiaries of TP currently accommodated by the State who, following the introduction of the revised accommodation arrangements, are expected to remain eligible for State-supported accommodation on grounds such as age, disability or other vulnerability; the projected capacity required to accommodate this cohort; whether sufficient designated accommodation capacity is currently available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60891/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2250, 2253 and 2254 together. My Department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My Department also registers arrivals at points of entry and provides Temporary Protection Certificates. Under the Local Integration Model, my Department funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including those with Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in 2025. Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Other Departments and Agencies are also involved in the whole-of-Government response to this crisis: The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage and local authorities provide assistance to people with Temporary Protection in sourcing hosted accommodation. The Department of Health has responsibility for policy relating to the healthcare needs of people fleeing the conflict. The Department of Social Protection has responsibility for the provision of access to social welfare benefits and income supports. The Government has approved the phased withdrawal of State-funded accommodation for people from Ukraine who arrived before March 2024 and who have been in receipt of State accommodation on an ongoing basis. Ireland's State-funded accommodation model for people fleeing Ukraine has been more extensive than that available in many other EU Member States. There are currently over 13,000 people in non-time bound State-contracted commercial accommodation who will be affected by the accommodation wind-down. An application process for people currently residing in State-contracted commercial accommodation who require ongoing State accommodation support and who meet specified criteria opened on 4 August 2026 and will remain open until 11 September 2026. Individuals seeking continued State-supported accommodation are required to self-declare their need for support and provide appropriate documentary evidence in support of their circumstances. As the application process remains open, data on the number of applicants seeking ongoing State accommodation will not be available until the application period has closed and all applications have been assessed and processed. Accordingly, the number of people with Temporary Protection who will remain eligible for State-supported accommodation on grounds such as age, disability or other vulnerability criteria is not yet available. My Department will remain in contract with a number of accommodation centres to accommodate those who are eligible for ongoing accommodation support. The changes are being introduced on a phased basis to allow residents who are impacted time to access the information and supports available to them. My Department is not currently procuring any further new accommodation centres for use as Designated Accommodation Centres. Based on current assessments of accommodation demand, my Department is satisfied that sufficient accommodation capacity is available at present and will continue to keep requirements under review as applications are processed. People with Temporary Protection who are no longer eligible for State-supported accommodation may apply for housing and income supports, subject to the statutory eligibility criteria applying to those schemes. Responsibility for the administration of these supports and any guidance relating to their operation rests with the relevant Department. My Department will continue to work closely with all relevant Government Departments to ensure a coordinated approach to supporting beneficiaries of Temporary Protection in Ireland.

question: 2255. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 2204 of 28 July 2026, the number of FCNs that were paid, broken down by month, from the total of 8,374 issued for non-compliant number plates; the number that were unpaid resulting in a summons being issued; and the number that were convicted in court. [60843/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Further to my reply to Parliamentary Question No. 2204 of 28 July 2026, I am informed by the Garda authorities that 8,404 Fixed Charge Notices (FCNs) were issued for non-compliant vehicle registration plates from October 2025 to June 2026. The updated figure reflects the fact that FCN data may be subject to change as notices are processed. A monthly breakdown is set out below: Month FCNs issued June 2026 863 May 2026 886 April 2026 706 March 2026 841 Feb 2026 889 Jan 2026 912 Dec 2025 939 Nov 2025 1451 Oct 2025 917 Total 8,404 I am further informed that 7,313 of these FCNs were paid. A monthly breakdown is set out below: Month FCNs paid June 2026 733 May 2026 744 April 2026 613 March 2026 727 February 2026 780 January 2026 797 December 2025 826 November 2025 1,276 October 2025 817 Total 7,313 The following table provides a monthly breakdown of the number of these FCNs which resulted in a summons being issued, were sent to court, or where the summons process was initiated: Month Summons/Court June 2026 69 May 2026 102 April 2026 72 March 2026 86 Feb 2026 91 Jan 2026 93 Dec 2025 86 Nov 2025 153 Oct 2025 84 Total 836 I am further informed that 11 summonses were created over the same period for possession of an unregistered vehicle. This offence does not proceed by way of Fixed Charge Notice. The figures relate to incidents which occurred between 1 October 2025 and 30 June 2026, inclusive. question: 2256. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total amounts paid by his Department to private insurance companies for insurance for each year from 2016 to 2025 and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61355/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Department’s activities are indemnified under the General Indemnity Scheme (GIS) in respect of any claims for personal injury and/or third-party property damage. This is essentially a form of State 'self-insurance' rather than policy-based insurance. This negates the need for the Department to purchase personal injury or third-party property cover.

question: 2257. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of emails received through the dedicated helpdesk at ipasinbox@justice.ie from persons applying for international protection regarding concerns in relation to their accommodation in each year from 2020 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60815/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The safety and well-being of all residents and staff in our accommodation centres is a priority for the Department and IPAS. IPAS is always available to deal with any complaints from residents and residents are encouraged to engage with IPAS if they are unhappy with any aspect of their accommodation. Each resident has access to details of the IPAS complaints procedure, and how residents can submit complaints about issues and problems in their accommodation. Complaints are handled sensitively and in confidence. Residents can make complaints verbally or in writing to the centre manager. If residents are not satisfied with how a centre has dealt with a complaint, they can submit a formal written complaint to IPAS. Residents can also submit written complaints directly to IPAS if they prefer. If a resident is not comfortable contacting centre management or the Department directly, the Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) operate a confidential support helpline for all residents being accommodated by IPAS. If a resident is not satisfied with the outcome of a complaint submitted to IPAS, a complaint can be submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman or the Office of the Ombudsman for Children. The following number of emails were received by the IPAS Helpdesk from residents regarding concerns in relation to their accommodation in each year since 2020. To note, the number of IPAS residents in IPAS accommodation has grown from 7,000 in 2020 to 33,000 in 2026. Year Emails 2020 213 2021 244 2022 564 2023 889 2024 1,668 2025 1,703 2026 YTD 1,172 These issues are raised with centre management and most can be resolved locally or with IPAS support. Residents are also offered the opportunity to proceed with a formal written complaint. The IPAS customer services team conduct clinics at IPAS accommodation centres and individual residents may raise a query or complaint directly with IPAS at any time by email through a dedicated contact centre, and may also seek support from external advocates as needed. All IPAS Accommodation Centres, whether state-owned or contracted emergency accommodation, are subject to oversight arrangements through the Department's Centre Management and Compliance Team, and inspected either by HIQA, department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the Department. HIQA reports are available online here: www.hiqa.ie/reports-and-publications/inspection-reports. Reports of IPAS inspections are available online here: www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/publications/ipas-inspection-reports/.

[60813/26]

The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. The Garda authorities have provided the following table detailing the number of Garda vehicles carrying Pride or Diversity themed livery from 2019 to date in 2026. Year Number of Vehicles 2019 2 2020 1 2021 1 2022 1 2023 1 2024 1 2025 1 2026 1 An Garda Síochána advise that in June 2019 two Garda patrol cars were marked with the Pride “rainbow” colours to mark the occasion of uniform Gardaí participating in the Dublin Pride Parade for the first time.
