question: 2261. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the organisations, persons and stakeholders that have been consulted to date with respect to the formulation and drafting of the national Migration and Integration Strategy due to be published in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60792/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands and the opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy later this year. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level. The ten Departments represented on the SMPG are: • Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Chair) • Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment • Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science • Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage • Department of Finance • Department of Social Protection • Department of an Taoiseach • Department of Health • Department of Education and Youth • Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht Each Department is in a position to convey the perspectives of the agencies under their remit which have also provided inputs to the Group as required. The SMPG and its working group has now met on 14 occasions for detailed discussions on different aspects of the Strategy. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs. With specific regard to integration, work previously undertaken, including a detailed consultation process with stakeholders, will be taken into account in the development of this strategy. The first phase of consultation consisted of a public survey, stakeholder submissions, and stakeholder workshops to gather insights into the needs, challenges, and opportunities for supporting migrant integration. Further engagement will take place as the strategy is developed.

question: 2262. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether passport control checks at ports of entry automatically identify individuals who are subject to Irish entry bans, exclusion orders, deportation orders or other immigration restrictions; the systems used to facilitate such checks; the number of alerts generated in each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60778/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2262, 2504 and 2526 together. The Border Management Unit (BMU) is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. Immigration officers are responsible for carrying out border management functions in order to protect the integrity of the State's immigration system and ensure compliance with immigration law. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, neither I nor my Department can comment on specific operational procedures of the BMU or the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB). However, I can assure the Deputy that all persons arriving at ports of entry are examined, and their travel documentation verified, using a range of border management and security systems. This includes checks against relevant national and international databases to assist in confirming identity, detecting fraudulent documentation, and identifying people who may be the subject of immigration, law enforcement, or security alerts. In relation to the sharing of biometric data with the UK, I can advise the Deputy that, at the UK-Ireland Summit in March, it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data-sharing arrangements, particularly to prevent abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits.

question: 2263. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a contract (details supplied) for IPAS accommodation will be renewed; if there has been engagement with the property owners in terms of its future use; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60768/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Providing reception conditions, including accommodation and other basic supports, to international protection applicants is a requirement of Irish and EU law. There are currently 298 IPAS Accommodation Centres located around the country, with over 32,000 residents.? The Department has a contract in place to provide accommodation seeking international protection at this location, which is due to expire in March 2027. This location was previously used to provide accommodation to people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Details of individual contractual processes are treated as confidential and commercially sensitive while they are ongoing. With respect to potential for contract renewals, the provision of accommodation for international protection applicants is demand-led, which remains high, and each premises is considered on a case-by-case basis to decide if the contract will be renewed as it approaches its end date. At potential renewal stage, consideration will be given to the current and projected demand for accommodation, the provider's performance under contract, and compliance with standards and legal obligations.

question: 2264. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to report on progress to meet his commitments under the National Human Rights Strategy for disabled people; the measures taken since the strategy was introduced; the key metrics identified to measure progress; and if he will make a statement on the matter [60743/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits Government Departments and public bodies to lead by example in creating meaningful employment opportunities for disabled people. Since the introduction of the Strategy, my Department has implemented a range of measures designed to advance the inclusion, participation and progression of disabled people. Details of my Department's progress under the commitments of the Strategy relevant to the Department's work are outlined below. Commitment 4: Civil & Public Sector Under Commitment 4, the Government has committed to maximising opportunities and access for disabled people to obtain meaningful work in the civil and public sector, enhancing disability inclusion policies and practices, supporting career progression, and providing clear pathways to permanent employment for participants in work placement programmes who perform well. Strengthening Workplace Supports My Department has appointed a full-time Disability Liaison Officer (DLO) who acts as a central point of contact for staff and managers on disability and accessibility matters. The DLO provides guidance to employees and managers and coordinates reasonable accommodations to support disabled staff in carrying out their roles effectively. My Department has also committed to implementing the forthcoming cross-Civil Service Reasonable Accommodation Policy once finalised by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. This will further strengthen and standardise workplace supports available to disabled employees. Establishment of a Disability Staff Network In 2025, my Department established a Disability Staff Network to support disabled employees across the organisation. The network: • Promotes peer support and connection among disabled staff; • Provides a structured forum for engagement and feedback; • Supports the development of a more inclusive workplace culture; and • Assists the Department in identifying opportunities for continuous improvement in disability inclusion. This measure directly supports the Strategy's objective of strengthening workplace inclusion and employee engagement. Inclusive Recruitment and Assignment Practices My Department continues to ensure that recruitment and onboarding processes are accessible and inclusive. Measures include: • Offering reasonable accommodations at all stages of recruitment and selection; • Providing accommodations throughout onboarding and induction; • Early engagement by the Disability Liaison Officer with successful candidates who require supports; and • Assigning staff, where possible, to roles that maximise opportunities for success, development and career progression. These arrangements are intended to reduce barriers to entry and support long-term retention and advancement. Supporting Pathways to Employment My Department continues its participation in the Willing Able Mentoring (WAM) Programme, a national initiative that provides work experience opportunities for disabled graduates and supports progression to employment. Since 2016, my Department has hosted WAM placements and has continued this commitment following publication of the Strategy. I am informed my Department currently employs two former WAM graduates at Executive Officer level, demonstrating progress in creating routes from placement programmes to permanent employment. This directly contributes to the strategic objective of providing clear pathways to sustainable employment for disabled people. Workforce Representation Percentage of staff who identify as disabled • 2025 Disability Census result: 15% • Public sector statutory target: 6% My Department's disability representation rate significantly exceeds the statutory target and provides strong evidence of success in attracting and retaining disabled employees. While the National Human Rights Strategy provides that detailed Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) will be set out in subsequent Programme Plans of Action, several measurable indicators are already being used or can be identified to track progress in the Department. The Strategy states that Programme Plans will specify delivery actions, timelines and relevant KPIs for each commitment. My Department has identified the following metrics as indicators of progress: Recruitment and Accessibility Metrics Indicators include: • Number of applicants requesting reasonable accommodations; • Number of accommodations provided during recruitment and onboarding; • Number of disabled candidates recruited; • Employee retention rates among disabled staff; and • Participation rates in disability inclusion initiatives. Career Progression Metrics Indicators include: • Promotions achieved by disabled staff; • Representation of disabled employees at different grades; and • Employee engagement through the Disability Staff Network. Employment Pathway Metrics Indicators include: • Number of WAM placements offered annually; • Number of WAM participants progressing to employment; • Number of former WAM participants retained in the Department; and • Conversion of placement opportunities into permanent roles. Assessment of Progress Against Commitment 4 The measures introduced by the Department demonstrate substantial progress towards the objectives of commitment 4. Achievements include: • Dedicated disability leadership through the appointment of a full-time DLO; • Enhanced workplace supports and accommodation processes; • Creation of a Disability Staff Network; • Inclusive recruitment and onboarding practices; • Continued participation in the WAM programme and support for pathways to employment; and • Exceeding the statutory public sector disability employment target, with 15% of staff identifying as disabled. Collectively, these actions show that my Department is progressing the Strategy's commitment to lead by example within the civil and public service and is working to ensure that disabled people can access, participate in and progress within employment on an equal basis with others. Commitment 13: Criminal Justice System The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits to ensuring that disabled people can access justice on an equal basis with others, that they do not unnecessarily enter the criminal justice system, and that disabled people in custody can access appropriate services and supports. Since the introduction of the Strategy, my Department has been progressing actions under Commitment 13. Criminal Justice Pathways In circumstances where a specific need has been identified and ongoing treatment is required on release, I am advised that the Irish Prison Service and in-reach services will take all reasonable steps to ensure that the necessary links are made with community services prior to release. The Irish Prison Service and Health Service Executive continue to engage in relation to improved care pathways from prison to community across all areas of clinical need, including disability through various fora including ‘Sharing the Vision’ and the ‘High-Level Taskforce on Mental Health and Addiction Challenges of persons interacting with the Criminal Justice System. Registered Intermediaries My Department supported the establishment of the Registered Intermediaries Scheme through a pilot programme, which concluded earlier this year. As part of the pilot, the Department funded several cohorts of eligible applicants (registered Speech and Language Therapists, Occupational Therapist or Social Workers) to undertake a Professional Diploma in Intermediary Studies at the University of Limerick in successive academic years from 2022 to 2026. A review of the pilot programme is currently underway to assess its operation and effectiveness and to inform the future development of the Scheme, including consideration of measures to increase awareness of its availability.

question: 2265. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the anticipated impact of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact on Ireland's border control, immigration screening and security procedures; the preparations being undertaken for its implementation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60638/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Pact is designed to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for the standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for applicants who have previously applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. In addition, under the International Protection Act 2026, people who apply for international protection are subject to initial security and identity checks and will be registered on the Eurodac system. The Eurodac Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1358) expands the data collection requirements to individuals aged six and over. It broadens data collection beyond fingerprints to include facial images and travel documents. Those seeking to claim asylum attend a designated Screening Centre at Citywest, where they lodge an application for international protection. During the screening process, applicants undergo further security, identity, health and vulnerability checks. The Screening Centre has staff from asylum processing, appeals, returns, reception, the HSE, the Department of Social Protection, legal representatives and other agencies co-located on site to engage with applicants. The new system has been in place since 12 June and is operating as intended. My Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact.

question: 2266. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland's current position in relation to European Union initiatives on migration management, border security and protection of the EU's external borders; the specific measures Ireland is advocating at EU level to reduce undocumented migration; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60635/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland has shown its commitment to a common EU-wide solution to migration through opting in to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the measures of the Pact which Ireland has opted into, and provides for appropriate alignment with the Schengen measures of the Pact. The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in the EU. Harmonisation in the area of returns is equally important and it is the Government’s preference that Ireland would participate in the Returns Regulation. Additionally, the Deputy may wish to know that the Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands and the opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy in the coming months. The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision including housing, amongst other issues relating to migration. As of the 1 July of this year, Ireland took over the Presidency of the Council of the European Union and for six months from that date, we will be driving an ambitious programme of work to advance the interests of the Union. Under the Justice and Home Affairs Council, which I Chair, one of the three overarching priorities for our Presidency is advancing a fair, firm, rules-based approach to migration, asylum and returns. Central to this is of course the effective implementation of the Pact, as well as preparing for the implementation of the recently agreed returns measure. I will also focus on the external dimensions of migration, including through partnerships with third countries and using the tools at our disposal to improve the rate of return and readmission of those with no right to remain in the Union. The Irish Presidency will also prioritise advancing actions that support Member States to secure our borders, fight serious and organised crime and respond to new and emerging threats.

question: 2267. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the resources and supports provided to local authorities and communities affected by the accommodation and processing of persons admitted to the State through international protection and immigration procedures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60630/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department runs a number of funding schemes to support communities and enable migrant integration in Ireland. In 2025, the Integration Fund was established combining the former International Protection Integration Fund (IPIF) and Communities Integration Fund (CIF). The results of the 2025 Integration Fund were announced in November 2025, with 117 projects receiving a total of €3.6 million in funding. Separately, the National Integration Fund (NIF), a multi-annual funding programme open to organisations operating at regional and national level. The results of the NIF 2023 call were announced in April 2024, with 18 projects awarded grants totalling more than €2.8 million over a three-year period. Building on these initiatives, the 2026 Integration Fund now includes a new multi-annual funding stream that replaces the NIF. The 2026 fund closed to applicants on 2 September 2026, with €4.5 million made available, and the results will be announced later this year. My Department also manages two EU funding schemes aimed at migrant integration. Firstly, my Department is the managing authority for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF). AMIF provides a range of supports for International Protection applicants, programme refugees, individuals granted Temporary Protection and other third country nationals arriving in Ireland. Since 2023, two open calls for proposals were published for projects suitable for funding under the AMIF 2021-2027 national programme. Arising from these two Open Call for Proposals, €11.5m of grant funding has been awarded to 19 successful projects to provide reception and integration supports and rehabilitative services to third country nationals. The second EU funding scheme to assist migrants is the Integration and Employment of Migrants action under the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) 2021-2027 programme. This action is aimed at legally resident migrants who are experiencing barriers to participation and employment because of language difficulties, lack of training or social exclusion. A total allocation of €5.4m was assigned to this action for the period 2021-2027, which is now fully committed. In 2022, seven projects were approved total. funding of €2.7m for a three-year period. In December 2025, a further eight projects were approved for funding to the value of €2.7m. Under the Local Integration Model, my Department funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including individuals granted Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred my Department in 2025. The Model makes use of existing organisations and initiatives, supported by co-ordination and collaboration across government bodies, agencies and NGOs. The Local Government Management Agency (LGMA) is responsible for coordinating and supporting the Local Authorities in the delivery of integration services. The approach rests heavily on interrelated and complementary work carried out by a DJHAM-funded network of Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) and Community Integration Fora (CIFs) in each Local Authority across the country, via programmes aimed at supporting the long-term integration into local communities of: • Individuals granted Temporary Protection • Applicants for International Protection • Persons granted Refugee status, Subsidiary Protection status, or Permission to Remain • Refugees resettled under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) LAITs provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Communication and collaboration between the actors in the integration space is facilitated by a Community Integration Forum (CIF) in each Local Authority. CIFs bring together a network of Government and Non-Government Organisations, voluntary and community groups, including LAITs, to collaborate on a community-led integration approach. CIFs are chaired at a senior level within the Local Authority and provide strategic oversight for the promotion of integration, social inclusion and civic participation of the relevant cohorts. My Department's Community Engagement Team (CET) was established in late 2023 to engage directly with elected representatives, local authorities, An Garda Síochána, community members, and other service providers in advance of a new accommodation centre opening. The CET team also links with other stakeholders outside of immediate openings of centres to build relationships and networks with key groups. This includes meetings with Community Integration Fora, Local Development Companies (LDCs) and other non-governmental organisations. Finally, the Programme for Government 2025 provides a commitment to developing a new Migration and Integration Strategy for Ireland, detailing how we intend to meet the demands and the opportunities facing our society and economy over the next decade. Work is well advanced on this project, with a view to the Strategy being launched later this year.

question: 2268. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the penalties, sanctions or enforcement actions available in respect of airlines or carriers that transport passengers to the State without valid travel documentation; the number of such actions taken in each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60625/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2271. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda resources assigned to Operation Tombola in 2026 to combat the illegal importation, sale and use of fireworks; whether these resources have been increased or decreased from previous years; and if he will make a statement on the matter [60471/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2271 and 2310 together. An Garda Síochána’s Operation Tombola combats the illegal importation, sale and use of fireworks through a nationwide policing plan focused on the prevention and detection of the sale of fireworks and associated public order and anti-social behaviour issues during the Halloween period. The operation encompasses all aspects of policing the Halloween period each year. It combats the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, through intelligence-led operations, searches and seizures, as well as focusing on preventing associated public disorder and anti-social behaviour. The penalties for importing, selling or using unlicensed fireworks are significant and Part 6 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 gives Gardaí power to arrest people found with unlicensed fireworks and sets out significant penalties on conviction, including fines up to €10,000 or up to five years imprisonment for possession with intent to sell or supply. These penalties, which can also apply to those convicted of throwing an ignited firework at a person or property, demonstrate the seriousness attached to breaches of the legislation governing the importation and use of fireworks. I am advised that a key component of Operation Tombola is active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each Garda Division. Gardaí collaborate closely with community stakeholders. Operation Tombola is actively implemented in the lead-up to and during the Halloween period, with each Chief Superintendent overseeing measures to address the sale, supply, and possession of fireworks, as well as anti-social behaviour. These measures include increased overt and covert patrols in key areas, including usual gathering locations for young people and areas likely to stockpile bonfire materials, as well as regular patrols on Dublin Bus, LUAS, and DART services in the days leading up to Halloween, ensuring a visible presence to deter anti-social behaviour continues. An Garda Síochána also conduct talks and sessions in schools and youth services throughout the region, specifically targeting young individuals who may be involved in the sale, supply, or use of firework continues, and there is active monitoring of open-source media to identify potential locations where individuals were engaging in the illegal sale and supply of fireworks continues. An Garda Síochána co-ordinates with local authorities to remove any stockpiled bonfire materials before Halloween will take place. A key component of Operation Tombola involves active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each division. Gardaí have collaborated closely with these stakeholders to ensure a unified approach to preventing anti-social behaviour during the Halloween period. I am advised that since 2016 Gardaí have sized 1,883 fireworks, with an estimated value of €347,516. These seizures have undoubtedly contributed to reducing harm associated with the illegal use of fireworks. The attached table counts the number of fireworks offences reported, the number of those sanctioned (charge/summons/caution), the number of objects seized and the estimated value thereof, for the period 2016 to 26 August 2026. An Garda Síochána have advised that the data was extracted from PULSE, it is operational and is subject to change. Fireworks offences

question: 2272. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to examine the case of a person (details supplied); the reason that after three years a decision has not yet been made on the application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61405/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2273. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the proposed voluntary return and re-integration programme for Ukrainian beneficiaries of TP, the number of persons his Department estimates may avail of the programme in 2027. [61329/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2274. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of beneficiaries currently in ARP-supported accommodation who are not in employment or self-employment and therefore may not meet the proposed eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme. [61325/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced in July 2022 to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to people arriving in Ireland from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive. The eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme sets out that the principal applicant must be employment or self-employment for six months, with a minimum yearly salary of €29,432. More information on the criteria can be found at Ukraine Updates (EN) on www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. I am unable to provide the current numbers for those hosted in ARP accommodation who are unemployed or self-employed. This information is not compiled as part of the administration of the ARP scheme and is not separately compiled. From the ARP scheme’s launch on 26 July 2022 to date approx. 29,500 hosts have hosted approx. 67,500 people with Temporary Protection. Currently, there are approx. 22,500 active claims in payment in respect of hosting approx. 40,000 people granted Temporary Protection from Ukraine. Recent CSO data shows that for the 31,069 BoTPs in employment, the mean weekly earnings in May 2026 for these employments was €573: www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/p-aui/arrivalsfromukraineinirelandseries19/. Based on this data, it is likely that a large proportion of these can meet the income requirement. However, it is not possible to pre-empt the number of people in ARP supported accommodation who may not meet the proposed eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme.

Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2278. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will confirm whether a period of residence in the State held under Stamp 0 permission is reckonable for the purposes of section 16A of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended, noting that Stamp 0 is not among the categories of residence excluded by that section; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61435/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2278, 2279, 2295 and 2304 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Stamp 0 may be granted to a person who wishes to come to Ireland to retire or to live as an elderly dependent of a sponsoring family member. This immigration permission is granted only where there is proof that the applicant is financially self-sufficient or that the sponsor can fully support them financially. Holders of Stamp 0 are not permitted to work or engage in any business, trade, or profession (unless specified in a letter of permission from Immigration Service Delivery). They cannot receive any State benefits or use publicly funded services and must have comprehensive medical insurance with full private hospital cover. Time spent in the State on a Stamp 0 is currently reckonable residence for citizenship. My Department does not collate statistics on the immigration permission or permissions held by applicants who were granted naturalisation. The Deputy will be aware that people may change their immigration permissions and may rely on a number of different permissions when applying for naturalisation, provided those permissions are reckonable under the 1956 Act. Last November, Government approved a package of policy and legislative reforms to strengthen Ireland's migration and asylum system, ensuring it is rules-based, efficient, and more closely aligned with those of other EU Member States. As part of this work, my Department is reviewing aspects of Ireland's citizenship legislation and developing proposed amendments. Draft legislative proposals will be brought to Government shortly. Any proposals approved by Government will be subject to scrutiny through the normal Oireachtas legislative process.

question: 2281. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there are plans to modernise the Garda vetting process; whether consideration has been given to linking Garda vetting applications to an individual's PPS number as a means of streamlining identity verification and reducing unnecessary administrative burdens on An Garda Síochána, employers, volunteers and community organisations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60336/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2282. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to legislate for how guardianship rights are determined when a parent has been accused of intimate partner violence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60316/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Guardianship of Infants and Child Care (Amendment) Act 2026 was signed into law by President Connolly on 21 July 2026 and will allow for the removal of guardianship rights of a person who has been convicted of killing the other parent of their child. The primary aim of the legislative changes under the Act is the promotion of child protection and welfare. The Court will be required to consider in these cases whether a revocation of guardianship would be in the best interests of the child. It is not planned at the moment to make further changes to the 1964 Act in this regard, however I would like to assure the Deputy that all legislation is this area is kept under review to ensure that it remains effective and that any further changes needed to protect victims and hold perpetrators to account are considered. The legislation will be reviewed in accordance with Oireachtas Standing Orders and a report laid before the houses one year following its enactment. The Deputy will be aware that Article 42A.4 of the Constitution requires that provision be made by law that in the resolution of all proceedings concerning the guardianship or custody of, or access to, any child, the best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration. The Article requires that provision be made by law for securing, as far as practicable, that in all such proceedings in respect of any child who is capable of forming his or her own views, the views of the child shall be ascertained and given due weight having regard to the age and maturity of the child. Section 3 of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 provides that the best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration for the court in any proceedings where guardianship, custody or upbringing of, or access to, a child is in question. However, it is important to note in the context of a situation where an issue such as violence or harm arises, Section 11 of the Act allows the court on application of a guardian to apply to the court for its direction on any question affecting the welfare of the child – the court may under that section make such order as it thinks proper regarding the custody of the child and the right of access to the child of each of his or her parents. In addition existing legislation already provides mechanisms to address circumstances where concerns arise regarding the welfare or safety of a child in the context of family law proceedings. Where it appears to a court that there may be a risk to a child, the court may, of its own motion or on application by any person, direct the Child and Family Agency to investigate the child’s circumstances. Pending the outcome of such an investigation, the court may make directions regarding the care and custody of the child. Following investigation, the Child and Family Agency may apply for a care order, supervision order or take such other action as may be considered appropriate in the interests of the child. Section 25 of the 1964 Act requires the court, as it thinks appropriate and practicable, to take into account the child’s wishes in such proceedings, having regard to the age and understanding of the child. Section 31 of the 1964 Act sets out a wide range of factors that the court is required to take into account when determining the best interests of the child in such proceedings. The courts shall have regard to all of these factors or circumstances that it regards as being relevant to the child concerned and his or her family and make its decision accordingly. Section 32(1) of the 1964 Act provides that in any such proceedings, the court may do either or both of the following: (a) give directions for the purpose of procuring a written report from an expert on any question affecting the welfare of the child; or (b) appoint an expert to determine and convey the child’s views. Section 47 of the Family Law Act 1995 provides that the Circuit Court or High Court may order a report in writing on any question affecting the welfare of a party to family law proceedings or any other person to whom they relate.

question: 2284. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any engagement he has had with the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science in relation to the refusal of visas for Palestinian students (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61527/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. question: 2285. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide information regarding the new family visits policy introduced by the Irish Prison Service (IPS) in November 2025, including the aim of the policy and the reasoning for its introduction; whether siblings and nieces/nephews under the age of 18 are excluded from family visits under the new policy; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61554/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Irish Prison Service is committed to making visiting a prison as easy and as safe as possible for visitors. The Irish Prison Service understands the importance of helping prisoners maintain and develop relationships with family and friends and is committed to enhancing where possible, and subject to appropriate security considerations, the visiting facilities and regimes for prisoners. I am advised that, from the 3rd November 2025, the Irish Prison Service introduced a new policy whereby all child visitors (persons under 18 years of age) visiting closed prisons are now required to produce a form of identification to enter a prison, similar to the process already applied to adult visitors. This is an important component of the overall security strategy, ensuring that appropriate measures are in place to prevent any potential misuse of child visitation as a means to compromise the safety and integrity of our prisons. The categories of child visitors permitted to visit a person in prison are: - Son/Daughter - Step-Son/Step-Daughter - Grandchildren Prisoners can make applications to their Governor for permission for other child visitors, including siblings, to be admitted outside of the cohort listed above. Each case is considered on its individual merit, where the Governor has satisfied themselves that there are familial links and all known risk and protective factors are taken into account. The following form of ID for Child Visitors are accepted: Birth Cert Passport Driver’s License National ID Card Public Service Card UK National Insurance Card Garda National Immigration Card I am further advised that the Irish Prison Service implemented a full public information campaign in advance of this new policy. Further information is available on the Irish Prison Service website (www.irishprisons.ie). This information is located in the ‘Visit a Prison’ section – under Prison Visit Information.

question: 2286. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update regarding the establishment of the Penal Policy Consultative Council by 31 December 2026; the timeframe for it to be established; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61553/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The 2020 Programme for Government committed to the establishment of a Penal Policy Consultative Council to provide advice to the Minister on matters relating to penal policy. However, while work was undertaken within my Department to progress this initiative at that time, addressing developments in the Prison Service, particularly in relation to overcrowding, have since taken precedence in this area. I can advise the Deputy that there are no current plans to establish the Consultative Council as I believe the Council’s proposed objectives are being achieved through other means, including collaboration across a number of interagency and cross-sectoral working groups. A Prison Overcrowding Response Group (PORG) was established in July 2023 to develop proposed actions to address the problem of Irish prisons operating above capacity. The group comprises representatives from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, An Garda Síochána, the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, and the Courts Service. Actions agreed by the PORG include developing new responses to deliver structured temporary release for suitable prisoners, actions to encourage greater use of community service, and advancing legislative changes to support delivery of community-based sanctions. The PORG continues to meet and work to implement these actions is ongoing. The High Level Taskforce on Mental Health and Addiction (HLTF) Steering Committee supports and monitors the implementation of recommendations cited in the HLTF Final Report published in 2022. The Report, jointly led by my Department and the Department of Health, identified the need to take a holistic approach when considering the mental health and addiction challenges of those who come into contact with the criminal justice sector from initial contact right through to release and support in the community. A Prison Education Taskforce (PET) commenced in May 2023 with the aim of ensuring greater alignment between prison education, work training and the tertiary education system to support people in prison to have education and training opportunities while in custody that support their rehabilitation and access to employment post-release. The taskforce is jointly chaired by the Minister of State for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science and the Minister of State for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, and comprises representatives from the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, SOLAS, Education and Training Boards, and Maynooth University. Finally, the Criminal Justice Strategic Committee was established in 2015 and is chaired by the Secretary General of this Department. It is comprised of members of the Department’s management board and the heads of An Garda Síochána, the Courts Service, Forensic Science Ireland, the Irish Prison Service, the Legal Aid Board, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, the Office of the State Pathologist, and the Probation Service. The Committee meets quarterly and its objective is to facilitate inter-agency collaboration by providing a forum for the identification, discussion and resolution of structural or operational issues that require senior management awareness and engagement.

question: 2295. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for a certificate of naturalisation granted in each of the years 2020 to 2026 to date, in which a period of residence held under Stamp 0 permission was counted as reckonable residence, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61434/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2278, 2279, 2295 and 2304 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Stamp 0 may be granted to a person who wishes to come to Ireland to retire or to live as an elderly dependent of a sponsoring family member. This immigration permission is granted only where there is proof that the applicant is financially self-sufficient or that the sponsor can fully support them financially. Holders of Stamp 0 are not permitted to work or engage in any business, trade, or profession (unless specified in a letter of permission from Immigration Service Delivery). They cannot receive any State benefits or use publicly funded services and must have comprehensive medical insurance with full private hospital cover. Time spent in the State on a Stamp 0 is currently reckonable residence for citizenship. My Department does not collate statistics on the immigration permission or permissions held by applicants who were granted naturalisation. The Deputy will be aware that people may change their immigration permissions and may rely on a number of different permissions when applying for naturalisation, provided those permissions are reckonable under the 1956 Act. Last November, Government approved a package of policy and legislative reforms to strengthen Ireland's migration and asylum system, ensuring it is rules-based, efficient, and more closely aligned with those of other EU Member States. As part of this work, my Department is reviewing aspects of Ireland's citizenship legislation and developing proposed amendments. Draft legislative proposals will be brought to Government shortly. Any proposals approved by Government will be subject to scrutiny through the normal Oireachtas legislative process.

question: 2298. [61471/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2128, 2298, 2377 and 2411 together. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the training of Garda personnel and the distribution of Garda resources throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of An Garda Síochána is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. I have been advised by the Garda authorities that while driver response training is provided to specific members of An Garda Síochána, with specialist units receiving advanced driving training, no Gardaí have been trained to conduct tactical pursuits. However, as recently confirmed by the Commissioner, An Garda Síochána is currently upskilling Garda Driving Instructors to enable the delivery of pursuit training to the organisation. In this regard I am advised that Garda College driving instructors attended training at the Devon and Cornwall Police in early 2025 to observe their training and determined that it was in line with the needs of the training requirement of An Garda Síochána. Thereafter, the instructors commenced the first of three stages of training. In 2026, driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall Police attended the Garda College and continued the training of Garda College driver training instructors, which is currently on-going. Officials in my Department have submitted a draft proposal to the Department of Transport, which is currently under review. question: 2306. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the strategies he has in place to address the growing problem of shoplifting; the powers a retailer or retail worker has to confront possible shoplifters; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61372/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2225 and 2306 together. I take any risk to retailers, retail staff and communities very seriously and I am acutely aware of the personal and economic impact that retail crime is having on businesses, retail workers and communities. I recognise that shoplifting and organised retail crime pose a significant threat to the economic welfare of Irish retailers and that retail theft is not a victimless crime. The Government is taking a number of strategic, tactical and integrated measures to address retail crime. The Programme for Government makes several commitments in relation to retail crime. Together with the ongoing roll-out of high visibility policing by An Garda Síochána, further measures are also under consideration. These include: • Improving data sharing between retailers and Gardaí to support enforcement; • Expanding the use of community sanctions for retail crime; and • Updating the Public Order Acts to allow prolific offenders to be excluded from retail premises for a certain period of time. My Department is in the process of drafting a Retail Crime Strategy and work is well advanced. I expect to receive a draft copy of this strategy in the coming weeks for my consideration. The Government intends to publish the Strategy within the next few months. An Garda Síochána commenced a dedicated operation in 2023, ‘Operation Táirge’, to tackle organised retail crime. Under ‘Táirge’, Gardaí nationwide use an intelligence-led approach to identify criminals engaging in retail crime. The approach is to disrupt the most prolific groups using organised crime legislation and proceeds of crime legislation and to work with retailers to strengthen their security and prevent them becoming victims of this criminality. It should also be noted that my Departments work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions, probation supervision schemes and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment and increasing high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Additionally, An Garda Síochána is currently developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy for 2026-2029. On a tactical level, getting more Gardaí on our streets is my first priority. The overall Garda workforce has increased from 15,980 in 2016 to over 18,500 in 2026. With three recruitment competitions to join An Garda Síochána in the last 18 months, there is a strong pipeline of recruits regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College. More Gardaí proactively patrolling in our cities, towns and rural areas as well as more Garda staff will help to maintain law and order and make everyone feel safer.

question: 2307. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the mechanisms through which Dáil Éireann exercises legislative and regulatory oversight of border control, immigration screening and airport entry procedures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60629/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2308. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the details of the way in which the Irish Prison Service carries out individualised, security risk assessments for individuals upon their committal to prison. [60608/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by my officials in the Irish Prison Service that an initial risk assessment process is conducted during the Governors' committal interview to which all prisoners are subject upon committal or transfer. This process, alongside existing information contained on the Prisoner Information Management System, allows the Governor of a prison to make an informed decision with regard to appropriate accommodation and initial sentence management activity, where a risk or need has been identified. I am further advised that on occasion additional information is provided during the court process or by An Garda Síochána when lodging a prisoner and this information will also be considered during the Governors committal interview. Additionally, where a person is committed late in the evening or at weekends the committal interview may not be completed in advance of the assignment of cell accommodation. However, a newly committed prisoner may declare that they are under threat from a particular person or factions and this would be factored into cell allocation.

question: 2310. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí assigned to Operation Tombola for each year since its commencement, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60477/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2271 and 2310 together. An Garda Síochána’s Operation Tombola combats the illegal importation, sale and use of fireworks through a nationwide policing plan focused on the prevention and detection of the sale of fireworks and associated public order and anti-social behaviour issues during the Halloween period. The operation encompasses all aspects of policing the Halloween period each year. It combats the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, through intelligence-led operations, searches and seizures, as well as focusing on preventing associated public disorder and anti-social behaviour. The penalties for importing, selling or using unlicensed fireworks are significant and Part 6 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 gives Gardaí power to arrest people found with unlicensed fireworks and sets out significant penalties on conviction, including fines up to €10,000 or up to five years imprisonment for possession with intent to sell or supply. These penalties, which can also apply to those convicted of throwing an ignited firework at a person or property, demonstrate the seriousness attached to breaches of the legislation governing the importation and use of fireworks. I am advised that a key component of Operation Tombola is active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each Garda Division. Gardaí collaborate closely with community stakeholders. Operation Tombola is actively implemented in the lead-up to and during the Halloween period, with each Chief Superintendent overseeing measures to address the sale, supply, and possession of fireworks, as well as anti-social behaviour. These measures include increased overt and covert patrols in key areas, including usual gathering locations for young people and areas likely to stockpile bonfire materials, as well as regular patrols on Dublin Bus, LUAS, and DART services in the days leading up to Halloween, ensuring a visible presence to deter anti-social behaviour continues. An Garda Síochána also conduct talks and sessions in schools and youth services throughout the region, specifically targeting young individuals who may be involved in the sale, supply, or use of firework continues, and there is active monitoring of open-source media to identify potential locations where individuals were engaging in the illegal sale and supply of fireworks continues. An Garda Síochána co-ordinates with local authorities to remove any stockpiled bonfire materials before Halloween will take place. A key component of Operation Tombola involves active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each division. Gardaí have collaborated closely with these stakeholders to ensure a unified approach to preventing anti-social behaviour during the Halloween period. I am advised that since 2016 Gardaí have sized 1,883 fireworks, with an estimated value of €347,516. These seizures have undoubtedly contributed to reducing harm associated with the illegal use of fireworks. question: 2311. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for naturalisation via Irish association received in the years 2023 to date; the number of which were successful and unsuccessful; and if he will make a statement on the matter.' [60469/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2141, 2227, 2311 and 2312 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Last year, my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. These guidelines set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or has Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department's website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. In April 2025, 1,358 fair procedures letters were issued to applicants, affording them the opportunity to provide a submission or submit additional documentation in support of their Irish Association application. All submissions received have been reviewed and added to the relevant applications. I can advise the Deputy that, in devising and introducing the new guidelines, full policy and operational consideration was undertaken, including transitional arrangements. Under the provisions of Section 16 of the Act, the Minister is afforded absolute discretion. I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications and decisions based on Section 16 'Irish Association' received each year, during the past four years. This would require the manual examination of hundreds of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time to compile. Following the recent introduction of the new Section 16 'Irish Association' guidelines, arrangements to separately record such applications have been put in place. The total number of decisions issued on Irish Association applications since the introduction of the guidelines in April 2025 is 444, of which 300 were refusals and 144 were approvals.
