question: 2364. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number who may not meet the minimum income requirement for that scheme; the accommodation options will be available to such persons following the termination of ARP; whether any alternative housing support or transitional financial assistance is being considered for households that cannot secure private accommodation. [61326/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Following a recent Government decision, my Department is progressing to develop an alternative permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland. This is known as the Temporary Protections Transition Scheme. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year as a beneficiary of temporary protection prior to the opening of the application process. Applicants must provide evidence of independent accommodation at the time of application. Each application will be considered on a case-by-case basis. Further information is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. This webpage will be updated over the next few weeks to include details of the application process. Recent CSO data shows that for the 31,069 BoTPs in employment, the mean weekly earnings in May 2026 for these employments was €573: Arrivals from Ukraine in Ireland Series 19 - Central Statistics Office: (www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/p-aui/arrivalsfromukraineinirelandseries19/). Based on this data, it is likely that a large proportion of these can meet the income requirement. However, the principal applicant can apply on behalf of a family unit and as such It is not possible to pre-empt the number of people who will not be eligible under the income requirement for the scheme due to the unknown family composition of each applicant. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, hosts can continue to have private arrangements with Ukrainians if they so wish. Other measures, such as the rent a room scheme are also available. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation. Following Council Implementing Decision 2026/1912 of 30 July 2026, the Temporary Protection Directive is currently in place across the EU until March 2028. Those granted Temporary Protection in Ireland will remain entitled to this protection and associated rights under Section 60 of the International Protection Act 2015 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/66/section/60/enacted/en/html) and Section 237 of the International Protection Act 2026 www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/9/section/237/enacted/en/html). (while the Directive remains in effect. These rights, include access to the labour market, access to education and training, and access to medical care in the State in the like manner and to the like extent in all respects as an Irish citizen. Similarly, such persons (other than persons resident in Designated Accommodation Centres), may apply for social welfare benefits in a like manner and subject to the same eligibility criteria as Irish Citizens.

question: 2365. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left, State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number for whom his Department has no recorded accommodation outcome following departure from State-provided accommodation. [61306/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2229, 2230, 2231, 2232, 2233, 2234, 2235, 2240 and 2365 together. My department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My department has no role in private accommodation arrangements and cannot assist with long-term housing matters. Those granted Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own accommodation arrangements through their own means, with the support of schemes and services provided by other bodies where appropriate. People may seek private rented accommodation independently and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Further information on Rent Supplement is available through local Intreo Centres and Department of Social Protection offices. Alternatively, people with Temporary Protection may seek hosted accommodation through their Local Authority or through the Irish Red Cross. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation should contact their Local Authority or the Irish Red Cross directly. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or on 1800 753 343. Information on the Offer a Home scheme is available at www.offerahome.ie. Once a person with Temporary Protection leaves State-provided accommodation, my department does not have a role in, or visibility of, their subsequent private accommodation arrangements. Accordingly, my department cannot track whether an individual has returned to Ukraine, secured accommodation through private means, or accessed accommodation supports through other agencies. Further information regarding accommodation supports and policy updates is available at gov.ie under the Ukraine Updates portal.

question: 2366. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of persons who presented or were assessed as being under 18 years-of-age and were subsequently determined to be adults, whether any cases in each of the years 2021 to 2025 were identified as involving suspected deliberate misrepresentation of age or identity; the number of such cases referred to An Garda Síochána or another relevant authority for investigation; the number resulting in any legal proceedings; the outcome of any such proceedings; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61228/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2352, 2353, 2366 and 2367 together. The International Protection Act 2026 has set out the legislative basis for carrying out an age assessment in line with the best interests of the child. Both this Act and the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum set out a series of safeguards in relation to presumed minors, including the procedures governing age assessment. Prior to the 2026 Act, a practice developed whereby, if an individual presented for asylum and claimed to be a minor, they were generally referred to Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. The International Protection Office (IPO) accepted Tusla's determination as to whether an individual was entitled to access its services as a proxy for an age assessment process. Under the 2026 Act, where doubts arise regarding the applicant's claimed age, an age assessment is scheduled. Each applicant is required to provide any identity documents in their possession. In conducting an age assessment, the Determining Authority (the International Protection Office) may consider statements made by the applicant to an officer of the Minister, a member of An Garda Síochána, their appointed representative, an immigration officer, a member of staff of Tusla, and any documentary evidence available. The applicant is provided with an opportunity to receive legal counselling and/or to appoint a legal representative, and a dedicated child representative supports them throughout all procedures. A professionally trained social care worker carries out a psychosocial assessment to support the age assessment decision. If the applicant is deemed to be a minor, they are referred by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to Tusla. Tusla will then undertake its own internal eligibility-for-services process. If, following completion of this process, Tusla disagrees with the Department's decision and believes the applicant to be an adult, it may refer the applicant back to the Department for a subsequent age assessment under Section 60 of the 2026 Act. In cases where Tusla has determined that an individual is not eligible to access its services, the individual's application is managed through the international protection process as an adult and they are accommodated accordingly. Individuals who apply as unaccompanied minors, undergo the age assessment process, and are subsequently determined to be adults are not subject to any further investigation on that basis. Their applications are progressed in the normal way as adult applications and, as with all applications, all relevant factors are taken into account before a decision is made. In terms of verification of familial relationships, the IPO team will seek documentary evidence of the relationship and observe behaviours between the child and the accompanying adult. Where concerns arise, the child is referred to Tusla for a comprehensive review of the child's wellbeing. Tusla can work with the child to initiate family tracing where the parent is not in Ireland. The table below shows the number of referrals from the IPO to Tusla for individuals claiming to be under 18 years of age from 2021 to 2025. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 39 181 186 233 353 The Department does not retain statistics on the number of individuals deemed ineligible for Tusla services. The table below shows the number of international protection applications made by Tusla on behalf of unaccompanied minors from 2021 to 2025. Please note that the difference between the number of IPO referrals to Tusla and the number of international protection applications made on behalf of unaccompanied minors does not equate to the number of referrals that were determined not to be minors. Decisions on whether to apply for international protection on behalf of an unaccompanied minor are carefully considered by Tusla on a case-by-case basis. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 53 58 189 250 224

question: 2368. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported suspected drink-spiking cases in County Kerry and throughout the country; the number that were investigated; the number that were brought before the courts; the number that were convicted in the past five years and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61187/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2368 and 2369 together. Spiking is a crime that preys on vulnerability, that undermines consent and that can have devastating consequences for victims. As Minister, I am committed to fostering a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). Spiking a person’s drink or spiking someone by injection are, in effect, poisoning, which is a criminal offence under section 12 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, that can result in a three-year prison term. Section 12 applies to anyone who intentionally or recklessly administers a substance which is capable of interfering substantially with another person’s bodily functions, which explicitly includes inducing unconsciousness or sleep. Depending on the nature of the substance that is administered, it may be possible to charge a perpetrator with endangerment under section 13 of the Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997. This provides that it is an offence to intentionally or recklessly engage in conduct which creates a substantial risk of death or serious harm to another. The offence of endangerment carries a maximum penalty of seven years imprisonment. Where spiking is perpetrated in order to facilitate the commission of a further substantive offence (for example rape, sexual assault or theft), the perpetrator may also be charged with that offence or, where that offence was not completed, an attempt to commit that offence. An Garda Síochána has clear protocols in place in responding to reports of any crime. Gardaí undertake comprehensive investigations into each case, including toxicology analysis where necessary, to determine the circumstances and nature of the incident. Where evidence indicates a criminal offence linked to suspected spiking, the investigation will be conducted by local Gardaí, supported by or working in conjunction with Divisional Protective Services Units. An Garda Síochána takes all reports of spiking seriously and thoroughly investigates to determine the exact nature of each incident including results of toxicology reports in each case. I would advise any victims of similar incidents or any form of spiking to come forward and report same. On the measures in place to ensure timely Garda statements and preservation of evidence where a victim is incapacitated, I’m informed that on receipt of a report of any crime, Gardaí are duty bound to gather and seize evidence at a crime scene. Statements form part of the evidence-gathering process and will be taken from injured parties at an appropriate time and in a timely manner by the investigating member or the Senior Investigating Officer, if it is an SIO led investigation. Considerations such as the victim’s health and welfare, readiness and availability to provide a statement will be considered in preparing to take a statement of evidence. Preliminary notes and details may however be taken from the injured party and witnesses if available at the earliest time possible to initiate the investigation with a view to the early gathering of evidence and identification of the suspect(s). All victims of crime are dealt with by Gardaí in line with the Victims Charter: (www.garda.ie/en/victim-services/garda-victim-service/victims-charter.pdf) I’m informed by the Courts Service that there is no specific offence on the statute book for spiking. As a result, there is no offence code on their case management systems and therefore there is no data available in relation to spiking. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that the following publication may be of assistance to the Deputy and provides an analysis of spiking incidents reported between 2010 and 2023: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/spiking-incidents-may-2024.pdf. I am further advised that, according to the published data, there were 107 reported spiking incidents in 2022 and 52 reported incidents in 2023. An Garda Síochána has advised that there were 61 reported incidents in 2024 and 58 reported incidents in 2025. Each of these reported incidents was investigated. An Garda Síochána has advised that volumes were not sufficient to summarise beyond a regional breakdown. Data relating to spiking incidents will continue to be made available through annual proactive publications by An Garda Síochána.

question: 2370. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expedite an application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60572/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2372. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a response will issue to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60413/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Matters in regard to court fees are set by Statutory Instrument made by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, with the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The court fee structures currently in place are designed to be proportionate and balanced to ensure continued access to justice, while supporting appropriate contribution to the efficient running of the court system overall. The current fees system reflects the need to ensure the interests of applicants, as well as considering the public interest in the smooth operation of the court system. Matters arising relating to court fees are kept under consideration by my Department.

question: 2374. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any initiative that seeks to re-enforce the requirement that passports and any other required travel documents are checked at all ports of entry to the country; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61839/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2375. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any work ongoing to ensure that the circumstances that occurred in a case (details supplied) cannot be replicated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61838/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2375 and 2376 together. I do not comment on individual cases or active investigations. The establishment of a person’s identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. At ports of entry, Immigration officials conduct passport checks, and run operations as required, to ensure passengers arriving in the State are properly documented in accordance with Section 11 of the Immigration Act 2004. Section 12 of the Act also provides that every non-national shall produce on demand their passport or IRP card to an Immigration Officer or a member of the Garda Síochána.

question: 2377. Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the engagement that has taken place with an organisation (details supplied) regarding their publicly stated concerns and calls for specialist pursuit training, a comprehensive pursuit framework and a dedicated professional driving licence for Gardaí carrying out this work. [61834/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2128, 2298, 2377 and 2411 together. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the training of Garda personnel and the distribution of Garda resources throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of An Garda Síochána is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. I have been advised by the Garda authorities that while driver response training is provided to specific members of An Garda Síochána, with specialist units receiving advanced driving training, no Gardaí have been trained to conduct tactical pursuits. However, as recently confirmed by the Commissioner, An Garda Síochána is currently upskilling Garda Driving Instructors to enable the delivery of pursuit training to the organisation. In this regard I am advised that Garda College driving instructors attended training at the Devon and Cornwall Police in early 2025 to observe their training and determined that it was in line with the needs of the training requirement of An Garda Síochána. Thereafter, the instructors commenced the first of three stages of training. In 2026, driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall Police attended the Garda College and continued the training of Garda College driver training instructors, which is currently on-going. This “train-the-trainer” approach will allow the Garda College to become self-sufficient to train further garda instructors and enable training of Gardaí to commence before the end of 2026. Officials from my Department and the Department of Transport are continuing to engage with a view to considering whether legislative changes may be required to provide appropriate legal protections for members of An Garda Síochána undertaking pursuits in the course of their duties. As Minister, I recognise the importance of ensuring that An Garda Síochána can carry out its operational responsibilities effectively while maintaining an appropriate legal and regulatory framework. question: 2378. Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide data for the Louth/Cavan/Monaghan division for the number of Gardaí who have requested, received and completed any form of pursuit training. [61833/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2378 and 2538 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. The Act states that the Commissioner is responsible for the training and professional development of Garda personnel and the Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. I have been advised by the Garda authorities that while the current suite of competency based driving courses provided does not include specific training on tactical pursuits an updated ‘Spontaneous Pursuits Policy’ was issued in late 2024. This policy provides direction to Garda personnel who engage in the use of pursuit tactics to reduce the risk associated with pursuits. The Commissioner has recently confirmed that he will introduce Garda pursuit training before the end of this year. This is the first time Gardaí will receive this specialist training. Currently, response training is provided to specific members of An Garda Síochána, with specialist units receiving advanced driving training. I welcome the the introduction of this training a and remain committed to ensuring that our Gardaí have the resources, equipment, and legislation they need to fulfil their vital policing role.

question: 2379. Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of calls received to the Garda regional control centre from on duty Gardaí seeking consent to pursue mechanically propelled vehicles for the Louth/Cavan/Monaghan division for each of the years 2020 to date in 2026. [61831/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is by law responsible for all operational policing matters, including responses by An Garda Síochána to emergency calls. I am informed by the Garda authorities that a search of their records for incidents recorded as 'Traffic - Failed to Stop' within the Louth and Cavan Monaghan Dispatch Groups from April 2023 returned 388 incidents. The Garda authorities have advised that this figure is approximate, as some incidents originated from callers other than on-duty Gardaí and an individual examination of records would be required to identify the precise number of relevant incidents. I am advised that the GardaSAFE system was rolled out incrementally across the organisation in 2023 and, accordingly, it is not possible to provide the requested information for the period prior to April 2023.

question: 2380. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether orientation and induction on the laws of the State and expected standards of behaviour is delivered to residents of emergency accommodation centres and emergency reception and orientation centres, as distinct from permanent IPAS centres; and the number of each category of centre currently in operation. [61945/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2380 to 2382, inclusive, 2392, 2393 and 2396 together. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and has passed into law. The new rules came into effect on 12 June. In line with Section 82 of the International Protection Act 2026, international protection applicants are provided with information, including on rights and obligations on reception, during the screening stage of their international protection journey. These documents can be found, including in translation, at www.irishimmigration.ie. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and Jesuit Refugee Service provide orientation supports to new international protection arrivals covering rights and responsibilities for individuals living in Ireland and information on how to access services: topics include cultural awareness, mental health care and social engagement. On arrival at an accommodation centre, people seeking international protection are provided with the ‘IPAS House Rules’ which explains the rules and procedures that are designed to make accommodation centres safe and effective. IPAS House Rules set out the rules that must be followed while living in accommodation provided by IPAS. All new residents are made aware that, by residing in IPAS accommodation, they are agreeing to abide by the IPAS House Rules. The IPAS House Rules, updated June 2026, explicitly prohibits sexual harassment, racism, homophobia and intimidation of any kind, and note that such conduct is illegal under Irish law. The IPAS Code of Practice 2025 is binding on all centre staff and explicitly names sexual orientation, among others, as a protected ground. The Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) operates three Reception and Orientation Centres (ROCs). Beneficiaries travelling to Ireland under IRPP receive Pre-Departure Orientation (PDO) in advance of their arrival in the State. This PDO is delivered by International Organisation for Migration (IOM) in conjunction with staff from IRPP. The PDO programme provides practical information to prepare beneficiaries for life in Ireland. This includes a dedicated session on rights and responsibilities covering, among other matters, the law in Ireland, child protection, gender equality, domestic abuse, female genital mutilation, marriage and honour-based abuse. After arrival, all residents with receive orientation training from the managers of the centres. A number of NGOs also provide orientation training sessions on an ongoing basis. IRPP staff also engage with residents on an ongoing basis, through monthly information clinics at which questions around various aspects of life in Ireland are addressed. Under the Local Integration Model, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in 2025. The Model makes use of existing organisations and initiatives, supported by co-ordination and collaboration across government bodies, agencies and NGOs. The Local Government Management Agency (LGMA) is responsible for coordinating and supporting the Local Authorities in the delivery of integration services. The approach rests heavily on interrelated and complementary work carried out by a DJHAM-funded network of Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) and Community Integration Fora (CIFs) in each Local Authority across the country, via programmes aimed at supporting the long term integration into local communities of: - Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs). - Applicants for International Protection. - Persons granted Refugee status, Subsidiary Protection status, or Permission to Remain. - Refugees resettled under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP). LAITs provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Communication and collaboration between the actors in the integration space is facilitated by a Community Integration Forum (CIF) in each Local Authority. CIFs bring together a network of Government and Non-Government Organisations, voluntary and community groups, including LAITs, to collaborate on a community-led integration approach. CIFs are chaired at a senior level within the Local Authority and provide strategic oversight for the promotion of integration, social inclusion and civic participation of the relevant cohorts.

question: 2383. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposed arrangements that will apply to Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection who apply for the temporary protection transition scheme but are refused; whether such persons will be eligible to participate in the proposed voluntary return and reintegration programme; whether eligibility for voluntary return will be automatic (details supplied); the legal status that will apply to a person following refusal; the time available to such persons to regularise their immigration status or make arrangements to leave the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61967/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government has agreed to introduce an alternative residence permission for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection who wish to remain in Ireland independently and who satisfy certain eligibility criteria. It is important to note that the alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection but to provide an additional pathway for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland on an independent basis. Persons who do not satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to benefit from Temporary Protection status and its associated rights and entitlements while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. Further information regarding the scheme is available at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/a-new-permission-en/. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. If a person takes the decision to return to Ukraine and the region becomes unsafe, they can reapply for temporary protection in Ireland for as long as the Temporary Protection Directive remains in force. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2385. Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the assessment his Department has made of the risks posed by the use of artificial intelligence to facilitate cyberattacks against Ireland’s critical infrastructure; the measures being taken, in conjunction with relevant Departments and agencies, to strengthen the State’s cyber-defence capabilities against AI-enabled threats; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61991/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government recognises the benefits that artificial intelligence (AI) can bring, while also acknowledging that it can present risks which require careful consideration. The recently published National Digital and AI Strategy identified secure and trustworthy AI, cyber resilience and digital security as strategic priorities. The Strategy includes commitments to undertake a national AI cyber risk assessment, strengthen the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), enhance the capabilities of the Joint Cyber Defence Command, update the National Cyber Emergency Response Plan, implement the EU AI Act and strengthen governance arrangements for the use of AI across the public service. The NCSC which is an operational arm of my Department monitors developments in AI-enabled cyber capabilities on a continuous basis and collaborates with our international partners in the EU and globally. The latest National Cyber Risk Assessment (NCRA), published last December, highlighted how AI drives systemic risk by increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of cyberattacks. In June 2026, the NCSC published Securing AI Adoption in the Public Sector, providing guidance to public bodies on identifying and managing cyber security risks associated with AI systems. This complements the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service framework which sets out governance, risk management, transparency and human oversight requirements for the use of AI by public bodies. The drafting of a new National Cyber Security Strategy, which is being led out by my Department and at an advanced stage, aims to build resilience against AI-enabled threats by tasking the NCSC to develop AI readiness across government, small businesses, and critical national infrastructure (CNI). It further proposes leveraging AI to enhance national defence capabilities, which the NCSC will progress through the development of an AI readiness plan.

question: 2388. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the total number of persons in each of the years 2023 to 2025 that were convicted of offenses related to the sale of cannabis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61974/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2388 to 2390, inclusive, and 2410 together. Management of the courts, operational matters and logistical functions including the recording of conviction data is the responsibility of the Courts Service who are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998. As Minister, I have no role in these independent matters. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. However, to be of assistance, I am advised by the Courts service that convictions are recorded on Courts Service case management systems by reference to the offence concerned. In this regard it should be noted that the consumption of synthetic cannabinoids or cannabis is not a standalone offence. As such the Courts Service is unable to provide the specific information requested. Similarly, regarding the sale of synthetic cannabinoids or cannabis, such activities fall under the general offences for possession for sale or supply under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 (as amended). As recorded court data does not categorise convictions by specific substance type, it is not possible to disaggregate this information to produce a report on convictions relating to the specific substance to which the Deputy has referred. The Deputy may be interested to note that on the 28 August 2026 the Minister for Public Health, Wellbeing and the National Drugs Strategy, Jennifer Murnane O’Connor TD, and I announced the establishment of a joint Working Group to address the availability and use of synthetic and semi-synthetic cannabinoids. The Working Group brings together the Department of Health, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Health Service Executive (HSE), An Garda Síochána and other relevant agencies. The group will strengthen enforcement of existing legislation, improve coordination across government, and support a rapid response to emerging drug risks, including synthetic cannabinoids found in products sold in shops, online and through other markets.

question: 2391. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether legislative changes are being considered in relation to parental responsibility for persistent youth offending; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62014/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2391, 2401, 2402 and 2404 together. The role of parental supervision orders , which are already provided for under the Children Act 2021 and other parental measures, will be further considered in the development of a new Youth Justice Strategy over the coming year. The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention, and the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, standing at a record €43 million. The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. As of this year, youth diversion services are now available nationwide. There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects across the country that are funded by this Department. The Government also funds specialised Youth Justice Workers and Programmes in Youth Diversion Projects catering to Early Intervention, Family Support and harder-to-reach, serious and prolific young offenders. The Government recognises the critical role that strong family relationships and effective parental supervision play in preventing youth offending. Since 2018, my Department has embedded family support initiatives within Youth Diversion Projects, and in 2026 there are 68 Family Support Worker posts funded across the YDP Network. Family support interventions are evidence-based and are designed to support families to build on their competencies, promoting a strengths-based approach. Alongside the network of 92 Youth Diversion Projects, my Department, in collaboration with the Probation Service, also operates a number of initiatives designed to address serious and prolific youth offending for those who may be deemed unsuitable for the Diversion Programme. Targeted YDPs provide intensive interventions specifically designed to address this cohort and I am examining the possibility of expanding these intensive interventions to areas of the country where they might be of particular benefit. It is also the case that engagement with the youth justice system can provide an opportunity for practitioners to work with parents to improve their parenting skills to better equip them to deal with their children's behaviour. The causes of, and our responses to, recent tragic events cannot be addressed through a lens of juvenile justice alone. The Departments of Health and Children, Disability and Equality play important roles and deliver a number of parental and child interventions and supports. For example, the HSE has responsibility for delivering Parenting Capacity Assessments, and Tusla has responsibility for child interventions and related parental supports. It is important to recognise that our existing Youth Justice Strategy has been successful in diverting children who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Youth Diversion Projects work with up to 5,000 children and their families each year, with the vast majority of these young people successfully disengaging from offending behaviour. There is also evidence of a strong relationship between increased investment in youth diversion and reductions in youth offending. Since 2020, An Garda Síochána has recorded a decline in youth offences. This reduction has occurred despite growth in the population of 12 to 17-year-olds. While the size of this age cohort has increased, the number of children coming to the attention of An Garda Síochána has remained relatively stable, indicating an overall reduction in youth offending rates.

question: 2392. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total expenditure incurred on the development, translation and delivery of orientation, induction and integration materials and programmes for international protection applicants in each of the years 2023, 2024 and 2025. [61949/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2380 to 2382, inclusive, 2392, 2393 and 2396 together. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and has passed into law. The new rules came into effect on 12 June. In line with Section 82 of the International Protection Act 2026, international protection applicants are provided with information, including on rights and obligations on reception, during the screening stage of their international protection journey. These documents can be found, including in translation, at www.irishimmigration.ie. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and Jesuit Refugee Service provide orientation supports to new international protection arrivals covering rights and responsibilities for individuals living in Ireland and information on how to access services: topics include cultural awareness, mental health care and social engagement. On arrival at an accommodation centre, people seeking international protection are provided with the ‘IPAS House Rules’ which explains the rules and procedures that are designed to make accommodation centres safe and effective. IPAS House Rules set out the rules that must be followed while living in accommodation provided by IPAS. All new residents are made aware that, by residing in IPAS accommodation, they are agreeing to abide by the IPAS House Rules. The IPAS House Rules, updated June 2026, explicitly prohibits sexual harassment, racism, homophobia and intimidation of any kind, and note that such conduct is illegal under Irish law. The IPAS Code of Practice 2025 is binding on all centre staff and explicitly names sexual orientation, among others, as a protected ground. The Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) operates three Reception and Orientation Centres (ROCs). Beneficiaries travelling to Ireland under IRPP receive Pre-Departure Orientation (PDO) in advance of their arrival in the State. This PDO is delivered by International Organisation for Migration (IOM) in conjunction with staff from IRPP. The PDO programme provides practical information to prepare beneficiaries for life in Ireland. This includes a dedicated session on rights and responsibilities covering, among other matters, the law in Ireland, child protection, gender equality, domestic abuse, female genital mutilation, marriage and honour-based abuse. After arrival, all residents with receive orientation training from the managers of the centres. A number of NGOs also provide orientation training sessions on an ongoing basis. IRPP staff also engage with residents on an ongoing basis, through monthly information clinics at which questions around various aspects of life in Ireland are addressed. Under the Local Integration Model, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in 2025. The Model makes use of existing organisations and initiatives, supported by co-ordination and collaboration across government bodies, agencies and NGOs. The Local Government Management Agency (LGMA) is responsible for coordinating and supporting the Local Authorities in the delivery of integration services. The approach rests heavily on interrelated and complementary work carried out by a DJHAM-funded network of Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) and Community Integration Fora (CIFs) in each Local Authority across the country, via programmes aimed at supporting the long term integration into local communities of: - Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs). - Applicants for International Protection. - Persons granted Refugee status, Subsidiary Protection status, or Permission to Remain. - Refugees resettled under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP). LAITs provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Communication and collaboration between the actors in the integration space is facilitated by a Community Integration Forum (CIF) in each Local Authority. CIFs bring together a network of Government and Non-Government Organisations, voluntary and community groups, including LAITs, to collaborate on a community-led integration approach. CIFs are chaired at a senior level within the Local Authority and provide strategic oversight for the promotion of integration, social inclusion and civic participation of the relevant cohorts.

question: 2394. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to a case (details supplied); and if he will instruct his Department to address the matter. [62059/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration IPAS is currently accommodating more than 32,000 residents; this is comprised mainly of individuals whose applications for International Protection remain under consideration but include also a number of individuals whose applications have been fully assessed and rejected and who are now the subject of Deportation Orders. Where an individual is no longer an applicant for International Protection they are not entitled to IPAS accommodation; if they are the subject of a Deportation Order they do not have any legal basis to remain in the State. The accommodation system continues to operate under significant pressure, and IPAS must prioritise accommodation for international protection applicants who are entitled to accommodation under the International Protection Act 2026. If a person’s application for international protection is refused and they are ordered to leave the State, they must do so. Their case to remain in the State has been considered in detail and any appeals processes have concluded. As part of the process leading to the making of a Deportation Order these individuals will have been advised of the options open to them, including the possibility of supported voluntary return; where this option is not availed of the process moves on to the issuance of the Deportation Order and the requirement on the individual to leave the State. These individuals will have been given contact details and scheduled appointment to engage with the Immigration Authorities to arrange their removal from the State; it is, of course, open to these individuals to make their own arrangements to comply with the Deportation Order and remove themselves from the State.

question: 2395. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on a citizens application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62050/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2397. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the target processing times his Department has set for naturalisation applications for each of the years 2026 and 2027; the priority afforded to citizenship processing within his Departments work programme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62108/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2397, 2398, 2399, 2400 and 2451 together. It is important to note that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of Irish citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place in respect of each application. Unfortunately, some checks, including international enquiries and verifications, can take a considerable amount of time and are largely outside the control of Immigration Service Delivery. While I expect that, going forward, most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in every case due to the individual circumstances and complexity of applications. The Citizenship Division currently has 81 staff assigned across all grades. Staffing levels are kept under constant review, taking account of operational needs, application volumes and available resources, and additional staff have been assigned to the team as required. The number of naturalisation applications received by the Department in recent years is set out in the table below. Table 1. Citizenship applications received 2021-2026 Year Applications Received 2021 11,975 2022 17,202 2023 22,690 2024 27,032 2025 41,511 2026 (to date) 22,055 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Citizenship Division has taken a significant number of steps in recent years to improve the application process and support more efficient case processing. These measures include the introduction of an online citizenship application process, online payment facilities and eVetting arrangements. These initiatives continue to improve the customer experience and support more streamlined processing. Approximately 6,000 applicants who have recently been approved for naturalisation are awaiting attendance at a citizenship ceremony. Each such applicant has received an invitation to attend the Citizenship Ceremonies being held on 17 and 18 September 2026. In 2025, 25 citizenship ceremonies were held and 29,300 certificates of naturalisation were conferred (adult and minor). In 2026 to date, 5 ceremonies have been held and 6,750 certificates have been conferred (adult and minor). My Department does not maintain statistics on the average length of time between the issue of an approval letter and an applicant's attendance at a citizenship ceremony. The scheduling of ceremonies is dependent on a range of operational factors, including venue availability and the number of applicants to be accommodated. The timeframe is also affected by the time taken by an applicant making the payment. There is no statutory processing time for naturalisation applications. However, the general objective of the Citizenship Division is to process straightforward applications as efficiently as possible. Citizenship processing remains a significant operational priority for my Department and I am committed to ensuring that the necessary resources and process improvements continue to be put in place to support the timely delivery of decisions. As of 31 August 2026, there were 51,882 active naturalisation applications being processed by the Citizenship Division of my Department. Of these, 38,748 applications (74%) had been in the system for less than 12 months, while 8,064 applications had been in the system for between 12 and 24 months and 5,070 applications had been in the system for more than 24 months.

question: 2401. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has reviewed parental responsibility laws, parenting orders, parental fines, compensation schemes or welfare-linked sanctions operating in other jurisdictions, including England and Wales, Australia and New Zealand; the findings of any such review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62130/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2391, 2401, 2402 and 2404 together. The role of parental supervision orders , which are already provided for under the Children Act 2021 and other parental measures, will be further considered in the development of a new Youth Justice Strategy over the coming year. The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention, and the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, standing at a record €43 million. The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. As of this year, youth diversion services are now available nationwide. There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects across the country that are funded by this Department. The Government also funds specialised Youth Justice Workers and Programmes in Youth Diversion Projects catering to Early Intervention, Family Support and harder-to-reach, serious and prolific young offenders. The Government recognises the critical role that strong family relationships and effective parental supervision play in preventing youth offending. Since 2018, my Department has embedded family support initiatives within Youth Diversion Projects, and in 2026 there are 68 Family Support Worker posts funded across the YDP Network. Family support interventions are evidence-based and are designed to support families to build on their competencies, promoting a strengths-based approach. Alongside the network of 92 Youth Diversion Projects, my Department, in collaboration with the Probation Service, also operates a number of initiatives designed to address serious and prolific youth offending for those who may be deemed unsuitable for the Diversion Programme. Targeted YDPs provide intensive interventions specifically designed to address this cohort and I am examining the possibility of expanding these intensive interventions to areas of the country where they might be of particular benefit. It is also the case that engagement with the youth justice system can provide an opportunity for practitioners to work with parents to improve their parenting skills to better equip them to deal with their children's behaviour. The causes of, and our responses to, recent tragic events cannot be addressed through a lens of juvenile justice alone. The Departments of Health and Children, Disability and Equality play important roles and deliver a number of parental and child interventions and supports. For example, the HSE has responsibility for delivering Parenting Capacity Assessments, and Tusla has responsibility for child interventions and related parental supports. It is important to recognise that our existing Youth Justice Strategy has been successful in diverting children who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Youth Diversion Projects work with up to 5,000 children and their families each year, with the vast majority of these young people successfully disengaging from offending behaviour. There is also evidence of a strong relationship between increased investment in youth diversion and reductions in youth offending. Since 2020, An Garda Síochána has recorded a decline in youth offences. This reduction has occurred despite growth in the population of 12 to 17-year-olds. While the size of this age cohort has increased, the number of children coming to the attention of An Garda Síochána has remained relatively stable, indicating an overall reduction in youth offending rates.

question: 2402. question: 2405. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review the process in assessing the student visa applications from students coming from Palestine to take account of the unique difficulties of making an application in that country in the context of war and genocide; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62152/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. question: 2406. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the engagement he has had with An Garda Síochána in relation to the societal impact of the sale of cannabis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62018/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2406, 2407, 2408 and 2409 together. The response to illegal drugs is a whole of Government one, led by my colleagues the Minister for Health and the Minister of State with responsibility for Public Wellbeing and the National Drugs Strategy. All stakeholders, including my Department and An Garda Síochána, have a role to play in limiting the harms caused by the illegal drugs trade, while centering a health led approach to tackling drugs misuse. I regularly engage with the Garda Commissioner on these issues, and officials in my Department are also in regular contact with counterparts in the Department of Health and An Garda Síochána to support our efforts to minimise harm. On 28 August, Minister Murnane O’Connor and I established a joint Working Group to address the availability and use of synthetic and semi-synthetic cannabinoids. The Working Group, chaired by Minister Murnane O’Connor, brings together the Department of Health, my Department, the Health Service Executive (HSE), An Garda Síochána and other relevant agencies. The group will strengthen enforcement of existing legislation, improve coordination across government, and support a rapid response to emerging drug risks, including synthetic cannabinoids found in products sold in shops, online and through other markets.
