question: 2490. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken to address lengthy Garda vetting delays for childcare workers, which providers report are contributing to staffing shortages and room closures; whether consideration is being given to a transferable vetting system for childcare employees moving between services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62139/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2491. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider reviewing the family reunification rights for healthcare assistants and home care assistants who have completed two years of lawful full-time employment in Ireland in order that they can access family reunification rights similar to those available to critical skills employment permit holders; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62740/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2495. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current legislative position regarding the sale, supply and possession of nitrous oxide for recreational or intoxicating use (details supplied); if he has examined the legislative approach taken in other jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, in addressing the misuse of nitrous oxide; if additional legislation or enforcement measures are currently being considered here; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62326/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2127 and 2495 together. The classification of substances under the Misuse of Drugs Acts is a matter for my colleague the Minister for Health. Nitrous oxide has a number of legitimate uses, particularly in the medical and catering industries, and I am informed that it is for this reason that it is not listed under the Misuse of Drugs Acts, nor is it the intention to classify it as a substance under those Acts. However, the challenge, as with any substance open to misuse, is to regulate its supply chain effectively without unduly penalising legitimate enterprise. The Government is not currently intending to introduce its own legislation on this matter; however the Deputy may be interested to note that I am advised by my colleague Minister Burke at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment that from February 2027, nitrous oxide will be subject to EU classification harmonisation and will be designated as a substance that is potentially harmful to human reproductive health and the nervous system. This reclassification is not merely a technical change; it is the trigger for further regulatory action. The European Commission has also published a draft amendment to the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) that would restrict the placing on the market of nitrogen oxide for supply to the general public, subject to narrowly defined derogations. In April 2026, the REACH Committee voted to proceed with the restriction on placing on the market of nitrous oxide based on its reprotoxic characteristics, with strict derogations for legitimate uses already approved under EU law, such as food safety law. It is expected that the final restriction Regulation will be formally adopted and published later this year and will come into force in February 2027. The Deputy may also be interested to note that the misuse of nitrous oxide is already addressed under several pieces of legislation. The purpose of the Criminal Justice (Psychoactive Substances) Act 2010 includes the prevention of the misuse of dangerous or otherwise harmful psychoactive substances and the provision of offences relating to the sale, importation, exportation or advertisement of those substances. The Act provides that a person who sells, or who imports or exports, a psychoactive substance knowing, or being reckless as to whether that substance is being acquired or supplied for human consumption, shall be guilty of an offence. That legislation also provides An Garda Síochána with powers in relation to the issuing of prohibition notices to a person engaged in selling, importing, exporting, or advertising nitrous oxide, or any psychoactive substance, for human consumption. The 2010 Act also provides a member of An Garda Síochána with powers of entry, search, seizure and detention, powers to search persons and vehicles and powers of arrest for obstruction where, with reasonable cause, they suspect a person of committing an offence under the Act. The HSE and An Garda Síochána remain aware of the issues surrounding nitrous oxide misuse, and the HSE continues to support awareness of the associated health risks among young people, parents and youth organisations.

question: 2496. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 12569/26, the expected timeline for the legislative transposition of the NIS2 Directive; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62759/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Work is close to finalisation on the drafting of the National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose the NIS2 Directive and establish Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory basis, with a view to its publication in the autumn. The Bill will then commence its passage through the Houses of the Oireachtas. While transposition of the Directive is complex, considerable implementation milestones have been completed to date including: • The launch of a National Competent Authority (NCA) Forum, led by our National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) in 2024 • The development and publication of a NIS2 Risk Management Measures guidance booklet • Ireland becoming a co-owner of the Cyber Fundamentals Framework (CyFun) which provides a structured, risk-based approach for essential and important entities to help them organise and evidence their NIS2 security measures The NIS2 Directive is a revision of the Network and Information Security Directive (EU) 2016/1148 (NIS Directive), which is currently in force in the State (S.I. 360 of 2018). Until the NIS2 Directive is transposed and enacted, the NIS Directive will remain in full effect, covering the most critical operators of essential services and digital service providers in the State. Additionally, work is at an advanced stage in my department on the preparation of Ireland's third National Cyber Security Strategy. On completion, this will fulfil a requirement under the NIS2 Directive.

question: 2497. Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the supports available in cases in which a solicitor has identified arguable grounds for judicial review of IPAT decisions but the applicant lacks the means to pursue the case. [62795/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Legal Aid Board (LAB) is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to persons of modest means. This includes the provision of legal aid and advice to international protection applicants under the International Protection Act 2015 and the International Protection Act 2026. Applicants for international protection can avail of the following services: • Legal Counselling: This service is available to applicants for international protection who apply under the International Protection Act 2026. The service involves the provision of general information and guidance to the applicant on the different procedures under which the application for international protection may be examined as well as information and guidance on the applicant’s rights and obligations during the procedure and guidance on completing the international protection application during the screening stage. • Legal advice: This involves legal advice and assistance in respect of the application to the International Protection Office (IPO) for international protection. • Legal Representation: In the case of a negative decision on the first instance application, LAB provides legal advice to an applicant on the options available to them, on the prospects of success on appeal, and where the applicant instructs that they wish to appeal, LAB provides legal representation for the applicant in the preparation of the appeal and at the hearing of the appeal before the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) or the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA) as the case may be. • Judicial Review: Where an applicant seeks legal aid to bring judicial review proceedings against a negative decision of the IPAT, the Minister or TARA, legal aid may be granted in respect of such proceedings.

question: 2498. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the supports in place from the State for companies and organisations to ensure the implementation of the NIS2 Directive. [60482/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Work is close to finalisation on the drafting of the National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose the NIS2 Directive and establish Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) on a statutory basis, with a view to its publication in the autumn. The Bill will then commence its passage through the Houses of the Oireachtas. Ahead of that, significant supports for companies and organisations to ensure compliance and the implementation of the NIS2 Directive have been put in place. This includes the establishment of a dedicated NIS2 webpage which offers updates on the legislative status and practical steps for in-scope organisations. While full transposition is pending, the NCSC has advised organisations to treat NIS2 as a benchmark and start closing security gaps immediately. There are also practical supports for organisations by way of readiness assessments. The NCSC encourages organisations to assess their current cyber security posture against NIS2’s risk management and reporting obligations via NIS2 Risk Management Measure Guidance, incident reporting and senior leadership engagement. A new resource, titled ‘Guidance on Cyber Governance for Management Board Members in NIS2 Entities’ is specifically designed to support Accounting Officers and Management Board members to fulfil their leadership responsibilities and protect the continuity of essential services with confidence. Furthermore, there are dedicated sector-specific and SME supports in place. The NCSC is prioritising support for critical infrastructure and digital service providers which includes sectors like energy, transport, healthcare, and digital infrastructure, as they are most likely to be in scope for NIS2. The NCSC has also provided tailored guidance for SMEs. Resources include checklists and toolkits for gap analysis as well as training and workshops to raise awareness and build capacity. There are a variety of other publicly available NIS2 Directive Resources available on the NCSC website, include a ‘NIS2 Quick Reference Guide’, and FAQ page, and 'Am I in Scope?’ to allow entities ascertain if they are within the scope of NIS2. Finally, Ireland has joined the Cyber Fundamental Framework, which provides a structured, risk-based approach for essential and important entities to help entities organise and evidence their NIS2 security measures.

question: 2499. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if it is intended to carry out a public information campaign on the implementation of the NIS2 Directive. [60487/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The NIS2 Directive aims to enhance and strengthen security across sectors that are vital for our economy and society and that rely heavily on ICT, such as energy, transport, water, banking, healthcare and digital infrastructure. Work is close to finalisation on the drafting of the National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose the NIS2 Directive and establish Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) on a statutory basis, with a view to its publication in the autumn. The NCSC is engaging with its constituents and stakeholders to ensure that NIS2 requirements are communicated ahead of time. The NCSC has prepared a media campaign for launch when the Cyber Security Bill comes into force and has produced resources and guidance for organisations within the scope of NIS2. This includes the rollout of draft Risk Management Measures and the Cyber Fundamentals (CyFun) framework, designed to help organisations comply with NIS2 requirements and most recently, Guidance on Cyber Governance for Management Board Members in NIS2 Entities. This new resource is specifically designed to support Management Board members fulfil their leadership responsibilities and protect the continuity of essential services with confidence. Together with Enterprise Ireland, the NCSC has launched a cyber review & improve grant scheme which provides 80% funding, up to 60k per grant, to Enterprise SMEs to conduct a review of their current cyber security posture and implement recommended improvements. In anticipation of the transposition of the Directive, the NCSC has made numerous publicly available NIS2 Directive Resources available on the NCSC website, including a ‘NIS2 Quick Reference Guide’, an FAQ page, and an, 'Am I in Scope?’ tool to allow entities ascertain if they are within the scope of NIS2.

question: 2504. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason biometric data of migrants is currently not shared with authorities in Britain' and his plans to address this. [62804/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2262, 2504 and 2526 together. The Border Management Unit (BMU) is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. Immigration officers are responsible for carrying out border management functions in order to protect the integrity of the State's immigration system and ensure compliance with immigration law. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, neither I nor my Department can comment on specific operational procedures of the BMU or the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB). However, I can assure the Deputy that all persons arriving at ports of entry are examined, and their travel documentation verified, using a range of border management and security systems. This includes checks against relevant national and international databases to assist in confirming identity, detecting fraudulent documentation, and identifying people who may be the subject of immigration, law enforcement, or security alerts. In relation to the sharing of biometric data with the UK, I can advise the Deputy that, at the UK-Ireland Summit in March, it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data-sharing arrangements, particularly to prevent abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits.

question: 2509. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update and a timeline on the implementation framework for legal aid reforms following on from the Frank Clarke Civil Legal Aid Income Limits and Independent Review Group Report; and if he will outline when the income threshold for legal aid will be increased in line with the report recommendations. [62908/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2126, 2212, 2509 and 2524 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. A range of civil legal issues are covered by the scheme, including domestic violence applications, which are prioritised by the Board. While contributions from those legally aided are an aspect of the scheme, the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 2017 provide that no contribution is payable for those who are applying solely for orders under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. In particular, the majority report recommends increasing the disposable income threshold from €18,000 to €23,500. Having the Civil Legal Aid Scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. However, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. A critical aspect will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Officials in my Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process. Potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy will be taken into account. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis is underway, with officials in my Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 2511. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department is aware of recent UK Government measures providing information to persons entering the United Kingdom concerning the law relating to violence and sexual abuse; whether any such material has been reviewed by his Department; and if so, the outcome of that review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62999/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2511, 2512 and 2513 together. All persons present in the State are subject to Irish law and are expected to respect the laws and values of Irish society. The Government's approach is centred on successful integration, participation in Irish society and compliance with the laws of the State. In that regard, work is underway on a whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy which will address how Ireland responds to the opportunities and challenges associated with migration. My Department is aware of the measures referred to by the Deputy. My Department recognises the importance of awareness-raising and behavioural change measures as part of its preventative work to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and to support victims of these crimes. Cuan, the DSGBV Agency, is tasked with driving progress and implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. A key function of Cuan is the delivery of impactful awareness campaigns on sexual consent and pathways to safety. The major national awareness-raising campaign on the topic of sexual consent, Let's Have the Consent Conversation, was launched on 23 November 2023 and continues to run at regular intervals. The purpose of the campaign is to use consent in sexual relationships as a means of focusing on equality and respect in how we, as a society, relate to and engage with one another. The campaign has deepened public understanding of consent, with 98% recognising its message and two-thirds reporting that it made them more likely to discuss consent. It has also supported targeted outreach to men and young people. In 2023, my Department launched Serious Consequences to raise awareness that threatening to share intimate images of a person without their consent is a crime. The campaign has increased public awareness of Coco's Law to 96%, targeted young men through major sports broadcasts, and won multiple national advertising awards. Likewise, the Hardest Stories campaign, launched in February 2025, raises awareness of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, encourages victims and survivors to come forward, and uses television, radio and digital content featuring diverse survivor stories. In addition, the Always Here campaign signposts victims to support services through television, radio, print, digital, and GP and pharmacy settings. The campaign has achieved 99% agreement that victims will be believed and 97% agreement that it clearly directs people to help.

question: 2514. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration where the former IPAS residents at a location (details supplied) have been or are being relocated to; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62974/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration During their period in IPAS accommodation, people may have to move to alternative centres for a variety of reasons, including family needs, renovations, regulatory or compliance issues at their accommodation, and pressures on capacity within the system overall. In order to protect the privacy of people resident in International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) accommodation, the Department does not provide detailed information about relocations between IPAS centres. We appreciate that relocating can be very disruptive for people. IPAS is in contact with residents and centre management to keep them informed of relocations plans and to offer support. IPAS and the HSE work together to try to facilitate continuity of care for residents with a serious medical need. A resident can tell IPAS if they have a serious medical issue by emailing ipasinbox@justice.ie. In so far as possible, the IPAS team will take these issues into consideration when allocating the resident new accommodation. However, it is important to understand that suitable accommodation in the same area may not be available. IPAS engages directly with people accommodated in IPAS centres through the dedicated customer service team ipasinbox@justice.ie.

question: 2515. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the action he is taking to reduce the waiting time for long stay (D) visa applicants to support those working and living in Ireland, especially in the healthcare sector so their family can join them here in Ireland and keeping these vital workers in the country. [62963/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2517. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to set out the research, data analysis or evidence base relied upon by the Department in designing the fee structure of the revised criminal legal aid scheme introduced on 1 July 2026, in particular in respect of cases involving multiple separate charges listed on the same day and cases of extended duration; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63107/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2125, 2130, 2139, 2140, 2517, 2518, 2519, 2520 and 2521 together. Management of the courts, operational matters such as allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and logistical functions are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given the separation of powers in the Constitution. Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the Courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Information requested in relation to the issuance of criminal legal aid certificates by the Courts should be directed to the Courts Service. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas, at oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. The Review and Reform Proposal of the Criminal Legal Aid fee structure for the District Court published on 2 July 2026 provides detail on the analysis conducted on these reforms. I am committed to improving efficiencies for court users, legal practitioners and the Irish taxpayer. The new District Court Criminal Legal Aid Scheme will allow for those efficiencies. There has been ongoing engagement between officials in the Department of Justice and the Law Society and Bar Council in relation to proposed changes to criminal legal aid fee structure, since October 2025, and I also wrote to the Law Society on these matters as recently as last Thursday week, 27 August 2026. I met with the Law Society of Ireland in July and listened to the issues raised by criminal practitioners regarding the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme which commenced on 1 July 2026. On foot of that engagement and at the request of the Law Society, I agreed to pay two thirds of the new €520 fee at the commencement of a case, with the remaining third to be paid at the conclusion of the case or after 12 months, whichever is earlier. The fee of €520, up from €455, is equivalent to the payment for 5 appearances in a case under the old system, adjusted to reverse the outstanding 8% cut under FEMPI. In addition, I agreed to increase the proposed fee for District Court cases going to the Circuit or higher courts from €100 to €520 and also introduced a separate fee of €80 for certificates issued following the execution of bench warrants. The further changes sought by Law Society are not compatible with the objectives of the reforms introduced as they would in practice reintroduce the possibility of multiple certificates being awarded in circumstances where the intention is to move to a single fee per case. It should also be noted that the flat fee has been set at a level intended to compensate, across the overall caseload, for cases where multiple certificates would have been granted under the previous system. My Department continues to keep the operation of the new criminal legal aid arrangements in the District Court under review following their introduction. As part of this review process, I have already indicated the possibility of considering modifications to reflect the distinct nature of cases that may require a large number of hearings, such as cases before the Children’s Court and remand hearings.

question: 2523. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding Ireland’s preparedness for a significant cyber-attack on any Government Department or institution; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63031/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), an operational unit of my Department, leads on the State’s response to cyber risk. The primary roles of the NCSC are to monitor, detect and respond to cyber security incidents in the State, to build cyber security resilience within the country, and to carry out national and international engagement. The National Cyber Emergency Plan outlines the process by which a National Cyber Emergency is declared, managed and co-ordinated. It ensures that stakeholders across Government and critical infrastructure understand their roles and responsibilities during a cyber emergency, and that the Government's approach to serious cyber incidents is clearly explained and communicated to the public. Through this avenue, the NCSC leads the management of major cyber security incidents across Government, co-ordinating with the Office of Emergency Planning within the Department of Defence, and offering guidance and advice to citizens and organisations during incidents. The NCSC organises exercises to assess and test national cyber crisis management arrangements, including co-ordination between key stakeholders, and strategic communications under realistic conditions of heightened threat. The National Cyber Emergency Plan is available online here: ncsc.gov.ie/pdfs/National_Cyber_Emergency_Plan.pdf The NCSC also delivers a range of functions to improve the cyber security resilience of critical infrastructure and services. This includes the ongoing work of the NCSC’s dedicated incident response team (CSIRT-IE) in detecting and responding to incidents, and its close information-sharing partnerships at national, EU and international levels. The NCSC publishes technical guidance to help organisations strengthen their systems against common cyber attacks, providing step-by-step walk-throughs on preparedness and has also built a secure digital engagement platform to support engagement with our constituents, partners and the public. Similarly, the NCSC has at its disposal technical capabilities to stand up enhanced monitoring, coordination, and situational awareness during major events. The NCSC acts as the competent authority for the NIS Directive under SI 360/2018 which ensures a high level of cyber security in critical entities under that instrument including readiness for potential cyber-attacks. The work of the NCSC will be further supported and expanded by the upcoming National Cyber Security Bill, which will extend and further develop the existing regulatory regime to other sectors of high criticality by transposing the NIS2 Directive, while also establishing the NCSC on a statutory footing with a defined set of functions and statutory powers.

question: 2524. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to review the civil legal aid scheme; if he will consider increasing the income thresholds to facilitate equal access to justice for low-income families; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63168/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2126, 2212, 2509 and 2524 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. A range of civil legal issues are covered by the scheme, including domestic violence applications, which are prioritised by the Board. While contributions from those legally aided are an aspect of the scheme, the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 2017 provide that no contribution is payable for those who are applying solely for orders under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. In particular, the majority report recommends increasing the disposable income threshold from €18,000 to €23,500. Having the Civil Legal Aid Scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. However, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. A critical aspect will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Officials in my Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process. Potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy will be taken into account. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis is underway, with officials in my Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 2525. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total cost of all removal and charter flight operations conducted on grounds of criminality up to the end of July 2026, including operations for which invoicing was previously described as incomplete; and the amount reclaimed or expected to be reclaimed under the EU Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund. [63167/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2525 and 2527 together. The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland. Under section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999 (as amended), a deportation order may be made in respect of a non-national on a number of grounds, including: - under section 3(2)(a), a person who has served or is serving a term of imprisonment imposed on him or her by a court in the State; - under section 3(2)(b), a person whose deportation has been recommended by a court in the State before which that person was indicted for, or charged with, any crime or offence; - under section 3(2)(i), a person whose deportation would, in the opinion of the Minister, be conducive to the common good; and - under section 51 of the International Protection Act 2015, persons who have been refused international protection. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transpose the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, the European Economic Area and Switzerland. Such orders can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health. Legally, such orders must not be disproportionate, and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the State, integration (e.g. work history), age and health must be carried out. These orders, and their legal basis, are distinct from deportation orders, which are legal orders to leave the State and apply only in respect of non-EEA nationals. Under the provisions of section 24 of the Prisons Act 2015 (as amended), the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration may direct that a person serving a sentence of imprisonment who is subject to a deportation order, removal order or return decision may be taken from prison up to two years before the conclusion of the term of imprisonment where necessary or expedient to facilitate the person's deportation, removal or return. My Department endeavours to finalise decisions relating to deportation orders and removal orders while people are in prison. Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999 permits a person detained in relation to a deportation order to be held for not more than 56 days before their removal from the State. Regulation 22 of the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 (S.I. No. 548 of 2015) permits a person detained in relation to a removal order to be held for not more than 28 days before their removal from the State. When a Deportation Order or a Removal Order is imposed on individuals involved in criminality, whether while serving a custodial sentence or while in the community, their removal from the State becomes an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau. The table below sets out the number of people removed to 6th September 2026. Deportation Orders Removal Orders The number of people removed on grounds of criminality** 70 107 Those removed from the State prior to the end of their custodial sentence. 28 73 The number of individuals released from custody prior to their removal. *** 16 25 The average time a person was returned to the community on completion of their prison sentence where a valid Deportation or Removal Order was imposed prior to their release. 57 days 56 days * Please be advised that the above figures are subject to change as information becomes available and data is cleansed. ** Please note that not all people removed from the state on grounds of criminality received custodial sanctions. *** Please note that the above table reflects individuals who had orders imposed while serving a custodial sentence and were then subsequently released from custody. People may be removed from the State on commercial flights or as part of charters. The breakdown of people who were removed on completion of their sentence on commercial flights is not recorded in this format. To date in 2026, three charter flights removing people with criminal convictions to their home countries have been successfully completed. The table below shows the costs incurred in relation to these charter flight operations. These figures also include the costs of returning accompanying escorts to Ireland where a one-way charter flight is used. They do not include the costs of removals enforced through commercial flights or other charter operations where the majority of persons removed did not have criminal convictions. Costs for relevant charter flight operations in 2026 Date of charter flight operation Destination Total cost (incl. VAT) of flights 25/01/2026 Poland & Lithuania €191,286.76 24/05/2026 Poland & Lithuania €256,330.22 28/07/2026 Nigeria ** €123,085.67 Total €570,702.65 * The above are all provisional costs as the invoicing process has not yet been completed. ** This is the provisional cost for the charter operation from Ireland to Italy. The returnees were then transferred onto the Frontex Joint Return Operation charter to Nigeria.

question: 2526. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the mechanisms in place at the State's borders to detect and prevent the re-entry of persons subject to an exclusion order or re-entry ban; and the number of attempted or actual re-entries by such persons that have been detected to date. [63166/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2262, 2504 and 2526 together. The Border Management Unit (BMU) is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. Immigration officers are responsible for carrying out border management functions in order to protect the integrity of the State's immigration system and ensure compliance with immigration law. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, neither I nor my Department can comment on specific operational procedures of the BMU or the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB). However, I can assure the Deputy that all persons arriving at ports of entry are examined, and their travel documentation verified, using a range of border management and security systems. This includes checks against relevant national and international databases to assist in confirming identity, detecting fraudulent documentation, and identifying people who may be the subject of immigration, law enforcement, or security alerts. In relation to the sharing of biometric data with the UK, I can advise the Deputy that, at the UK-Ireland Summit in March, it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data-sharing arrangements, particularly to prevent abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits.

question: 2528. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of cars allocated to each Garda district, by district and station, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63203/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2528 and 2608 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes being responsible for the allocation and deployment of resources available to him including the Garda fleet. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. This Government is committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs to fight crime and a strengthened, well-resourced Garda organisation is central to this policy. Information in relation to the Garda fleet is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/finance-services/finance-fleet-management.html The Deputy should select Finance Fleet Management and access the file titled “Fleet Management Report to the most recent date” for a breakdown of vehicles currently in use. It is important to emphasise that An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis. Gardaí see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by all Divisional resources and units.

question: 2529. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a full and current update on the proposed new Dublin Family Courts complex at Hammond Lane, Smithfield; the present status of the project; the current stage of procurement; the anticipated contract award date; the confirmed or anticipated date for construction to commence; the estimated completion and opening date; the current estimated total cost; and will he make a statement on the matter. [63298/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2529, 2570 and 2597 together. The construction of a purpose-built family law courts complex at Hammond Lane is a key priority for the Courts Service and a key Justice sector project in the National Development Plan. The new Dublin Family Courts Complex will be a modern purpose-built 19 courtroom facility where family law cases can be held in a dignified, secure and non-threatening environment with a range of support services to hand. It has been designed and will be built with the specific needs of Family Law court users in mind and will benefit families who interact with the courts at some of the most challenging junctures in their lives. The provision of a safe and secure environment for all court users is a key objective for the facility. A variety of measures will be implemented to achieve this including separate circulation routes for staff, judges, members of the public and persons in custody, clear and simple layouts providing clear sightlines, a variety of waiting spaces located throughout the building, private interview rooms where Courts Service staff can meet with members of the public in private, security screening areas, a custody suite, CCTV and access control. The provision of an on site security service is also proposed. Specifically in relation to domestic violence, the design of the facility provides for dedicated domestic violence accommodation, where providers of domestic violence support services will be able to meet clients/victims of domestic violence in a safe and secure private environment. It is proposed that the dedicated domestic violence accommodation will include office space, meeting rooms, bathroom facilities, video conferencing facilities, waiting areas and tea/coffee making facilities. Good progress is being made in delivering this much needed facility. Key achievements to date include: • Approval in principle to proceed with the project was granted by my Department in July 2023, following submission of a preliminary business case by the Courts Service as sponsoring agency. • Detailed plans/layouts for the building were developed by the OPW and approved by the Courts Service. The plans provide for a 6 storey over basement building providing approximately 18,250 sq m of purpose built accommodation. • Planning permission was granted by the Commissioners of Public Works in April 2024. • Technical and legal advisors were appointed by the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) on behalf of the Courts Service in 2024. • The procurement process was initiated in July 2024. The project is being procured by the NDFA on behalf of the Courts Service in conjunction with the OPW, using the Competitive Dialogue procurement procedure pursuant to EU and national procurement law. • In November 2024 candidates were pre-qualified to participate in the tender competition for the project. • Following preparation of the tender documents the project was formally handed over to the NDFA for procurement in accordance with the project governance arrangements in August 2025. On 28 August 2025, the NDFA issued the tender documentation to the shortlisted candidates. • The competitive dialogue phase of the procurement process completed in Q1 2026. The closing date for receipt of tenders was 25th March. Subject to the successful completion of the procurement process, it is envisaged that construction will commence in 2027 with the building becoming operational during 2029. The Contract Notice for the project published in July 2024 shows an estimated capex cost of circa €150 million ex VAT. The actual costs will be informed by the procurement process.

question: 2530. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the formal consultation Cuan has undertaken directly with victims and survivors of domestic violence; the number of victims and survivors participated; the specific policy or service changes resulted from that consultation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63297/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2530, 2575 and 2589 together. I recognise the importance of ensuring that the voices and experiences of victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) inform the development of DSGBV policy, services and public awareness initiatives. The Zero Tolerance Strategy and, indeed, the Programme for Government clearly set out our commitments to listening to victims and survivors and ensuring that their voice informs service improvements, as well as policy and practice. This commitment is reflected in Action 4.7.1 of the assets.gov.ie/static/documents/Zero_Tolerance_Implementation_Plan_2025-2026.pdf which seeks to strengthen consultative structures to engage victims and survivors, children, civil society and sectoral organisations throughout implementation of the Strategy, particularly the development of services, research and public awareness campaigns. The purpose of this work is to ensure that actions to prevent and respond to DSGBV are informed by lived experience and victims and survivor voices. Last year, Cuan partnered with the National Women's Council and the Observatory on Violence Against Women to fund independent research on the development of survivor structures of engagement. This research included consultations undertaken by an independent expert with three distinct cohorts: victim-survivors themselves, the DSGBV sector and civil society, and civil and public servants. The researcher also undertook consultation on good practice in survivor engagement in other jurisdictions and was supported by an Advisory Group to the project which included representatives of civil society and the DSGBV sector, as well as officials from my Department and Cuan. This project concluded with the publication of www.nwci.ie/learn/publication/structures_of_engagement_for_survivors_of_violence_against_women which was launched in April 2026. Cuan and my Department have considered the report's recommendations and are at the early stages of progressing the development of dedicated survivor engagement structures. In parallel, officials from Cuan and my Department engage regularly with victims and survivors and their representative groups, including in the development of public awareness campaigns, research and service development, as well as through bilateral engagement at the request of survivors themselves. I regularly meet with victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and I commend their bravery in sharing their often traumatic experiences in order to strengthen protections for others in similar situations. My Department and Cuan are particularly conscious of the need for survivor engagement to be intersectional and inclusive of those from seldom-heard groups and continues to work with survivor representative groups, civil society organisations and other stakeholders to ensure this objective is achieved. My Department convenes regular meetings with sectoral stakeholders through a number of different fora including the DSGBV Forum, the Victims of Crime Forum, the Family Justice Development Forum and the Human Trafficking Stakeholders Forum. These meetings provide an invaluable opportunity to engage directly with frontline organisations working with victims and survivors with the aim of keeping updated on developments and trends, improving outcomes and supporting those engaging with the justice system. While no single consolidated figure is maintained for the number of victims and survivors who have participated across the wide range of consultation and engagement mechanisms supported by my Department or Cuan, engagement has taken place through multiple channels, and this will continue. My Department, supported by Cuan, has commenced initial preparations for development of the Fourth National Strategy on DSGBV. Early consultation activity has already taken place, including engagement with stakeholders and services through the National Women's Council which include victim-survivors and their representative groups, and further consultations will continue as work progresses, including engagement with children and young people. Through supporting these measures, I remain fully committed to ensuring that the lived experience of victims and survivors continues to shape the development of policy, services, research and public awareness initiatives, and that victims’ and survivors’ voices continue to be central to Ireland's response to domestic, sexual and gender-based violence.

question: 2531. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of additional domestic violence refuge and emergency accommodation spaces that have become fully operational since Cuan was established; the number of spaces available when Cuan commenced; the number available currently; the number currently under development; the expected opening date of each planned facility, by county; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63296/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge units and safe homes provide a vital place of safety for families in crisis. The Government is determined to continue to establish units across the country to ensure that those supports are available when they are most needed. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown expected to be operational in Q4 2026. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Furthermore, Cuan continues to explore additional opportunities for developing domestic violence accommodation, especially in areas where such facilities are currently lacking, while also considering interim refuges and alternative accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). By working with partners across the sector, Cuan is building capacity, accelerating delivery of accommodation and ensuring that frontline professionals and support staff are trained to respond effectively. The are nine counties currently without a domestic violence refuge, they are; Carlow, Cavan, Laois, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Offaly, Roscommon and Sligo. However, five of these counties have Safe Homes, which is another form of safe domestic violence accommodation. Work is underway to develop safe accommodation capacity in the remaining four counties; beginning with Leitrim and Laois, with Laois identified as a priority area for refuge development. Cuan is also working to support the provision of domestic violence accommodation in Cavan and Monaghan. Cuan is working with Safe Ireland to deliver six Safe Homes (3 in Monaghan and 3 in Cavan), and an interim refuge in Monaghan. It is anticipated that these will be operational by Q4 2026. Cuan has further advised that the attached table outlines safe accommodation units by county as of Q3 2026. Accommodation by County

question: 2532. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the specific additional services for victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, since the establishment of Cuan that have become fully operational, as distinct from services that have been announced, planned or funded but have not yet commenced; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63295/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.

question: 2533. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of cases since 7 April 2025 in which the possible revocation of a naturalised Irish citizen's citizenship has been considered; the number in which the person had a criminal conviction; the number involving national security concerns; the number in which a notice of intention to revoke was issued; the number in which citizenship was revoked the number in which a revocation decision was subsequently overturned by a committee of inquiry; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63286/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2533, 2534, 2535, 2536 and 2543 together. My Department actively reviews files relating to terrorism, fraud, and organised crime with a view to assessing whether citizenship revocation proceedings are appropriate. The loss of citizenship has serious consequences, and each case is considered very carefully. In the last 10 years, eight people have had their citizenship revoked, including two revocations since 7 April 2025. Given the number of revocations, it would not be appropriate for me to comment on the specific grounds on which citizenship was revoked in these cases as there is a possibility that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. Of the eight revocations, seven were made under section 19(1)(a) on the grounds that the issue of the certificate was procured by fraud, misrepresentation, whether innocent or fraudulent, or the concealment of material facts or circumstances. One revocation was made under section 19(1)(b) on the grounds that the person to whom it was granted had, by an overt act, shown themselves to have failed in their duty of fidelity to the nation and loyalty to the State.

question: 2537. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of Gardaí attached to Blanchardstown Garda Station; the current number of Gardaí in the K district as a whole; the number of Community Gardaí assigned to Blanchardstown Garda Station; and to indicate comparable figures for each year between 2021 and 2025 inclusive. [63302/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Information on the number of Community Gardaí are also published nationally, by Garda division. Data on the allocation of Gardaí for 2026 and previous years can be accessed at the link below. Historical data can be accessed via the December 2025 file. www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ It is important to emphasise that An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis. Gardaí see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area is be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by all Divisional resources and units.

question: 2538. Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the percentage of Gardaí in each Kildare Garda station who have successfully completed the pursuit driving courses in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63310/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2378 and 2538 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. The Act states that the Commissioner is responsible for the training and professional development of Garda personnel and the Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. I have been advised by the Garda authorities that while the current suite of competency based driving courses provided does not include specific training on tactical pursuits an updated ‘Spontaneous Pursuits Policy’ was issued in late 2024. This policy provides direction to Garda personnel who engage in the use of pursuit tactics to reduce the risk associated with pursuits. The Commissioner has recently confirmed that he will introduce Garda pursuit training before the end of this year. This is the first time Gardaí will receive this specialist training. Currently, response training is provided to specific members of An Garda Síochána, with specialist units receiving advanced driving training. I welcome the the introduction of this training a and remain committed to ensuring that our Gardaí have the resources, equipment, and legislation they need to fulfil their vital policing role.

question: 2539. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on an application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63327/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy is at the registration stage. I expect that going forward, the majority of applicants will receive a decision within one year, however, it is important to note that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. My Department has taken a significant number of steps to speed the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2540. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to request his Department to examine a case (details supplied). [63336/26]
