question: 2591. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the measurable performance indicators that are being used to determine whether the establishment of Cuan has resulted in victims receiving faster access to protection, accommodation, advocacy and other specialist supports; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63539/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2544, 2548, 2554, 2571, 2572, 2574, 2576, 2584, 2586, 2588, 2591 and 2616 together. Cuan is responsible for the coordination, monitoring, and reporting of Zero Tolerance – the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The Agency reports on progress to my Department and also to a High-Level Oversight Board, chaired by the Secretaries-General of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Department of an Taoiseach, a Senior Officials Group, and the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs. The provision of regular, timely, and accurate reporting on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy supports robust and accountable cross-Governmental coordination, maintains implementation momentum, and facilitates the timely identification and resolution of delivery challenges by Cabinet and Heads of Department. My Department puts in place annual performance delivery agreements with Cuan, which are published on Gov.ie. The agreements define targets by which the performance of Cuan is measured and the mechanisms for monitoring and appraising performance. Cuan’s annual reports provide comprehensive details on delivery and achievements of the agency and can be accessed at Gov.ie/Cuan. In July, I announced publication of the 2025 Cuan Annual Report, detailing the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan which marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made, and I would like to direct the Deputies to this publication for a more in-depth look at the statistics and information they requested. It can be read here: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf In June 2025, I launched the third and final implementation plan covering the remaining period of the Zero Tolerance Strategy - 2025 and 2026. The plan sets out 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution, and Policy Coordination, with 22 implementation partners responsible for leading on implementation across Government. Implementation partners report biannually to Cuan on actions and performance indicators through a bespoke online monitoring platform. These updates are analysed and collated to prepare regular progress reports on implementation for publication. The most recent progress reports on implementation are again available for review on Gov.ie. I announced publication of the Annual Progress Report for 2025 at the DSGBV Forum in March 2026 which was attended by stakeholders and services working to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This is another important mechanism which holds the Government to account on progress in meeting our objectives. While delivery of the Strategy’s objectives requires sustained effort over time, and significant work remains to ensure all victims and survivors are protected, supported, and able to access justice, this Progress Report demonstrates the measurable progress achieved in 2025 against key performance indicators. As we move into the final phase of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, our focus will be on consolidating progress, strengthening implementation efforts, and supporting the transition to the next phase, including the development of a Fourth National Strategy.

question: 2592. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the number of victims and survivors that have accessed Cuan-funded domestic violence services in each year since its establishment, how this compares with the equivalent figures before Cuan was established; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63538/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.

question: 2593. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Cuan's total budget in each year since its establishment; the amount that was actually expended in each year; and the amount of that expenditure that went directly to frontline services for victims and survivors; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63536/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2547, 2578, 2583 and 2593 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to confront the scourge of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Cuan, established in 2024, is the statutory agency responsible for the coordination and implementation of the Government’s response to DSGBV. The total budget for Cuan was €59.05 million in 2024, €66.9 million in 2025, and €79.2 million in 2026. Cuan’s overall budget each year includes spend on salaries for Cuan staff and business overheads, as well as funding for DSGBV services, and prevention measures including education and awareness raising campaigns. Cuan funds 78 DSGBV organisations nationally, including 20 domestic violence refuges. Cuan has provided the following levels of funding to organisations for the provision of DSGBV services, including refuges and support services: • €52.3 million in 2024; • €58.4 million in 2025; • the provisional allocation for 2026 is €69m. Prior to 2024, funding for DSGBV services was administered across a number of Government Departments and agencies, and consolidated funding figures for the sector are therefore not available. The establishment of Cuan has provided a more coordinated and strategic approach to funding and service development, ensuring that resources are directed towards identified needs and aligned with the objectives of the Zero Tolerance Strategy.

question: 2594. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the number of counties currently have no dedicated domestic violence refuge accommodation, the timeframe for providing appropriate services in each of those counties; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63535/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge units and safe homes provide a vital place of safety for families in crisis. The Government is determined to continue to establish units across the country to ensure that those supports are available when they are most needed. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown expected to be operational in Q4 2026. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Furthermore, Cuan continues to explore additional opportunities for developing domestic violence accommodation, especially in areas where such facilities are currently lacking, while also considering interim refuges and alternative accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). By working with partners across the sector, Cuan is building capacity, accelerating delivery of accommodation and ensuring that frontline professionals and support staff are trained to respond effectively. The are nine counties currently without a domestic violence refuge, they are; Carlow, Cavan, Laois, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Offaly, Roscommon and Sligo. However, five of these counties have Safe Homes, which is another form of safe domestic violence accommodation. Work is underway to develop safe accommodation capacity in the remaining four counties; beginning with Leitrim and Laois, with Laois identified as a priority area for refuge development. Cuan is also working to support the provision of domestic violence accommodation in Cavan and Monaghan. Cuan is working with Safe Ireland to deliver six Safe Homes (3 in Monaghan and 3 in Cavan), and an interim refuge in Monaghan. It is anticipated that these will be operational by Q4 2026. Cuan has further advised that the attached table outlines safe accommodation units by county as of Q3 2026. Accommodation by County

question: 2597. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the proposed Dublin Family Courts complex at Hammond Lane, Smithfield, including the present status of the project; the current stage of procurement; the anticipated contract award date; the confirmed or anticipated date for construction to commence; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63546/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2529, 2570 and 2597 together. The construction of a purpose-built family law courts complex at Hammond Lane is a key priority for the Courts Service and a key Justice sector project in the National Development Plan. The new Dublin Family Courts Complex will be a modern purpose-built 19 courtroom facility where family law cases can be held in a dignified, secure and non-threatening environment with a range of support services to hand. It has been designed and will be built with the specific needs of Family Law court users in mind and will benefit families who interact with the courts at some of the most challenging junctures in their lives. The provision of a safe and secure environment for all court users is a key objective for the facility. A variety of measures will be implemented to achieve this including separate circulation routes for staff, judges, members of the public and persons in custody, clear and simple layouts providing clear sightlines, a variety of waiting spaces located throughout the building, private interview rooms where Courts Service staff can meet with members of the public in private, security screening areas, a custody suite, CCTV and access control. The provision of an on site security service is also proposed. Specifically in relation to domestic violence, the design of the facility provides for dedicated domestic violence accommodation, where providers of domestic violence support services will be able to meet clients/victims of domestic violence in a safe and secure private environment. It is proposed that the dedicated domestic violence accommodation will include office space, meeting rooms, bathroom facilities, video conferencing facilities, waiting areas and tea/coffee making facilities. Good progress is being made in delivering this much needed facility. Key achievements to date include: • Approval in principle to proceed with the project was granted by my Department in July 2023, following submission of a preliminary business case by the Courts Service as sponsoring agency. • Detailed plans/layouts for the building were developed by the OPW and approved by the Courts Service. The plans provide for a 6 storey over basement building providing approximately 18,250 sq m of purpose built accommodation. • Planning permission was granted by the Commissioners of Public Works in April 2024. • Technical and legal advisors were appointed by the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) on behalf of the Courts Service in 2024. • The procurement process was initiated in July 2024. The project is being procured by the NDFA on behalf of the Courts Service in conjunction with the OPW, using the Competitive Dialogue procurement procedure pursuant to EU and national procurement law. • In November 2024 candidates were pre-qualified to participate in the tender competition for the project. • Following preparation of the tender documents the project was formally handed over to the NDFA for procurement in accordance with the project governance arrangements in August 2025. On 28 August 2025, the NDFA issued the tender documentation to the shortlisted candidates. • The competitive dialogue phase of the procurement process completed in Q1 2026. The closing date for receipt of tenders was 25th March. Subject to the successful completion of the procurement process, it is envisaged that construction will commence in 2027 with the building becoming operational during 2029. The Contract Notice for the project published in July 2024 shows an estimated capex cost of circa €150 million ex VAT. The actual costs will be informed by the procurement process.

question: 2600. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the case of a family (details supplied); the individual assessment that was undertaken; whether one child’s disability, specialist education and accessibility requirements were considered in allocating this location; whether another child’s ongoing medical treatment was considered; whether this family falls within the his stated commitment regarding those living under temporary protection with established HSE care plans to remain in the relevant community health organisation area for continuity of care; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63641/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Colm Brophy) The ending of the provision of commercial accommodation at the Citywest Hotel follows a Government decision of 26 May 2026. As previously communicated to all residents, no further accommodation for those granted Temporary Protection will be provided at the Citywest Hotel from 18th September 2026. Recognising that this is a significant change for residents, the Department, the Irish Red Cross and the International Organization for Migration commenced dedicated engagement with those affected, providing information and practical support regarding available options. At the same time, a self-declaration application process was made available to residents who believed they continued to require temporary accommodation following the closure of the Citywest facility. An offer of accommodation has now issued to all residents whose applications were approved, taking into account, where relevant, any identified vulnerabilities or accommodation requirements. Before the Department allocates accommodation to beneficiaries, available information regarding the composition of a family is considered, including any identified vulnerabilities or medical requirements, where known. The Department works with relevant agencies, including the HSE, to ensure that these factors are taken into consideration, insofar as practicable, when allocating accommodation. While every effort is made to continue to accommodate those with established HSE care plans to remain in the relevant Community Health Organisation area for continuity of care, there is no guarantee continued accommodation will be in the same area in which a person currently lives. The Department seeks to match accommodation to identified needs and remains committed to ensuring that vulnerable persons continue to receive appropriate supports throughout this transition. With specific reference to the question of specialist education needs, it should be noted that it is the Department’s practice to try to retain children with special educational needs in the same area where possible. In cases however where documented medical needs present along with special educational needs, medical requirements are considered to be the priority in the accommodation allocation process. In this context, medical requirements may necessitate relocation to a specific accommodation centre, even if it is not in immediate proximity to the current location. Relevant HSE Social Inclusion teams are kept informed of the allocations to ensure transfer of care packages and equipment within the timeframe. In the case referred to by the Deputy, the needs of all family members were carefully considered. When identifying suitable onward accommodation, priority was given to the father's submitted documented accommodation requirements, which had been assessed by his medical team as an absolute necessity. As a result, accommodation in Offaly was offered rather than in one of the centres closer to Citywest. I trust this provides clarification and reassurance that affected residents continue to receive appropriate supports as they transition from Citywest.

question: 2603. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a person (details supplied) is due to be deported following their release from prison on 17 September 2026. [63665/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As Minister, I do not comment on individual cases. I can advise the Deputy that the removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland who represent a danger to public policy or public security. These orders can be made on the grounds of that the individual’s personal conduct represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society. These orders, and their legal basis, are distinct from deportation orders which are legal orders to leave the State and remain outside of it, apply in respect of non-EEA nationals only.

question: 2613. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on his meeting on 19 July 2026 to discuss the new Garda station at Northern Cross; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61402/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration There is no record in my diary of a meeting to discuss a new Garda station at Northern Cross on Sunday, 19 July 2026. The Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities, and strengthening An Garda Síochána is at the core of that. This is reflected in the unprecedented allocation of over €2.74 billion to An Garda Síochána in Budget 2026. This funding allows for the continued recruitment of Garda personnel and provides the equipment, technology, facilities and fleet that Gardaí require to support their vital role of keeping communities safe. It is also extremely important that Gardaí across the country are stationed in modern workplaces that are up to standard. This is why following the review of the National Development Plan, I secured a landmark €2.18 billion for a Justice Investment Plan up to 2030. Of this, €911 million has been dedicated to the completion of Garda estate projects. This funding will support the completion of new Garda stations in Portlaoise, Newcastle West and Bailieborough in 2026 and early 2027, as well as work on new stations in Macroom, Clonmel, Castletroy, and Carndonagh. It will also provide €35 million for a rolling programme of minor refurbishment works in Garda stations across the country. As part of the overall investment, I also specifically secured funding for the development of a new divisional HQ and campus facilities for the Dublin Metropolitan Region North. The funding is in place for these works to commence in the second half of the 2026 – 2030 Garda Capital Plan, while efforts in the first half are focused on completing the several large-scale projects already in progress. The requirements for DMR North have been under review by An Garda Síochána, the OPW and my Department for some time now. This work will be progressed in line with the Infrastructure Guidelines, as required by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, which set out the value for money guidelines for capital appraisal. In line with this, work is commencing on the Strategic Assessment and Preliminary Business Case phase, which will set out the rationale, benefits, options and expected costs and timelines for the project. The Government is committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs to combat and prevent crime and keep us safe. The projects on the capital plan will provide modern work environments for Garda members and staff, supporting improved service delivery to local communities.

question: 2614. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the Community Safety Fund recipients for 2026 will be announced; and to outline the funding timetable. [63862/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration First opened in 2022, the Community Safety Fund (CSF) allows the proceeds of crime seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, to be redirected into local projects that support and enhance community safety. Details on the timetable for the 2026 CSF Funding Call are outlined below: Stages Date / Indicative period 1 Launch of Call 13 April 2026 2 Deadline for submitting applications 18 May 2026 3 Notification of results to applicants October 2026 4 Sign-off of grant agreements November 2026 5 Commencement of projects December 2026 This year’s fund, totalling €4.75 million, represents a significant increase on the initial allocation of €2 million in 2022. The Funding Call document describes the criteria used to assess applications, including the degree to which the planned outcomes meet the goals of the scheme and its strategic objectives; the overall strength of the project proposal having regard to the planned activities; and financial management, governance, and value for money. The guidance document can be found at the following link: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/564ce32b/2026_Community_Safety_Fund_Guidance_Document_.pdf A Selection Committee within my Department, including an independent panel member from outside the Department, will review all submitted CSF applications and assess each application in accordance with the published award criteria. Final recommendations on the award of grants will be made by the Selection Committee and submitted to me for approval. As this is a competitive grant process, applications will be assessed against the published criteria and established appraisal process.

question: 2615. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 2297 of 28 July 2026, if he will give consideration to a proposal (details supplied). [63801/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2616. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measurable performance indicators being used to determine whether the establishment of Cuan has resulted in victims receiving faster access to protection, accommodation, advocacy and other specialist supports. [63784/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2544, 2548, 2554, 2571, 2572, 2574, 2576, 2584, 2586, 2588, 2591 and 2616 together. Cuan is responsible for the coordination, monitoring, and reporting of Zero Tolerance – the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The Agency reports on progress to my Department and also to a High-Level Oversight Board, chaired by the Secretaries-General of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Department of an Taoiseach, a Senior Officials Group, and the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs. The provision of regular, timely, and accurate reporting on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy supports robust and accountable cross-Governmental coordination, maintains implementation momentum, and facilitates the timely identification and resolution of delivery challenges by Cabinet and Heads of Department. My Department puts in place annual performance delivery agreements with Cuan, which are published on Gov.ie. The agreements define targets by which the performance of Cuan is measured and the mechanisms for monitoring and appraising performance. Cuan’s annual reports provide comprehensive details on delivery and achievements of the agency and can be accessed at Gov.ie/Cuan. In July, I announced publication of the 2025 Cuan Annual Report, detailing the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan which marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made, and I would like to direct the Deputies to this publication for a more in-depth look at the statistics and information they requested. It can be read here: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf In June 2025, I launched the third and final implementation plan covering the remaining period of the Zero Tolerance Strategy - 2025 and 2026. The plan sets out 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution, and Policy Coordination, with 22 implementation partners responsible for leading on implementation across Government. Implementation partners report biannually to Cuan on actions and performance indicators through a bespoke online monitoring platform. These updates are analysed and collated to prepare regular progress reports on implementation for publication. The most recent progress reports on implementation are again available for review on Gov.ie. I announced publication of the Annual Progress Report for 2025 at the DSGBV Forum in March 2026 which was attended by stakeholders and services working to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This is another important mechanism which holds the Government to account on progress in meeting our objectives. While delivery of the Strategy’s objectives requires sustained effort over time, and significant work remains to ensure all victims and survivors are protected, supported, and able to access justice, this Progress Report demonstrates the measurable progress achieved in 2025 against key performance indicators. As we move into the final phase of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, our focus will be on consolidating progress, strengthening implementation efforts, and supporting the transition to the next phase, including the development of a Fourth National Strategy.

question: 2617. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of counties that currently have no dedicated domestic violence refuge accommodation; and the timeframe for providing appropriate services in each of those counties. [63781/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge units and safe homes provide a vital place of safety for families in crisis. The Government is determined to continue to establish units across the country to ensure that those supports are available when they are most needed. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown expected to be operational in Q4 2026. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Furthermore, Cuan continues to explore additional opportunities for developing domestic violence accommodation, especially in areas where such facilities are currently lacking, while also considering interim refuges and alternative accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). By working with partners across the sector, Cuan is building capacity, accelerating delivery of accommodation and ensuring that frontline professionals and support staff are trained to respond effectively. The are nine counties currently without a domestic violence refuge, they are; Carlow, Cavan, Laois, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Offaly, Roscommon and Sligo. However, five of these counties have Safe Homes, which is another form of safe domestic violence accommodation. Work is underway to develop safe accommodation capacity in the remaining four counties; beginning with Leitrim and Laois, with Laois identified as a priority area for refuge development. Cuan is also working to support the provision of domestic violence accommodation in Cavan and Monaghan. Cuan is working with Safe Ireland to deliver six Safe Homes (3 in Monaghan and 3 in Cavan), and an interim refuge in Monaghan. It is anticipated that these will be operational by Q4 2026. Cuan has further advised that the attached table outlines safe accommodation units by county as of Q3 2026. Accommodation by County

question: 2619. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the specific additional services for victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence that have become fully operational, as distinct from services that have been announced, planned or funded but have not yet commenced, since the establishment of Cuan. [63777/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.

answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation applications referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2626. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to correspondence from this Deputy, if he has reviewed the continued operation of the IPAS contract at a location (details supplied) following the determination by An Coimisiún Pleanála that the change of use constitutes development and is not exempted development; if he is satisfied that continued State funding of the facility is appropriate in these circumstances; and if he will now consider terminating the contract. [63903/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The State has a legal obligation to provide reception conditions – accommodation and other basic supports – to people seeking international protection. The accommodation centre at Dundrum House, Tipperary, has been providing accommodation under contract to the Department since 2022, for people fleeing the war in Ukraine and people applying for international protection. The Department notes the recent decision by An Coimisiún Pleanála in relation to Dundrum House and will consider its implications for the accommodation centre and its residents. Since 2025, the Department requires valid confirmation of compliance with planning regulations for all IPAS properties that are newly contracted or renewed. While matters related to planning are between the Local Authority and the accommodation service provider, the Department will comply with any regulatory issues that are notified to us, either by the Local Authority or the accommodation service provider.

question: 2627. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total cost to the State to date of the interim arrangement for the provision of coronial post-mortems at University Hospital Waterford by locum pathologists sourced from the UK; the breakdown of costs relating to professional fees, flights, accommodation, transport and agency or contractual charges; and the projected annual cost if the arrangement continues. [63901/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The post-mortem examination service, which supports the work of the Coroner Service, is supported by several departments and agencies. My Department is responsible for the legislation underpinning the work of coroners, while the provision of the post-mortem examination service is largely provided through the health service and its personnel. Where a post-mortem examination is deemed to be required, the coroner will arrange for it to be conducted as expeditiously as possible in order to ensure the timely release of remains to the deceased’s next of kin. Securing the provision of the post-mortem examination service for the coronial death investigation function is challenging and I have been engaging with the Minister for Health to address this. There are issues arising within the pathology profession, including relating to training and recruitment, as well as competing demands on pathologists in areas of diagnostic and research work. I acknowledge those concerns. The situation in University Hospital Waterford (UHW) reached a critical juncture in January this year when pathologists employed at that location indicated that they were no longer available to carry out post-mortem examinations. Coroner directed post-mortem examinations for counties Waterford, Wexford, Kilkenny, Carlow, and Tipperary are carried out in UHW. My Department has introduced a short-term solution where locum pathologists are providing a coronial post-mortem examination service on a three-day per week rota since 1 January in UHW. This approach is necessary to minimise any impact on bereaved family members who would otherwise experience lengthy wait times for the release of remains which are the subject of coroners’ inquiries. However, the use of locum pathologists to conduct coroner directed post-mortem examinations is not a long-term solution to these issues and my Department is aware that a more sustainable solution is required in this regard. My Department engaged with a number of potential providers to secure an appropriate solution for University Hospital Waterford and, following an evaluation of several options, entered into a contract for service provision. The annual cost to the Exchequer is largely dependent on the number of post-mortem examinations conducted and, as a consequence, details of contractual arrangements are commercially sensitive. Therefore, my Department does not publish details of contractual arrangements on the basis that it could place the State at a disadvantage in other commercial negotiations.

question: 2628. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether Attenti technology, hardware, software or technical services form any part of the Irish Electronic Monitoring Managed Service contract; the location in which data generated by the service will be processed and stored; and the supply-chain, data-protection and ethical due diligence undertaken before the contract was awarded. [63676/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Allied Universal Electronic Monitoring (AUEM), to whom the contract for an Electronic Monitoring pilot was awarded, are a company registered in the United Kingdom. AUEM were selected through an open procurement competition carried out in accordance with Irish and EU public procurement rules. The company was assessed against the published selection, mandatory and award criteria and was found to be compliant with all mandatory requirements and all tenderers were assessed on the same basis. My Department is required to conduct procurements in accordance with the principles of equal treatment, transparency, proportionality and non-discrimination and all tenderers were assessed on the same basis. The contract award decision was made following completion of the evaluation process, including compliance checks and operational product testing of the proposed solution. All data will be stored, hosted, and processed only in data centres located within the EEA.

question: 2629. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether exemptions will apply to residents of the North of Ireland under the new travel arrangements due to come into effect on 28 September 2026; the categories of persons who will be exempt; and if he will make a statement on the matter [63577/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2629, 2630, 2639, 2640, 2643 and 2646 together. Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). The CTA facilitates Irish and British citizens to move and reside freely across Ireland and the UK while maintaining access for citizens to a range of reciprocal rights and privileges central to everyday life. The CTA arrangements apply only to Irish and British citizens. All other nationalities remain subject to the immigration requirements in each jurisdiction. While there is excellent cooperation on CTA matters, the immigration rules that apply in the UK and Ireland are a matter for each jurisdiction. Each carrier must comply with the requirements of the jurisdictions in which they operate. It is a standard border management function to impose carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. There is no requirement for Irish or UK citizens to produce passports when travelling within the CTA. However, airline and ferry carriers may require their passengers to have a passport in their possession before allowing them to board the craft. This is not an immigration requirement.

question: 2631. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the mechanism available for a minor Irish citizen and their mother (details supplied) to assert their rights of residency under article 20 TFEU in Ireland. [63987/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the applicant concerned applied for permission to remain in the State pursuant to the Chen/Teixeira/Ibrahim judgments. These judgements apply in circumstances where an EU citizen child has moved to reside in a Member State other than that of their nationality and is accompanied by their primary carer. These judgments set out rights that are not expressly provided for in the Free Movement of Persons Directive. The application referred to by the Deputy was based on a child who is an Irish citizen. Accordingly, the above judgments were not applicable in the circumstances of the case and the application was refused both at first instance and following review. The decision letter issued to the applicant on 20 July 2026 sets out the reasons for refusal in this regard. As the parent of an Irish citizen child, it is open to the applicant to apply for permission to reside in the State on that basis. More information is available on the Immigration Service Delivery web site at: www.irishimmigration.ie/my-situation-has-changed-since-i-arrived-in-ireland/the-parent-of-an-irish-citizen-child/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2634. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals there are to roll out new CCTV schemes in Cavan and Monaghan in view of the value of these schemes in strengthening local crime prevention and community safety. [63966/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Community safety is a top priority for my Department and everyone has the right to be safe and to feel safe in their communities. CCTV in public places has a role in giving people a greater sense of security. It can also be effective in deterring criminal activity and antisocial behaviour and assists with the investigation of crime. The consideration and operation of CCTV by local authorities is a matter for the local authority concerned. As Minister, I have no role in relation to local authorities and updates on the rollout of individual community CCTV schemes should be sought from the relevant local authority. Local authorities work closely with An Garda Síochána in relation to CCTV schemes. The Garda National Community Engagement Bureau offer support and assistance in relation to all applications and processes. Each application is evaluated on the principles of necessity, proportionality and legality to ensure the CCTV application meets necessary human rights and privacy standards. All applications must be presented to the CCTV Advisory Committee and the need for each camera justified. The Deputy may wish to note that the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 provides for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes, allowing for a member of Garda personnel or a Local Authority to apply in writing to the Commissioner of An Garda Síochána for an authorisation of CCTV. Pending the commencement of part 5 of the Act and the introduction of new arrangements, no new applications are being accepted. Prior to commencement, an amendment to section 7 of the Act that provides for transitional arrangements for existing CCTV applications, was also required. That amendment was included in the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Act 2026 which was signed into law by the President on 16 July 2026. The Commencement and Ministerial Orders are currently with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel (OPC) for drafting and I expect that the new CCTV provisions set out in Part 5 will be commenced at the end of the month. It should also be noted that under the Act there is a requirement for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures to be followed. As part of developing this new Code of Practice, An Garda Síochána consulted with the bodies listed in Part 8 of the Act and conducted a public consultation for any views or observations on the draft Code of Practice. The completion of the draft Code of Practice is an operational matter for the Garda Commissioner and I am unable to provide any timelines associated with the completion of this work by An Garda Síochána.

question: 2635. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals to intensify cross-Border collaboration to deal with criminality with particular reference to the increasing prevalence of illegal drugs throughout the Island. [63965/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am pleased to inform the Deputy that there continues to be excellent ongoing cross-border engagement and co-operation with counterparts in Northern Ireland to tackle cross-border crime. I am in regular contact with my counterparts in the Ministry for Justice in Northern Ireland and I met with Minister Long in May for a meeting under the auspices of the Inter-Governmental Agreement on Co-operation on Criminal Justice Matters (IGA), in Armagh. At the meeting, Minister Long and I formally finalised the 2023-2025 IGA work plan and agreed a new plan to run from January 2026 to January 2028. The new work plan provides for continued cooperation across a range of criminal justice, public protection, forensic science, victim support and youth justice issues. This political level engagement is supported by close co-operation between my officials and officials in the Northern Ireland Department of Justice on a range of issues, between An Garda Síochána and the Police Service of Northern Ireland, and other agencies with their counterparts. Significant engagement also took place at Ministerial, senior official and operational level at the Cross Border Police Conference on Organised and Serious Crime in Co. Cavan in March of this year. This annual event, reinforces the aim of my Department to enhance understanding and cooperation between law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, particularly in relation to cross border organised criminality and related issues. The objectives of the Conference include sharing experiences, identifying effective approaches and recommending actions to the Joint Agency Task Force aimed at enhancing cross-border working relationships to enhance our collective ability to tackle organised crime. As the Deputy will appreciate, the specific matters discussed at the Conference are sensitive and operational in nature, however I can advise the Deputy that robust and fruitful discussions around tackling cross border criminality took place. The 19th Cross Border Joint Agency Task Force report also highlights the ongoing commitment of law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, which has been effective in disrupting their activities. The Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau leads in tackling all forms of drug trafficking and the supply of illicit drugs in Ireland. An Garda Síochána continues to implement an enhanced national anti-drugs strategy through Operation Tara. The focus of this operation is to disrupt, dismantle and prosecute drug trafficking networks, at all levels - international, national and local. The long-standing excellent cooperation between An Garda Síochána and their counterparts in Northern Ireland has been key to tackling cross border crime and ensuring security on the Island. I know that the Garda authorities will continue to work effectively with their counterparts in tackling crime and promoting safety for all communities on this Island.

question: 2636. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals to establish new youth diversion projects in Cavan and Monaghan. [63964/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of Youth Diversion Projects (YDP) throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service. Cavan 365 and Monaghan Neighbourhood Youth Project (MNYP) are the YDPs in Cavan and Monaghan respectively, both operating in partnership with Foróige as the Community Based Organisation. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone of the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. This Department has, in recent years, significantly increased funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. With these funds, YDPs employ dedicated Youth Justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country. More than 570 full-time equivalent youth justice workers have been recruited in recent years.

question: 2638. Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of visa applications received from Palestinian nationals who have secured places in Irish higher education institutions for the current and upcoming academic years; the number approved, refused and pending; whether any measures are in place to expedite applications from students offered places in Irish colleges and universities; and if he will consider flexibility in documentation requirements where applicants are unable to obtain records due to the conflict in Gaza and the Occupied Palestinian Territories. [63947/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. Short Stay (C) Study Received 6 Long Stay (D) Study Received 134 Short Stay (C) Study Granted 5 Long Stay (D) Study Granted 41 Short Stay (C) Study Refused <5 Long Stay (D) Study Refused 108 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. * A decision made in 2026 may relate to an application received in a previous year. * It is the policy of my Department not to release numbers where there are fewer than 5 in respect of any nationality, as there is a possibility that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. * The Department does not collate information on the sponsorship details of applicants.

question: 2641. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reasons for the current delays in individuals applying for GNIB cards. [64053/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2439, 2440, 2441, 2442, 2443, 2444 and 2641 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience exceptionally high demand for first-time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended waiting times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every available avenue to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers in processing both first-time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact, and waiting times are reducing. I expect them to reduce further over the coming months. I am happy to inform the Deputy that the time taken for a Stamp 4 renewal application to be reached for processing after submission has been significantly reduced in recent weeks, from over 17 weeks to fewer than 11 weeks. Work is continuing to further reduce this timeframe. The processing times for individual nationalities are not recorded by my Department. Immigration renewal applications are processed chronologically based on permission stamp type rather than nationality. The Registration Office provides a live processing date for each stamp category, which is updated every Monday and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing. Customers may submit their renewal application up to 12 weeks prior to the expiry of their permission to allow sufficient time for the application to be reached and processed before their current permission expires. The standard 12-week provision remains in place, as does the notice to employers regarding any concerns individuals may have about their eligibility to work while their application is being processed. Further information is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.
