question: 2644. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardai assigned to roads policing units in July 2026, by garda division; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64104/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Information on the number of Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing are also published nationally, by Garda division. Historical data on the allocation of Gardaí 2006 - 2025, along with the same sheet for 2026 can be found here: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ It should be noted that road traffic laws are enforced by both Roads Policing personnel and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies. In addition uniform Garda members are to be deployed on high visibility roads policing operations, of 30 minutes duration, in each tour of duty. Technology also continues to play a significant role in supporting roads policing enforcement.

question: 2645. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of scrambler bikes seized by Gardai under the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026 known as 'Grace's Law'; and the number returned on payment of a fine. [64105/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Our road safety strategy takes a whole of government approach and is a shared responsibility. Development and implementation of road traffic legislation and policy falls within the remit of my colleague, the Minister for Transport, and the vital role of enforcing road traffic laws is carried out by An Garda Síochána. To support An Garda Síochána, we now have an enhanced legislative framework following the signing into law of the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026, known as Grace's Law. Gardaí also have additional, and significant, legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of scramblers, quad bikes, e-scooters and other such vehicles under the Road Traffic Act 1961, the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023. I commend An Garda Síochána on the progress they have made regarding the seizure and detention of scrambler bikes and other such vehicles. I am informed by Garda authorities of substantial increases in the seizure and detention of these vehicles when comparing the first half of 2026 against the full year of both 2024 and 2025. The Garda Authorities has provided me with the below table which shows the total Scramblers, e-Scooters, e-Bikes and Quad Bikes which were seized in 2024, 2025 and the 1st half of 2026. 2024 2025 2026 (1st half) Scramblers 165 159 180 e-Scooters 310 931 1,412 e- Bikes 144 237 287 Quad Bikes 39 40 26 The data for 2026 includes incidents where multiple vehicles of varying types may be seized and are subject to change. Please be advised that data on the number of vehicles released by Gardaí after the payment of a fine is not currently available.

question: 2646. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the mechanisms in place to accommodate Irish citizens who do not have a passport in terms of travel to the UK by ferry following the decision to amend travel requirements (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64023/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2629, 2630, 2639, 2640, 2643 and 2646 together. Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). The CTA facilitates Irish and British citizens to move and reside freely across Ireland and the UK while maintaining access for citizens to a range of reciprocal rights and privileges central to everyday life. The CTA arrangements apply only to Irish and British citizens. All other nationalities remain subject to the immigration requirements in each jurisdiction. While there is excellent cooperation on CTA matters, the immigration rules that apply in the UK and Ireland are a matter for each jurisdiction. Each carrier must comply with the requirements of the jurisdictions in which they operate. It is a standard border management function to impose carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. There is no requirement for Irish or UK citizens to produce passports when travelling within the CTA. However, airline and ferry carriers may require their passengers to have a passport in their possession before allowing them to board the craft. This is not an immigration requirement.

question: 2647. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the decision on the future use of 654 rapid-build housing units (details supplied); following the conclusion of their current use, to confirm if the units will be transferred to local authority housing stock, made available for allocation to households on local authority social housing waiting lists, or for other forms of housing provision; whether his Department assessed the suitability of these units for long-term social housing use; when the Government will make a final decision on the future ownership, management and allocation of these units; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61752/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Future use of these units following the end of the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) has always been an integral element of the rapid build project in order to provide value to the State and local communities. While the units are highly durable with a 60-year lifespan, the sites were built with future use in mind with all necessary infrastructure to support long term residency and are finished to enhance the local area. Under the Rapid Build Programme, the Office of Public Works (OPW) developed an exemplar single-storey modular design and specification to ensure Building Regulation compliance. The design is also aligned with the Department of Housing’s equivalent space standards to allow the units to be potentially utilised for social housing at a future date. Further to the first iteration, OPW leveraged this learning to also provide a modular two-storey housing option as a proof of concept. Twelve such units were built into the design at Backweston, Lucan, Co. Dublin. While the planning exemption remains in place for the current use of these units by people fleeing the war in Ukraine granted Temporary Protection, under the current Temporary Directive set to expire in March 2028, these units cannot be utilised for any other purpose. To determine the long-term strategy for the sites post-TPD, a multi-stakeholder process commenced in March 2025, chaired by officials from my department and including representation from the OPW and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH). In tandem with the consideration of the feasibility of potential future uses, this work involves exploring planning regularisation at each site. Work is also underway to determine the appropriate planning application process for each of the sites. To date, there has been no final decision made on long term future use, as discussions are ongoing with the need to explore all potential options within the local areas. However, these options include Social Housing and lower cost affordable housing such as Cost Rental. While current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until March 2028, they will be free to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process opens. To meet the conditions of the scheme, they must surrender their unit and leave their state provided accommodation in line with those in commercial accommodation. To date, full occupancy has been maintained, and we will continue to do so with eligible families to avoid having vacant units as developments and plans for their long-term future use have been finalised.

question: 2648. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the rapid-build modular housing sites at Ballinure Way, Mahon, Cork city, and at Charleville, County Cork, are to be transferred to Cork City Council and Cork County Council respectively for social housing use; and the timeline for any such transfer. [60611/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2182, 2183, 2184 and 2648 together. The rapid build programme has delivered 654 homes at 11 sites nationwide which are providing temporary accommodation for just over 2,600 people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Together, the two sites in Co Cork, referred to by the Deputy, comprise a total of 130 units designed for families of four, with 64 units at Ballinure Way in Mahon and 66 units at Charleville. These rapid build sites have a combined maximum occupancy of 520 people and there are currently no vacant units. A licence agreement is signed by each adult occupant allowing them to remain in their allocated unit while the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) is in force. Residents must adhere to the conditions of the agreement and fulfil satisfactory annual unit inspections undertaken by the Approved Housing Body, Tuath Housing, who manage all rapid builds across the 11 sites. At present, the licence agreements are dated to 4th March 2027. Now that the TPD has been extended to 4th March 2028, these licenses can be extended on expiry of the current license period. Contributions are payable at a rate of 16% of income plus a flat fee of €40 per household per week towards utility costs. The same contribution is payable at all rapid build sites and there has been no change in the contribution percentage or utility amount since the sites were initially occupied. These contributions are offset against the management costs of the sites. The rapid build sites fall outside of the scope of the commercial accommodation wind down and, subject to meeting license conditions, current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until the end of the TPD. Rapid build residents will be able to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process becomes available. In order to meet the conditions of the scheme, however, they must first surrender their unit and leave state-provided accommodation. This same requirement also applies to those in commercial accommodation.
